Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
Recently, I have been struggling a lot with figuring how to live up to the expectations of always being that “perfectly good girl”. Growing up I was the girl who my relatives adored because I was respectful, kind and I always had good grades. They loved and pampered me because of all the good things I have achieved and I was the “role model” used in comparison amongst my cousins. This may seem like a positive trait, but beneath the surface, all I felt through the past 19 years of my life was pressure. The pressure to excel in all areas of my life, the pressure to put others before myself in order for them to be happy, the pressure to live up to the standards that others have for me, that I felt like I was so drained and I lost motivation to do anything in life. I felt trapped, anxious and uncertain of who I was. If I lost the “good girl” image, would I still be who I claim to be?

Hence, for this assignment, I wanted to use ChatGPT to understand where all these overwhelming emotions are stemming from and how I could potentially solve this issue I have. The goal in mind was not to find a fix, but to understand the root causes of the mentality I have now as well as finding healthier ways to cope with it.
I chose to use ChatGPT out of the rest as my conversational agent because of how it had the ability to replicate an almost human conversation with its emotional tone and guide reflective dialogue. I crafted my prompts so that it created a safe, therapeutic-like space rather than a problem-solving one. I asked the AI to help me break down my emotions and where they could possibly stem from instead of giving me concretely cold solutions.
My initial prompt was: "I am feeling really conflicted about why I keep having the feeling of needing to live up to the name of being the perfectly good girl and I wish to explore how to cope with it .”
From there, I experimented with prompt engineering to guide the direction, tone and depth of our conversation. For example, I told the AI to respond empathetically and to avoid giving me single solutions. I also asked it to help me identify the emotions behind certain thoughts as well as how I could shift away from my current mindset slowly . I wanted it to help me think, not tell me what to do. I also asked it to help me figure out what emotions were behind my thoughts. This made the conversation feel like talking to someone who was guiding me, not judging me.
The AI helped me break down my feelings step by step. For example, when I said, “I feel guilty when I rest,” it helped me see that this guilt came from a belief that “being good means being productive.” Or, when I said, “I feel like I have to be good to be liked,” the AI replied, “What you might be craving deep down isn’t more perfection — it’s permission to just be human.” That really hit me. It helped me realize how much of my thinking was shaped by the idea that I had to earn love and approval by being perfect.
Through reconstruction of social realities, I started to see how my “good girl” image was not just about me, it was built by what others expected. Society and family often praise girls who are kind, quiet, and hardworking. The AI helped me see that I don’t have to follow that version of “goodness” all the time.

Being good can also mean being kind to myself, honest about how I feel, and allowing myself to make mistakes.
I also learnt how prompt engineering was very important for having a meaningful conversation as the right questions paved the way for self-discovery. The better my questions were, the more meaningful the answers became. For example, when I changed my question from “How can I stop having this expectation for myself?” to “What might my expectations and feelings be protecting me from?”, the tone changed completely. It made me reflect with more compassion instead of guilt. I realized that how I ask questions, both to the AI and to myself, really affects how I understand my emotions.
During this reflection, I also thought about how a multi-agent model could be like different parts of me having a conversation. One side wanting to please everyone, and another side just wanting to be real. This helped me see that my inner conflict isn’t such a bad thing, it’s just two parts of me trying to be heard and seen.
Through this reflection, I understood that my need to be the “perfectly good girl” comes from fear; the fear of disappointing people or losing their love. I realized I connected being “good” with being “worthy.” The AI helped me see that even though this mindset once kept me safe and accepted, it also stopped me from being my true self. I learned that being truly good doesn’t mean being perfect, it means being honest and kind, even when I’m not at my best.
One message that really struck me was when AI said: “You feel this way because you’ve spent a long time earning love instead of simply receiving it — and now your heart is tired.” That felt so real. It made me see that I don’t need to keep proving myself to be loved. That people will love and accept me for who I am regardless.
Talking to an AI about something so personal like that felt so weird and strange, but it turned out to be surprisingly comforting. Prompting the AI tone I wanted made it easier for me to open up. It didn’t judge me or rush to fix things, it just listened and prompted me to reflect. Of course, I know it’s still a machine and can’t truly understand emotions like a human would. But as a tool for thinking and self-reflection, it was really helpful.
After this experience, I feel like a weight has been lifted off my shoulder. Of course I will still need time to shift to a new reality but I am comforted by the conversation I just had. It was truly an experiential memory.
In the end, I believe that asking correct questions is really important in solving the problems we have or just merely figuring out our thought processes. And now I know that AI is such a helpful tool in pointing us in the right direction and helping to relieve some of the queries that we have. I’m glad to have this assignment and that it has helped me to learn so much more about what AI can do for us.

Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
For this assignment, the situation I explored was a recent disagreement with my father, where our differing viewpoints led to me feeling frustrated and confused. I think an emotional encounter like this provided meaningful context for me to explore how cognitive behavioural techniques could support reflection, self-understanding, and constructive reframing of thoughts. Hence, this personal experience became the basis for designing a conversational agent which could guide me through a structured CBT exercise.

I learnt that developing this conversational agent requires integrating multiple areas of knowledge. In relation to reconstructing social realities, I had to consider how individual perception shaped emotional responses in social interactions. Prompt engineering, as seen from the video, was also critical to create precise instructions that would guide the LLM to respond empathetically and ask reflective questions step-by-step. My conversational agent used chain-of-thought reasoning to encourage systematic exploration of thoughts, emotions, evidence, and alternative perspectives, which mirrored the cognitive restructuring process in CBT. I didn’t really explore multi-agent LLMs, but I would imagine it to have potential dialogue flows where multiple agents could simulate different perspectives or ask targeted questions to deepen reflection.

The conversational agent was implemented using the free version of ChatGPT and the design process involved :
●structuring the conversation into sequential steps, to facilitate progressive self-reflection
●emphasising on empathy and non-judgemental responses, so that I could have a safe reflection space
●iteratively testing prompts to ensure it responds adequately to my inputs
●including reflective checkpoints like intermediate guiding questions to help me observe emotional changes and internalise balanced thoughts

Through this process, I gained insights into how structured questioning and reflective dialogue can help in analysis of cognitive distortions, especially because they are biased interpretations that arise automatically and can go unrecognised in the moment. I found identifying evidence-based alternatives to be beneficial in reshaping

my perception of the situation and reducing the intensity of emotions I felt (though only slightly). This assignment also made me realise the value of acknowledging conflicting internal beliefs, which in my case was the tension between filial duty and independent thinking. I think having my thoughts reframed in a more balanced manner would contribute to my personal growth in the long run. I was genuinely impressed by how conversational AI could facilitate structured self-reflection and emotional regulation, and was seemingly almost as capable as an actual psychiatric counsellor.

Designing and interacting with the CBT conversational agent was not as challenging as I thought because I had the video tutorial for reference, but I felt making my own tweaks to create my own conversational agent was rewarding. To me, this assignment also highlighted the potential of LLMs as tools that support structured reflection and self-awareness. In terms of personal growth, the assignment reinforced the importance of self-compassion and the benefits of cognitive reframing in situations where I may feel negative emotions.

Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
For as long as I can remember, I have been caught in a frustrating and stressful cycle. I am inclined to procrastinate on tasks, especially those I have little interest in, until the very last moment. This habit invariably leads to a period of intense,
last-minute cramming, significant stress, and a powerful wave of regret. I would experience the negative consequences, tell myself I would never repeat the mistake, and then, inevitably, find myself caught in the exact same downward spiral. This assignment presented a unique opportunity to move beyond simple "productivity
hacks," which had never worked. My goal was to use a conversational AI not for advice, but for awareness - to dissect the internal mechanism of this habit and understand why it held such power over me.
My personal area of awareness was this repeating pattern of procrastination. To explore it, I used Google's Gemini as my conversational agent. My intention was to "design" the AI to act as a Socratic, reflective partner rather than a prescriptive
coach. I did not want a 10-step plan to "beat" procrastination; I wanted to co-create a map of my internal experience.
My design process focused on two key techniques:

1.Introspective Prompting: I initiated the dialogue by describing the feeling of procrastination, not just the act. I focused on the "short-term sense of comfort" I felt, which prompted the AI to ask deeper, more probing questions about the quality of that comfort.
2."Meta-Reflection" Pauses: A core part of my design was to periodically pause the self-discovery process and analyze the conversation itself. We would "zoom out" to discuss the internal "agents" we were identifying (like the
"Comfort-Seeker" and the "Rationalizer"). This allowed us to consciously apply assignment concepts like "intrapersonal intelligence" in real-time, effectively using the AI-human synergy to build my final reflection as we went. This process itself was a "chain-of-thought" model, where we traced the habit from trigger to consequence.
This reflective process was incredibly effective. I was able to move past the simple, one-dimensional label of "procrastinator" and identify the complex, interacting system that runs this pattern. The map of my procrastination mechanism became clear:
1.The "Comfort-Seeker": The part of my mind that is triggered by a low-interest task. Its sole motivation is to seek immediate, guaranteed relief and engage in an activity I enjoy.
2.The "Rationaliser": This voice provides the logical cover for the "Comfort-Seeker." It says, "I can always do it later," effectively giving "permission" and enabling procrastination.

3.The "Shadow": This was the most critical discovery. I described it as a "faint reminder like a shadow that keeps bugging me." It’s a quiet, underlying anxiety that taints the "comfort" and makes it feel borrowed and restless.
For my entire life, I had seen this "Shadow" as the enemy. It was the annoying buzz of my own failure, the voice of self-criticism, and the first step on the "downward
spiral." I tried to ignore it, to drown it out with my chosen distraction.

The true "Ah-Ha" moment of this assignment came when the dialogue helped me completely reframe this. The core message of the "Shadow" was one I had always heard negatively: "Are you going to regret this later?"
Through this conversation, I had a sudden shift in perspective, very much like the "protective response" insight from the example paper. My "Shadow" is not my critic; it is my wisest and most compassionate ally.
This "Shadow" is the voice of my own past self - the one who vividly remembers the stress and regret - trying to gently send a signal to protect my future self. The
"Comfort-Seeker's" promise of relief is the illusion; the "Shadow's" faint warning is the truth.
This realization was profoundly transformative. My problem is not a "flaw" in my character, like laziness. It is an imbalance in my internal system. The
"Comfort-Seeker's" reward is immediate and powerful, while the "Shadow-Ally's" reward (long-term peace) is abstract and distant. I haven't been "failing"; I've been stuck in an unfair fight.
This insight, co-created with the AI, completely changes my path forward. The goal is no longer to silence the Shadow with more force or shame. The goal is to listen to it with compassion and curiosity.
This exercise demonstrated that a transactional, transformative conversation is possible with AI. By designing an agent for reflection, I turned a piece of information ("I procrastinate") into a piece of transformation ("My internal 'shadow' is an ally trying to help me"). Moving forward, when I feel that "bugging" reminder, I will no longer treat it as an annoyance. I will treat it as an invitation from the wisest part of myself to pause and ask, "What is one small thing I can do right now to honor this message and be kind to my future self?"

Whenever I accomplish assignments, it’s almost always out of the need to finish it quickly so I can submit it and move on to the next task at hand. However with this task, it felt like a weight was lifted off my shoulders. The situation I used was something that nagged me a lot for the past year. It was due to the fear that my parents secretly resent me for pursuing my dream because it required that I leave them in the process. As an international student from a third-world country, it has always been my dream to pursue my tertiary education abroad. When the opportunity came, my parents were very supportive of my choice but as the days before moving to a new country came closer, they became a bit more hesitant. Even if I don’t regret my decision a year after, I still can’t help but think they secretly resent me for leaving them. With ChatGPT, it helped me process my thoughts and think of a different perspective to this situation.


After first feeding the information, ChatGPT broke it down into multiple categories like emotions and evidence that would produce a balanced thought. I was impressed by how it could compartmentalise different aspects into clear and distinct prompts. Thus, I ensured that the conversational agent was always straight to the point and would only ask clear cut questions to reduce any confusion or unnecessarily lengthen the conversation.
Applying my learnings from class, I recognized prompt engineering through providing clear answers to the questions so ChatGPT could come up with the best suited and most useful answer. Using the CO-STAR model, I provided the context and stated my objective. I wrote it from a first person point-of-view and with a serious tone as I wanted it to be catered to myself as the audience. Lastly, I requested that the answer be short so it would be easy to read and look back on. Besides prompt engineering, I also used zero shot learning and chain-of-thoughts (COT) prompting in terms of structuring the LLM. In terms of the emotions part, I noticed the use of the Arousal vector when the LLM asked me to rate the intensity of the emotion.
After finishing the task, I gained a refreshing perspective that provided me some more clarity on the situation. It felt like a weight was being lifted off my shoulders because it has been something nagging me for quite some time. I can now look back at the reframed thought reminder to reassure myself whenever I am in doubt.


“I chose to pursue my dream with their support, and I’m making the most of that choice — for myself and in honor of their love. Even though we’re far apart, I stay connected because we still belong to each other. Sadness and longing don’t mean resentment — they mean love.”
This reframed thought reminder that ChatGPT provided me with, really encapsulated and calmed my thoughts. It’s a testimony to why I made my decision–and why it was the best choice I could have made; not always concerned if it was the right choice. I can only make the most out of what life has thrown at me and do my best to balance my time. It’ll serve as a gentle reminder that I will always have my parents’ support and reaffirm how grateful I am for their love.

Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
The personal area that I sought greater awareness for is my perceived lack of social skills – not good at talking to people and making friends, and always making things awkward.
I used ChatGPT and selected GPT-5 LLM, as the LLM can process nuanced user input through Natural Language Processing, and produce coherent, empathetic responses. The model can also maintain context across a conversation, which is essential for stepwise CBT reasoning. It can adapt its tone, style, and depth of reasoning based on user instructions in the prompt.
I generated a prompt for an LLM to bring a user through a cognitive behavioural therapy to reframe thoughts. Then, I did prompt engineering by providing a structured meta- prompt that instructed the LLM to act as a CBT coach and guide the user step-by-step through identifying, understanding, and reframing unhelpful thoughts. I specified constraints like empathetic tone, structured stepwise guidance, and non-clinical advice, which shaped both the agent’s behaviour and the content it could safely produce. My interaction design emphasised incremental questioning and feedback.
This is analogous to chain-of-thought reasoning, where each stage builds on the previous user input to produce coherent, thoughtful output. The model is guided to explicitly articulate intermediate steps instead of jumping straight to conclusions.
The CBT session explored my subjective experiences (feeling awkward, anxious, or “performing” in conversations) and worked on the reconstruction of social realities. The agent helped to identify automatic thoughts, evaluate evidence, and reframe cognitive distortions. This mirrors psychological methods for reshaping perceptions and aligning beliefs with reality, with more accurate and actionable understandings.
The interaction also simulated aspects of multi-agent LLM collaboration, with the user (me) and agent engaging in a back-and-forth reasoning process. I acted as a guiding agent, providing context, reflections, and constraints, while the LLM applied cognitive frameworks to generate responses, creating a dynamic co-reasoning environment.
Through this exercise, I gained some valuable insights about how I think and interact socially. One big takeaway was identifying some of my common thinking traps:
-mind-reading: where I assume others find me boring or want to end the conversation
-comparison: judging myself against how others seem to connect
-catastrophising: worrying that awkward silences mean I’ve failed
-“should” statements: like feeling I need to be funny or lively for a conversation to count

Working through these thoughts helped me see that many of these assumptions aren’t entirely accurate. For example, seeing others laugh and chat easily doesn’t necessarily mean they’re effortlessly connecting — people often mask awkwardness with small talk or laughter. I also realised that “having fun” isn’t about being funny; it’s about feeling comfortable enough to be myself.
My biggest “aha” moment was noticing that social interactions feel difficult not because I’m inherently boring, but because I over-monitor myself, which makes it harder to relax and engage naturally.
I also saw that I actually have the ability to connect when I feel I have something meaningful to offer. When I share guidance or experiences, I feel confident, engaged, and authentic. That authenticity is what others respond to, not humour or performance.
The process also highlighted how useful and sometimes limited AI can be. It was validating to have my feelings recognised as normal, and AI helped uncover underlying thoughts I hadn’t articulated fully. But it also reminded me that some suggested reframes aren’t always practical. For instance, my original thought was, “I should be funny or interesting for people to like me.” ChatGPT suggested, “It’s okay if I’m not the most entertaining person; I connect best when I’m being myself.” I doubted this because I value quiet time and don’t always want to talk, so how does one connect when they don’t talk? After my input, AI tried to validate my preference and it suggested a possible reframe to be: “Ǫuiet connection is still connection.” However, this is not practical especially in new situations where some amount of talking is needed to build bridges, and being quiet may mean disinterest, causing others to ignore you. I had to point this out before AI helped me refine it to something more realistic: “Talking helps build connections, but I don’t need to perform. Small, sincere interactions can open the door to deeper friendships.”
Overall, this process gave me clarity, validation, and practical strategies. I now understand that socialising isn’t about performing or being constantly entertaining — it’s about being present, engaging in small ways that feel authentic, and letting meaningful connections develop naturally.

Intro to Transformation Assignment

Reflection pointers:
a.The context or personal area in which you sought greater awareness
I was feeling unhappy about the lack of consideration of my dad towards the family during eating times. Since another family member was still ordering, but the rest of our food had already come, I assumed we were all going to wait for her and say a prayer together before we all started. However, I realised that my dad had already started without saying anything, while my sister and I were still waiting, despite our food also having already arrived.
Immediately, I felt extremely frustrated, and I was mainly consumed by the thought that I did not understand why he could not just wait for everyone to get their food first, say a prayer, then eat together.

b.Integration of different topics (i.e. reconstruction social realities, prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, multi-agent LLMs, etc)
Firstly, there was the reconstruction of social realities. In CBT, the reframing process itself is about reconstructing reality. At first, my social interpretation was: “Dad eats first = he doesn’t value family togetherness.” Through guided reflection, this reality was reconstructed into: “Dad may not realize the meaning I attach to waiting; his action doesn’t necessarily equal disregard.” This shift creates a new social meaning, less charged with hurt, more open to compassion. Secondly, prompt engineering was used as well, the structured step-by-step framework created is essentially a “prompt-engineered protocol.” Each step (“describe the situation,” “identify automatic thought,” “rate intensity,” etc.) acted as a constraint to keep the dialogue aligned with CBT methodology, enabling ChatGPT to respond based on predicting the next most likely words following the input prompt. It relates to providing clear instructions, examples, or contexts, in the prompt, to get the most useful answers to answer my questions.

c.How you designed your conversational agent, including LLM/platform selection and development process.
Firstly I asked ChatGPT to come up with an outline, by asking:
“You are a compassionate therapist who specializes in familial relationships. Guide the user step by step through a cognitive-behavioral therapy exercise to reframe unhelpful thoughts. Be empathetic, inquisitive, and supportive.”
Then, I asked ChatGPT to further refine the framework given and summarise it into a single-line prompt, and it created this prompt:
I am going through frustrations in dealing with my family, and I would like your help to reframe my thoughts using Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT). Follow these steps in order, prompting the user before moving on:
1.Explore the Situation: Ask the user to describe a recent family situation that caused distress or tension, probing gently: “What exactly happened? Who was involved? Where and when did it occur?”
2.Identify Automatic Thoughts: Ask the user to recall their immediate thought or belief during the situation. Probe deeper: “What words or images went through your mind first?”
3.Explore Emotions: Ask the user to name the emotions they experienced (e.g., anger, sadness, guilt, anxiety) and rate each one on a scale from 0–100.

4.Identify Thinking Patterns: Introduce cognitive distortions and check for them in the thought (e.g., all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization, mind reading, catastrophizing, emotional reasoning).
5.Reframe the Thought: Help the user create a balanced, realistic reframe. Check emotional impact: “How does this new thought make you feel now?” Encourage reflection: “Does this new thought feel believable? How might it change your behavior or response?”
6.Plan a Small Action: Ask: “What is one small, practical step you could take to align with this new perspective?” Provide examples like expressing feelings calmly, setting boundaries, or self-care actions. Encourage realistic and achievable steps.
7.Reflection: Prompt reflection: “Looking back at this exercise, what insights have you gained about your original thought and emotions?” Encourage self-compassion: “What can you acknowledge about your effort in reflecting on this today?”

d.The new awareness or insights (if any) that emerged, and how they may influence your life.
Actually, I felt like I was quite pleasantly surprised by the new insight that I received from AI. I had this kind of stereotype that AI bots would never be able to provide help emotionally, and while the AI bot, ChatGPT in this case, may not have had the empathetic aspect of emotional help, it was able to provide me with logical reasonings. I was quite enlightened when the logical thinking process that ChatGPT offered enabled me to realise that maybe he was just really hungry and felt as though there was no need to wait since his food came first. Alternatively, they also offered the probability that he could have felt that the rest would not care if he started first. I guess it made me take a step back from being in the heat of the moment and realise that I may be annoyed, but actually, he does not do it to intentionally hurt me or my other family members, he just may not realise what that means to me.
One valuable piece of advice I received from this conversation with the ChatGPT bot is that I should practice pausing and taking a breath when frustration arises, reminding myself that he likely doesn’t mean harm. Personally, this is a new insight that I will truly value in my life moving forward, especially in dealing with such frustrating situations in the future. It has shifted my outlook on how I should cope with my emotions so that I will not act on impulse and unintentionally hurt others around me as well, prioritising a clear thought process over irrationally deciding in the moment.

e.Overall reflections on your process and experience in completing the assignment.
Overall, this assignment really opened my eyes to the wise way to deal with my emotions, especially in situations where emotions may run high. As I was watching the video done up by Prof, I was actually really inspired by the way that there was a hint of co-creation of meaning, although this communication model was not between humans. I have realised that my initial reactions, though valid, can sometimes be clouded by assumptions or emotions that make me interpret someone else’s actions in the worst possible light. This shift in perspective has taught me the importance of not letting my emotions dictate my immediate response. Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
In my daily life, I often find it difficult to balance being productive and allowing myself to rest. My problem is not about having too much work. It’s more about how I easily get distracted by my phone and environment. Apps like TikTok and constant notifications from random apps makes it hard for me to stay focused. I end up doomscrolling without realizing how much time has passed. This happens throughout the day, like when I’m on the bus or even during lessons. For this assignment, I decided to explore this problem through a conversation with an AI. I wanted to understand why I keep doing this even though I know it affects my focus and time. My goal was to gain some awareness of my habits and maybe find a small way to improve them.

For my experiment, I chose to have a conversation with an AI chatbot/ChatGPT that guided me to think more deeply about my habits. I wanted it to feel like I was talking to someone who could listen, ask questions, and help me notice patterns I usually ignore. I planned a simple flow before starting. I first shared my main issue, that I struggle to balance productivity and rest, and then let the AI ask follow-up questions. It asked about what distracts me the most (I said TikTok and notifications) and gradually guided me to think about why I reach for my phone so often. The questions came step by step, and each one made me reflect a bit more. From what we learned in class, I could recognize how prompt design and chain of thought questioning were at play. 

Instead of giving me direct solutions, the AI helped me look at my own reasoning more clearly. It also made me realize how AI can help us reconstruct our understanding of daily habits. I used to just label distractions as bad habits, but through this process, I began to see them as signals that my brain is seeking rest or relief. If I had more time, I’d like to experiment with multiple AIs working together, maybe one that tracks my screen time and another that helps me reflect on how I feel. That could give a fuller view of my behaviour and mindset.

A few key insights stood out during the conversation. First, I realized I don’t open social media because I’m lazy, it’s more about wanting quick relief from mental stress. Scrolling gives me small bursts of entertainment that let me escape pressure for a while, but it doesn’t recharge me. Second, I learned that I’ve been misunderstanding what rest really means. I used to think rest was separate from productivity, almost like wasted time. When the AI asked me what true rest looks like, my first instinct was to say sleeping. 

That moment made me see how real rest physical and mental recovery is, not just distraction. My biggest “Aha” moment was when the AI suggested I try pausing with intention. Instead of forcing myself to quit distractions completely, I could take a few seconds to notice why I’m reaching for my phone before I do it. That small pause builds awareness, and awareness is the first step toward change.

From this experience I learned that my time management is about my attention management. The issue is not about having or not having enough time, but how easily I’m distracted. Going forward, I hope to practice short pauses whenever I catch myself picking up my phone. Even though it is just a small action of picking up my phone, Maybe I will ask myself if I’m tired or bored. Using AI in this activity shows me how much more it can do instead of just quick answers or technical problems. It can act like a mirror and help us organize our thoughts and understand ourselves better. It didn’t tell me what to do but helped me look at it from another point of view that I didn’t notice.

This assignment showed me that we don’t always need to learn new things to gain self-awareness. Sometimes it’s about looking at a problem from a different angle, and having a third opinion gives us that “Aha” moment. Chatting with an AI made me slow down and think about my own “bad” habits in a more mindful way. It’s not about deleting apps or going cold turkey but about finding balance between productivity and rest. Overall, I enjoyed this process because it helped me understand myself better. But I do wonder if AI can be a little biased by always trying to be nice to me.

Essay:
Reflective Report: Finding the Real Reason Behind My Stress

1. What I Wanted to Figure Out

My goal is to understand why stress sometimes helps me focus and be productive, but at other times completely freezes me up. This was especially true when I was trying to work in my bedroom.

I initially thought the problem was my environment or a lack of discipline. I wanted my conversation with the AI to go much deeper than that and find the one core, unhelpful belief that was truly causing me to freeze.

2. Designing the Conversational Agent and Integrating Topics

I designed the AI to be a self-discovery engine, leveraging advanced prompting techniques to maintain therapeutic rigor.

LLM/Platform Selection and Development Process

I used Gemini for my AI platform. I designed the initial prompt to give the AI a decisive, blended role: a Cognitive Coach (to help me identify my thought patterns) and a Philosopher (to challenge my deep-seated self-worth issues).

The development process primarily involved refining the prompts. I started with the AI's persona suggestions, but its first answers were too complicated and philosophical. I had to prompt it repeatedly to simplify its language. I basically told it to talk like a wise, grounded friend instead of a distant professor.

Methodological Controls and Integration

The final design enforced two critical constraints:

The "No Answers" Rule: The most important rule was to instruct the AI not to provide me with a solution. This forced me to do all the hard thinking on my own. It created an honest coaching environment where the AI's role was solely to guide me, not to act as the expert.

The "Think Before You Ask" Rule (Chain-of-Thought): I built a special command into the prompt that forced the AI to perform a private analysis before asking any question. This made the AI act like a disciplined analyst: it would first diagnose my faulty thinking (such as exaggerating a problem) and then strategise the next question. This command kept the entire conversation deep, organised, and constantly moving toward my core belief.

 

 

 

3. The Big 'Ah-Ha' Moment

The structured conversation continued to press on why I avoided work, and the real reason emerged.

I realised my paralyzing stress isn't about being tired or overwhelmed, but I’ve been tricking my brain psychologically to protect my ego.

When I avoid work by staying in bed, I am intentionally creating a built-in excuse: "I couldn't start because I was too stressed/tired." That excuse is much easier to accept than the terrifying, deepest fear that lurks underneath: "I gave it my absolute best effort, and I still wasn't good enough. I always expect myself to get a high grade, but most of the time my expectations fall short”.

My 'Ah-Ha' moment was realising that the paralysis is an active choice to defend the limiting belief that I'm fundamentally inadequate, rather than an inability to act.

How This Changes My Life

This insight completely shifts my focus. The problem isn't the work, the environment, or the stress itself; the problem is the fear of testing my worth.

Now, the solution isn't to "get less stressed," but to reclaim control. I need to frequently commit to a small act of discipline, like the 5-minute sprint. I do this small act purely for the sake of internal self-worth and agency.

By successfully doing something small, I prove to myself that I have control over my focus and actions. These small, internal wins build up and dismantle the deep fear of powerlessness. I realised I have the freedom to think and act based on my own self-worth, not based on chasing external approval.

4. Overall Reflection

Using the AI this way was surprisingly powerful. The best thing about the LLM wasn't its general knowledge, but its unwavering discipline. A human coach might slip up or try to give me advice, but the AI stuck perfectly to the rules I gave it. This intense rigor forced me to keep digging until I found the root cause.

The experience showed me that one of the most significant values of AI in self-reflection isn't what it knows, but its ability to be a perfectly objective, constrained partner. It allowed me to discover a profound truth about myself that was hiding right beneath the surface.

Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
I’ve often wondered why certain negative situations seem to impact me more deeply than others. When faced with conflict, failure, or criticism, I tend to get caught between emotional chaos and overanalysis. Instead of allowing myself to fully experience my feelings, I instinctively try to dissect and rationalise them.


While watching the video for this assignment, I resonated strongly with the professor’s reflection on experiencing an “all-or-nothing” mindset, where if things aren’t going perfectly, it feels as though they’re going terribly. I recognised that I often react this way as well. When something goes wrong, even slightly, I tend to magnify
it in my mind. Only once my emotions have settled do I look back and wonder: Why was my reaction so sudden and intense? This realisation made me want to explore my inner dialogue more closely: Why do I respond so strongly to negativity, and what does that reveal about how I process my emotions?


For this assignment, I used ChatGPT (GPT-5) as a conversational AI agent as it tends to be more nuanced and conversational. My intention wasn’t to get advice but to use the AI as a reflective mirror, uncovering the patterns and beliefs behind my emotional reactions. I began by describing a recent experience of receiving a bad grade on an assignment I had worked hard on. My first prompt was:


“Can you help me understand what goes through my mind when I get a bad grade?”


The AI broke my experience into layers: external triggers, internal narratives, and underlying beliefs. This helped me see that my reactions followed a predictable pattern. I refined my prompts to encourage deeper introspection, asking questions like:


“What beliefs might be driving such a strong reaction to a disappointing result?”
“Can you package my thoughts such that they come from my emotions instead of my rational mind?”


These questions helped the AI highlight emotional nuances I normally overlook. I also used chain-of-thought prompting, asking the AI to trace how one event, like a low grade, could escalate into a larger story about self-worth. Through this, I noticed the loop I often fall into: an emotional trigger, followed by self-blame, then rationalisation, and finally emotional withdrawal. This essentially amounted to gaslighting myself out of my own emotions.

One of the biggest insights was recognising how much I intellectualise my emotions.
When something unpleasant happens, I immediately try to understand or explain it instead of letting it unfold naturally. The AI pointed out that “understanding” can sometimes be a way of avoiding discomfort—an observation that felt both accurate and confronting. I also saw how my “all-or-nothing” mindset shows up: I tend to
interpret small setbacks as total failures. When I received the bad grade, my mind jumped to thoughts like “I’m not good enough” or “I’ll never improve.” The AI helped me see that I subconsciously link achievement with self-worth, and that my rigid
internal language (“always,” “never,” “should”) amplifies emotional intensity. Recognising this pattern gave me a way to interrupt it by allowing myself to “feel” emotions instead of pushing them away.


The most meaningful moment came when the AI reframed my overreactions not as weaknesses, but as protective responses. It said:
“Your mind might be reacting so strongly because it’s trying to protect you from feeling inadequate or disappointed. The intensity itself shows how much you care.”
That simple line shifted something in me. Instead of judging myself for “overreacting,” I began to see my emotions as signals of care and sensitivity rather than flaws. This was my true “Ah-Ha” moment: the realisation that compassion for my reactions opens far more growth than constant self-criticism.


I also learned that the quality of the conversation depended on the quality of my prompts. Direct or analytical questions led to surface-level responses, while open,
emotionally grounded prompts led to deeper insight. This highlighted that emotional honesty in my questioning mirrors the clarity of the reflection I can achieve. Moving forward, I plan to use AI journaling regularly to process negative emotions, helping me slow down, articulate feelings, and notice thinking patterns I might otherwise
miss.


Ultimately, this exercise showed me that meaningful transformation can come even through a digital dialogue. By engaging in a reflective conversation with AI, I uncovered patterns in my thinking and developed a kinder, more compassionate relationship with myself. I learned that my “all-or-nothing” reactions are not flaws to suppress, but invitations to pause, reflect, and better understand my emotions.

Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
Personal Area of Awareness:
Consumerism culture has pushed society, including myself, to chase material possessions as a badge of status, belonging, and identity. While I am aware of the pressures and temptations to buy, buy, and buy, the dilemma still perpetuates itself unhealthily: give in to the urge to buy new clothes, skincare, bags, a nice meal (the list goes on), or be fiscally responsible and save the money? Moreover, the rise of the ‘treat yourself’ culture has grown into something bigger that justifies self-indulgence, often through irresponsible spending. Yet, breaking this spending cycle feels insurmountable. Through this assignment, I wish to learn how to better manage my finances.

Designing the Prompt:
In designing the prompt, I wanted help in a few areas:
●What emotions do I feel after spending money?
●What are the hidden triggers behind my spending habits?
●How can I manage finances for the future?

That said, the chatbot should not prescribe financial advice like investment tips, but instead, encourage reflection. I crafted my prompt to be step by step for greater co-creation of meaning, whereby the chatbot can build on my previous responses to suggest tailored ways to reframe my financial habits. Thus, I engineered my prompt to follow the COSTAR format: “Provide step by step prompts (response) for an LLM to help me (audience) deconstruct, understand, and reframe (objective) my unhealthy financial habits (context) in a thoughtful tone, (tone) similar to a reflective finance coach (style).”

Selection of LLM Chatbot:
To reduce familiarity bias toward ChatGPT, I also tested the prompt on DeepSeek to see how it compares to ChatGPT. DeepSeek provided a general 3-stage prompt using the keywords in my input – deconstructing, understanding, and reframing. On the other hand, ChatGPT automatically entered Chain-of-Thought by thinking for 48 seconds and listed a 5-stage process – Exploration, Meaning Making, Values Alignment, Reframing, and Integration. DeepSeek appeared more fact-driven and technical and lacked the conversational ‘human touch’ I was looking for. Thus, I selected ChatGPT for this assignment given its detailed prompt which suits the reflective nature of this assignment.
Being able to read ChatGPT’s Chain-of Thought process also helped me understand how its questions are formed in order to unpack my thoughts. For example, the thought process aimed to find out “emotional, cognitive, and behavioural patterns to guide the user through financial reflection and improvement”. Knowing this enabled me to dig deeper in my past spending experiences and be specific in pinpointing my feelings and needs when splurging. In other words, there was mutual engagement in the conversation which enhanced our transaction.

Main Personal Learnings:
After exploring my patterns toward financial decisions, I could relate it to the dimensional representation of emotions. ChatGPT helped me accept that contradicting emotions can be present at once, like feeling satisfied yet guilty when spending money – rather than a sign of ‘irresponsible spending’, I could reframe it as a way to gauge how much I need the item. For example, feeling greater intensity for guilt could mean the item is an impulse purchase, while a lower dominance

over satisfaction could imply an item that brings me insuppressible joy. Identifying my emotions as such to decide if something is worth buying can promote self-awareness in my finances.
Stage 2: Meaning Making benefitted me most in self discovery. It helped me uncover unconscious inferences that stemmed from my upbringing, where my dad was strict about saving while my mum took a carefree, ‘buy it if you like it’ approach. Recognising this internal tension meant that my relationship with money is driven by conflicting values, likely explaining why I love the joy of spending – it reflects my mum’s self-indulgent behaviour, but often followed by guilt because it misaligns with my father’s values. From now on, I aim to be more compassionate in my financial habits and strive to strike a balance between financial discipline and financial freedom.
While I continued the conversation, I gleaned that my financial needs were shifting. Compared to the past where I had no financial concerns and could spend freely, I now have considerations about my future in saving for housing, emergency funds, and taking care of my parents. It reminded me of the Shaker Room @ Botanical Gardens concept of handling complexities. In other words, as my long-term goals evolve, my current behaviours must shift to make space for things that matter. One thing I appreciated was how ChatGPT assured me that I was on the right track to integrate my financial goals into my current lifestyle which felt encouraging and heartening.
ChatGPT also provided practical and actionable advice to start managing my finances, like implementing a spending cap, a cool-off period before making big purchases, or simple tasks like turning off promotional notifications on my devices to curb temptations.

Overall Reflections:
The conversation provided insights on my emotions, the environmental factors affecting my financial habits, future-oriented outlook on my financial needs, and useful tips to spend less. It was helpful and enjoyable, and it felt like I was talking to a friend. With the non-judgemental nature of the AI, I could revert back to previous stages or ask clarifying questions at any point without feeling like I inconvenienced anyone, which is perfect for introspection and expressing my thoughts freely as they come. This relates back to the conversation design as an ongoing process, allowing me to tweak the conversation to align with their needs. For instance, I could ask the AI to be more humorous midway through the conversation to better suit the lighthearted tone I’m looking for.
The assignment also highlighted that crafting the prompt well and asking the right questions play a pivotal role in getting ideal responses from ChatGPT. However, one downside I noticed was that the AI tends to be agreeable to everything I say, at times lacking nuance. I wonder if this can lead users to develop biased opinions or self-righteousness after engaging with an AI, in turn failing to uncover deeper implications or behaviours. Thus, implying that AI must be used with discretion; we must still take personal ownership when forming conclusions.
While communicating my issues to an AI felt foreign at first, it provided guidance to help me understand my financial habits. I would definitely try this again in the future in other areas of my life.

Essay:
The Area of Introspection

 

I have always built my life around optimisation, around systems, routines, automation and flow. It has served me well in life so far, bringing me to law school and helping me carry out life with a certain feeling of control. However, I recognise that this has downsides, a certain level of rigidity, an intolerance for inefficiency, a fear of losing control and a fear of failure that sometimes paralyses me into inaction. 

 

Recently, I met with a friend and junior in law school, and we ended up on the subject of our mutual goals. We spoke for a while about how most people don’t really take the time to introspect. The conversation stayed with me because I consider introspection a core part of my identity. He mentioned that Adler had said that human behaviour is teleological, that we act with purpose towards our goals.

 

Here, I suggest that we can use LLMs as a kind of Adlerian therapist, using teleological reasoning to uncover the underlying purpose behind our behaviour. In my case, I wanted to explore the question of: Why control matters so much to me. 

 

I will use ChatGPT as a reflective partner, it helps me interrogate my assumptions and trace them back to the goals I might be unconsciously striving toward.

The Framework

 

Teleological reasoning assumes behaviour is goal-driven. The purpose here is to understand the function or goal that “control” serves in my life. 

 

I adopt the CO-STAR Prompt Engineering framework. CO-STAR stands for Context, Objective, Style, Tone, Audience and Response. The prompt is as follows:

 

Context (C): I’ve built my life around systems, routines, and automation. This gives me a sense of control but also brings rigidity and anxiety about inefficiency or failure. 

Objective (O): You are an Adlerian reflective partner. Help me use teleological reasoning to understand what deeper goal this need for control serves in my life, and how it aligns with/obstructs my growth.

Tone (T): Tone should be reflective, candid, slightly philosophical, but grounded in fact.

Audience (A): Self

Response (R): Lead me through reasoning that identifies (1) the likely purpose that my control-seeking behaviour aims to achieve, how this purpose shapes my mindset, productivity, and relationship, whether this purpose continues to serve me well, and how might I recalibrate that to a healthier and adaptive guiding principle.

Frame your analysis teleologically, treating each insight as a hypothesis about what goal my behaviour is pursuing. Use past context to inform your decision.

However, the surgery was quite costly, and though my parents thought that they were covered by insurance, in actuality, within the fine print of the insurance agreement, there was a carve-out for such conditions, and thus my family had to bear the heavy costs. Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
Reprogramming My Thoughts on Love
For this assignment, I decided to explore a deeply personal area: my conflicting feelings about love and dating in university. As someone who values faith as a muslim, commitment, and family expectations of getting an arranged marriage, I often feel torn between craving emotional intimacy and fearing that pursuing romance might lead me away from what I believe is right. I used this conversation with AI as a safe space to unpack the thought: “I’m afraid of love but I crave it so much. My goal was not to seek advice about dating but to understand why I feel so many emotions like fear, insecurity, longing, and guilt and to reframe them into something more digestible.
I designed my conversational AI on ChatGPT, grounding its tone and structure in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) principles. I crafted a detailed system prompt instructing the AI to be a supportive and culturally sensitive guide trained in CBT. It was told to:
1.Ask me to describe a recent emotionally charged situation related to romance or dating.
2.Help me identify unhelpful thought patterns (like catastrophising or all-or-nothing thinking).
3.Challenge those thoughts through gentle reflection (“What evidence supports this?” “Could there be another way to see it?”).
4.Guide me to reframe the thought into something kinder and truer to my values.

This design also intentionally avoided giving advice or moral judgment. Instead, the AI focused on emotional awareness, cultural sensitivity, and faith alignment. I chose ChatGPT because of its flexible tone control and ability to follow structured, reflective dialogue which aligns with the transactional model of communication, where meaning is co-created between both participants, as compared to Perplexity that’s focused more on research and facts.
This experience combined ideas from communication theory, prompt engineering, and AI-human synergy. By designing a CBT-inspired conversational flow, I effectively engaged in rapid prototyping of a therapeutic-style dialogue. The interaction embodied the transactional model of communication rather than a one-way exchange, the conversation became a co-creation of meaning where my emotions evolved in real-time through guided reflection.
In prompt engineering terms, I realised how critical precision and empathy were in the system instructions. For example, including phrases like “avoid assumptions about what is ‘normal’ or ‘right’ in relationships” and “respond with warmth and respect for cultural or religious sensitivities” prevented the AI from defaulting to Western dating norms. This created a psychologically safe space that felt surprisingly human and attuned to my context.
The turning point in the conversation came when I admitted: “It makes me feel like I’m afraid of love but crave it so much.” The AI identified this as a tension between two worlds: one part of me rooted in faith and values such as waiting for marriage, the other yearning for emotional connection in the present. When it named cognitive distortions like catastrophising

(“If I fall in love, I’ll lose myself or my family’s approval”) and all-or-nothing thinking (“I can either honor my faith or experience love, but not both”), I recognised patterns I hadn’t consciously acknowledged.
Through the AI’s questioning, I discovered that what I truly longed for was deep companionship, not casual romance, but the kind of love that aligns with long-term faith and emotional maturity. The reframing exercise, turning “I’m missing out on love” into “I’m waiting and preparing for the kind of love that aligns with who I am”, brought genuine comfort. I realised that patience was not passive waiting but trusting timing.
This insight shifted my mindset. I no longer saw my singleness as deprivation but as preparation. When I concluded the session with, “What they have is beautiful, but one day my turn will come too… there’s greater value in waiting,” I felt a profound emotional release. It was an “Ah-ha” moment: love and faith are not in conflict: they can coexist through patience, self-awareness, and trust.
This conversation reminded me how transformative communication can be, even with AI. It mirrored the transformative dialogue described in the transactional model, a process through which both parties (human and AI) co-construct meaning. Although the AI lacked human emotion, its structured empathy and reflective questioning enabled me to engage in deep introspection.
The experience also highlighted the delicate balance between AI as a mirror and AI as a guide. The AI did not tell me what to think; it helped me see my own thoughts more clearly. Its neutrality made me feel safe to explore guilt and longing without fear of judgment, which can sometimes be harder in conversations with peers or mentors.
From a design perspective, I learned that effective AI-mediated reflection depends heavily on the clarity of the prompt and the emotional sensitivity of its language. Even subtle wording choices (“gently challenge,” “aligned with your personal values”) shaped the entire tone of the conversation, turning what could have been a mechanical exchange into an emotionally restorative one.
In conclusion, through this AI-guided reflection, I developed a new awareness of how technology can facilitate emotional growth when designed intentionally. The conversation not only helped me reframe my fear of love but also reminded me that self-discovery is not always about finding answers, sometimes it’s about learning to sit with uncertainty and trust one’s journey.Moving forward, I plan to apply this method of AI-assisted self-reflection to other areas of my life, such as academic stress and self-esteem. This experience convinced me that AI can serve as a compassionate thinking partner, one that doesn’t replace human connection but enhances it by helping us articulate the meanings and contradictions within ourselves.
Ultimately, this exercise showed me that even a digital conversation can lead to a very human outcome: greater self-compassion, clarity, and peace.

Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
Information and transformation assignment 

Write a reflection on your experience (max 2 pages) and upload to eLearn as a PDF. Below are some (non-exhaustive) points you can consider:

The context or personal area in which you sought greater awareness

My grandmother has dementia and thus our family hired a caregiver to take care of her. Last Sunday, it was the caregiver’s off day. My parents had to go to work, and thus I am responsible for taking care of my grandmother. However, my day was ruined as I could not control my temper and shouted at my grandmother when she was not listening to my instructions. 

Integration of different topics 

I provided the clear context in my prompt in order to get the most useful answers. I also told the conversational agent my objective of this interaction: cognitive behavioural therapy techniques to reframe my thoughts. This fulfils the C and O in CO-STAR under prompt engineering. 

Chain-Of-Thought: Instead of generating an immediate answer, ChatGPT internally “thinks through” multiple reasoning steps before producing a response. This can be seen in screenshot 5, where after my prompt, ChatGPT thought for 13 seconds before giving me a response. Afterwards, ChatGPT uses a step-by-step reasoning to prompt me for my inputs, customising the output response according to what my inputs are. 

How you designed your conversational agent, including LLM/platform selection and development process.

I chose to use ChatGPT as my conversational agent (screenshots attached below).  I first started off with asking ChatGPT to provide me with prompts for an LLM to bring me through cognitive behavioural therapy techniques to reframe my thoughts. After that, I asked it to combine into a single prompt for me to paste it in another browser’s ChatGPT. I then begin my journey to heal my soul by allowing ChatGPT to comfort me through its various questions and responses. 

The new awareness or insights (if any) that emerged, and how they may influence your life.

Whenever I am feeling stressed or frustrated with my grandmother, I will always remember what ChatGPT told me – “I love my grandmother, but I am human too, it’s okay to feel stressed. One difficult moment doesn’t define me; I’m doing my best.” (shown in the last screenshot)

I will always tell myself this and will motivate myself to do better at both taking care of my grandmother as well as managing my emotions. 

Overall reflections on your process and experience in completing the assignment.

Although conversational agents can be intuitive sometimes and manage to encourage me by providing comforting words, I still prefer to interact with humans and share my thoughts with them. This is because humans can relate to me sometimes, especially when I have friends that experience the same thing as me before. Conversational agent might not have the same experience and feelings, and thus they sometimes cannot provide the comfort that humans want.

Question: In our daily lives, we engage in countless conversations with others and with ourselves. Some resemble the transmission or interaction models of communication, while others are transformative—aligned with the transactional model—leading to new perspectives and the co-creation of meaning. Could such an “Ah-Ha” moment also emerge from a conversation with AI? We are living in a rapid prototyping era in which AI has accelerated the development of functional prototypes that allow us to explore the synergy between artificial intelligence and humanity. In this assignment, you will design and use conversational AI to guide a process of self-discovery and reflect critically on the experience.
Essay:
The area I wanted to seek greater awareness in was how to manage the stress arising from my school projects. I often felt overwhelmed by the workload and the challenges of collaborating with others. Through talking to a Large Language Model (LLM) I hope to gain insights and develop coping strategies.
When designing my LLM, I began by stating my objectives clearly. I instructed the first LLM to create a prompt for another LLM to act as a therapist to help me manage my stress. Using this prompt, the responses were disappointing as the LLM was returning generic advice such as breathing exercises and recommending me to take a break. After reflecting on this, I went back to the first LLM and told it to generate a new prompt, this time I was more specific with my expectations. I instructed it to design a therapist that can engage more deeply, ask questions to understand my situation and to provide tailored suggestions. This new prompt led to significantly better outcomes, the LLM asked me follow up questions and helped me to better understand and manage my stress. This process has made me realise the importance of prompt engineering in shaping the quality and depth of a LLM’s response.
Several concepts came together in the creation of this conversational agent. Firstly, prompt engineering as described above played a central role. I learnt how small changes in phrasing and structure could alter the LLM’s behaviour. By being specific with my tone, objectives and expectations, I could design more effective prompts.
Secondly, the concept of chain-of-thought reasoning guided how I structured the LLM’s response. By encouraging the LLM to think step by step and to ask clarifying questions, the conversation became more comprehensive and emotionally aware. This approach allowed the LLM not just to respond to my inputs but to reason through them, like how a therapist might read between the lines and understand my underlying issues.
Next the idea of reconstructing social realties, the use of AI chatbots can shape societal views towards seeking help. Although speaking to a LLM cannot completely replace the experience of talking to a real human therapist, the experience of being listened to and guided still had a positive impact on how I deal with stress. This shows how AI can shape social norms around seeking help and normalise discussions about mental health.
While I did not build a full multi-agent system, I did have a simple 2 agent process, where one LLM acted as a “designer” translating my requests into prompts while the other acted as the “therapist” that was helping me deal with stress. In this case, I was the link between the 2 LLMs, allowing me to experience at a much simpler scale how different agents given distinct taskings can collaborate to produce an effective outcome together.
During the conversation, the LLM asked me questions to get more context on my situation. The LLM then helped me to uncover two main pain points causing my stress. The first one which I was already aware of the tight deadlines across numerous projects with overlapping timelines. The second one, which I only discovered through my conversation and reflections with the LLM was my frustration with a groupmate that was not contributing sufficiently. I

realised much of the stress came from not only the workload but also from the emotional burden of managing team dynamics. The conversation I had with the LLM allowed me to see things more clearly. Since I am non-confrontational in nature, I often choose to avoid addressing conflicts directly. The LLM suggested practical solutions for me to advocate for myself and communicate my concerns without being too aggressive. It recommended techniques such as using “I” statements, documenting my contributions and setting clear boundaries. The suggestions by the LLM seem realistic and I intend to apply them to better manage my workload and stress.
This conversation has also changed my perspective on stress management in general. I realised that at times the most obvious issue, the deadlines or heavy workload may not always be the main source of stress. Emotional and relationship factors, though less visible can be significant as well. Through reflecting and listing out all the things that are bothering me, I can better pinpoint the root cause and address them rather than only dealing with the obvious surface level issues.
Beyond the personal lessons that I have learned, this experience has exposed me to how LLMs can be used as reflective tools rather than being a problem solver or information provider. I learnt that with effective prompt engineering, I can create a LLM to facilitate a more reflective and exploratory conversation. Through asking thought provoking questions, listening and facilitating self-discovery, the LLM managed to create a safe and guided space for reflection.
I also realised how much my interactions with the LLM mirror us humans. Just as in real life where we have to convey our expectations and instructions to others when we give them a task. Similarly, LLM also requires clear and well-structured instructions, in this case the right prompt to be able to perform up to my expectations.
Overall, this assignment has allowed me to experience first-hand the process of designing testing and refining a conversational agent. Not only did I learn how to create better prompts for LLMs, I also gained deeper insights on my own emotions and stress triggers. I realised that talking about my stress even if it is with AI, helped me feel better and aware of my feelings. This exercise has shown that when carefully guided LLMs can serve as valuable companions for self-reflection and emotional regulation. The combination of prompt engineering and personal reflection has shown me that with the right questions and honest answers, AI can help us uncover truths that we might otherwise overlook in our daily lives.
