Essay:
TED Talk: “How to Make Stress Your Friend” by Kelly McGonigal
Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc
a) Summary of the TED Talk
In her TED Talk, health psychologist Kelly McGonigal argues that stress is not inherently harmful and argues that our mindset significantly influences its impact on our health. She cites a study that tracked 30,000 adults over eight years, revealing that those who experienced high levels of stress and believed it was harmful had a 43% higher risk of death. McGonigal uses this to argue that seeing stress as bodily signs of readiness, not danger, can lead to healthier physical reactions and more resilience. McGonigal also highlights oxytocin, a stress-related hormone that promotes social connection and resilience. Overall, McGonigal encourages viewing stress as a natural, helpful response to life’s challenges, fostering greater well-being.
b) Evaluation of the TED Talk
Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk, “How to Make Stress Your Friend,” aligns closely with key psychological concepts from NCO112. Her central proposition echoes the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping framework by Lazarus and Folkman (Eysenck, 1985), which conceptualizes stress responses into two categories: primary and secondary appraisals. McGonigal’s focus on reshaping how we perceive stress aligns with the primary appraisal stage, where individuals assess whether a situation is threatening, challenging, or harmless. By promoting a healthier mindset toward stress, McGonigal’s encourages a more adaptive interpretation that enhances perceived control and supports effective coping in the secondary appraisal phase, thereby improving overall well-being. Her approach also reflects the emotion-focused strategies within the Coping Strategy Matrix discussed in Seminar 2. This is further supported by a meta-analysis by Nes and Segerstrom, which found a correlation between dispositional optimism and approach-oriented coping, suggesting that individuals with a more optimistic outlook in life are likely to manage stress constructively rather than avoid or suppress it. (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006).
From a physiological perspective, McGonigal explains that positively reinterpreting stress responses can lead to healthier bodily states. She highlights research showing individuals who interpret stress responses – such as a pounding heart and rapid breathing – as helpful tend to exhibit improved cardiovascular patterns, such as the dilation of blood vessels. Similarly, another study by Pascoe et al. (2019) found that students with negative perceptions of stress and poor coping strategies were more likely to experience adverse health effects, including elevated blood pressure and a weakened immune system (Pascoe et al., 2019).
While McGonigal presents a compelling and evidence-based narrative, it is not without limitations. She cites a study estimating that 182,000 Americans deaths resulted from believing that stress was harmful. While this claim is attention-grabbing, it is based on correlational data, yet framed in her presentation as causal, demonstrating a classic example of the correlation-causation fallacy. In reality, chronic stress is rarely determined by mindset alone, but by complex factors such as socioeconomic conditions and systemic issues (Slavich, 2016), which were not adequately addressed by McGonigal. By overlooking broader social determinants, McGonigal risks oversimplifying the causes of stress and implies that mindset alone can resolve deeply rooted or systemic challenges.
The second area of contention lies in the assumption that mindset-based strategies are effective across all stress contexts. While McGonigal’s approach may benefit those facing short-term or manageable stress, it overlooks those facing persistent pressure, especially those raised in chronically adverse environments. Over time, prolonged psychological stress can lead to dysregulated stress systems, limiting one’s ability to benefit from cognitive reframing (Repetti et al., 2002). This highlights that positive thinking alone is often insufficient, and structural solutions are necessary alongside these individual-level strategies.
Overall, Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk offers a valuable perspective of stress, encouraging individuals to reframe their perceptions of stress as a catalyst for self-resilience and growth. While McGonigal presents an unorthodox narrative that challenges traditional beliefs, her approach aligns with the psychological frameworks taught in NCO112 and is supported by empirical evidence on the effectiveness of adaptive, approach-oriented coping strategies on stress. However, her message falls short of addressing the complexities of chronic or systemic stressors, where psychological agency alone may be insufficient to overcome. To effectively address stress, mindset-based interventions must be part of a holistic approach that includes policies targeting socioeconomic and structural factors. This empowers individuals not just to cope, but to thrive in environments that support lasting mental and physical well-being.
c) Personal Reflection
As someone who recognizes having a relatively low stress tolerance, I often struggle to maintain emotional equilibrium when faced with academic deadlines, social obligations and work-related pressures. My typical physiological responses – such as heart palpitations, rapid breathing and a tensed body – were always seen as signs of personal inadequacy or a malfunctioning nervous system. I developed a negative narration about myself, which reinforced a self-perpetuating belief that only intensified my stress responses.
Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk challenged this narrative, offering a space for introspection where I began rethinking the meaning I assigned to these bodily reactions. I began to see them as signs of engagement, my body’s way of preparing me to rise to the occasion, rather than indications of dysfunction. This shift marked a turning point in how I approached high-pressure situations, moving from a mindset of avoidance to embracing stress as an opportunity for me to tap into inner resilience and develop greater self-efficacy.
Reflecting on McGonigal’s talk and the concepts taught in NCO112, I realized many of the strategies that I use to manage stress – such as meditation, short walks, diaphragmatic breathing techniques – were forms of emotion-focused coping. However, I had not adjusted my primary appraisal of the stressor. According to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, my habit of framing stressors as threats constantly triggered my flight-or-fight response. This helped me understand why my nervous system was always on edge. Without reframing them at the primary appraisal stage, my strategies were merely short-term band aids, offering only momentary relief.
This shift in appraisal aligns with the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, which outlines how individuals respond to adversity through varying forms of reintegration (Richardson, 2002). My past stress responses reflected homeostatic reintegration, where my coping strategies focused primarily on restoring emotional balance, without fostering meaningful growth. McGonigal’s reframing of stress offered a roadmap towards resilient reintegration, where adversities in life can be seen as opportunities towards personal development rather than dysfunction.
Nonetheless, while McGonigal’s TED Talk was empowering, it also made me realize that lasting change requires broader systemic and contextual support beyond individual mindset shifts. I believe that truly addressing stress requires a holistic approach, one that combines approach-oriented coping strategies with collective efforts to create supportive environments, reduce structural stressors, and foster long-term well-being.

(a) Summary of TED Talk 
In Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk on “How to Relieve Stress when You’re Overwhelmed” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc), she highlighted that relieving stress can be challenging when overwhelmed as it may seem like another task to complete. To address this challenge, she emphasised three keys to stress relief. The first strategy is to let tension out of one’s body through physical activities, such as meditation or exercise, lowering cortisol levels. The second strategy is to limit information when feeling overwhelmed by taking breaks from constant input and allowing the brain to rest or engage in calming activities. The third strategy is having a low barrier to entry by selecting accessible and low-effort activities to encourage participation. By incorporating these strategies into daily life and work, individuals would experience reduced stress levels, increased energy, prevent burnout, and improved work productivity. 

(b) Alignment and Critique of TED Talk with Course Content on Stress and Coping
In Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk, she talked about stress and its negative effects on the body. Stress is defined as a state of “mental or emotional tension or strain” (Collins English Dictionary, 2023). First, she highlighted her personal experience of stress which arose from high coursework demands that exceeded the insufficient time and energy needed to complete them. Similarly, the concept of stress was discussed in the Transactional Model (“Model”) of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984) in NCO112 where it arises from an imbalance between the demands that an individual faces and the resources needed to cope with it (Ong, 2025). Additionally, Nesdoly discussed the negative effects of stress by presenting the results of a longitudinal study showing how continuous work without breaks can lead to stress accumulation, exhaustion, and reduced work productivity. These effects were also covered in the Model where negative stress can be detrimental to mental health. While Nesdoly highlighted the negative form of stress whereby there is an imbalance between demands and resources needed to cope with the stressful situation resulting in detrimental effects, her content did not cover eustress which is a positive outcome that can arise from a potentially stressful situation as covered in the Model. Eustress is a positive form of stress that helps individuals to achieve peak performance and promotes growth (Ong, 2025). To achieve eustress, the Model states that individuals must perceive that they have sufficient resources, such as adopting adaptive coping strategies, to better cope with the stressful situation for improved well-being.

In Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk, she emphasises three keys to stress relief when overwhelmed, which involves letting tension out, limiting information in, and having a low barrier to entry. Nesdoly provided an example of how overwhelmed individuals could relieve stress by choosing an enjoyable activity that requires little effort and time, such as meditation or journaling, as it would increase the likelihood of engaging in it and alleviate stress levels. Similarly, these keys are aligned with Nes and Segerstrom’s (2006) Two-dimensional Coping Framework (“Framework”) discussed in NCO112, specifically emotion-focused approach coping strategies, which involves individuals actively trying to improve their emotional responses to the stressful situation (Ong, 2025). While Nesdoly highlighted emotion-focused approach coping strategies for immediate stress relief, these keys do not address the root causes of stress. In contrast, the Framework considers both emotion-focused and problem-focused approach coping strategies for effective long-term stress management and improved holistic well-being. By utilising problem-focused approach coping, individuals can find solutions and address the root causes of their stress to prevent reaching the distress stage. For example, students could prepare for their examinations earlier to avoid last minute revision, reducing feelings of stress, overwhelm, and anxiety. This helps them to manage stress more effectively as they have the time and energy to cope with exam demands, thus reducing the likelihood of needing immediate stress relief from feeling overwhelmed. Similar to the Framework, George Engel’s (1977) Biopsychosocial Model posits that well-being is the combined influences of biological, psychological, and social factors, suggesting that stress can lead to poorer mental and physical outcomes. To effectively reduce stress, individuals take holistic approach to address emotion-focused (psychological) and problem-focused (social) coping strategies.

(c) Reflections and Summary 
The previous semester was stressful as I struggled to balance part-time tutoring commitments on top of demanding coursework. During the coursework submission period, I was nowhere close to completing assignments that had tight and even overlapping deadlines. I desperately needed more time to focus and complete them. However, due to my tutoring commitments, my study sessions were constantly disrupted as I had to pause and provide tuition. Furthermore, internal pressures such as my poor time management, procrastination, high self-expectations for academic excellence, and perfectionist tendencies resulted in additional stress. As deadlines caved in, I felt increasingly stressed by the overwhelming workload, while needing to maintain tutoring obligations. To have more time to complete my assignments, I indulged in quick social media breaks and neglected proper rest leading to prolonged stress and exhaustion. 

The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984) covered in NCO112 highlights that stress is a product of the imbalance between the demands that an individual faces and the perceived resources to cope. From the model, I learned that I was stressed due to an imbalance between high coursework demands and perceived insufficient time and energy needed to cope with it. Learning from that experience, I realised that my maladaptive coping strategies of neglecting proper rest to obtain extra time for coursework completion were ineffective as it only resulted in poor physical and mental health. 

Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk addressed the challenge of relieving stress when overwhelmed by emphasising three keys to stress relief which can be incorporated into daily routines. These keys involve letting tension out through physical activities, limiting information by taking intentional breaks from excessive information by allowing the brain to rest and immersing in stress-relieving activities, and having a low barrier to entry by choosing activities that are accessible and attainable, encouraging participation as it requires low effort and time. Reflecting on my experience, it was challenging to relieve stress and take breaks during my hectic coursework submission period due to insufficient time and lack of energy. Furthermore, I lacked knowledge on effective stress management especially when overwhelmed, where I pushed through the stress without proper breaks. 

Moving forward, I would utilise Nesdoly’s three keys of stress relief. Instead of taking social media breaks, I would disengage from work and take an intentional ten-minute stroll around my neighbourhood which relieves stress, reduce information input, and increase focus levels. While these are short-term practical strategies, I would also adopt Nes and Segerstrom (2006)’s Two-dimensional Coping Framework, specifically approach coping, which is defined as “an active form of coping that seeks to improve the situation that the person is in and reduce the negative impact of the stressor” to effectively cope with stress from a long-term view. There are two types of approach coping. First, problem-focused approach coping aims to problem solve, like working on coursework earlier, breaking down tasks into smaller parts, and discussing tuition cancellations with parents to reduce unnecessary last-minute stress. Secondly, emotion-focused coping aims to regulate emotional reactions, like talking to a friend about my stress for emotional support. By adopting these adaptive coping strategies, I would have sufficient time, more energy, and sustained motivation to cope with future work demands.

Essay:
TED talk selected: What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience 
Speaker:  Charles Hunt
YouTube link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qELiw_1Ddg 
In this Ted Talk, the speaker, Charles Hunt shared about his own experience about trauma. The trauma included having a drug addict as his mother and his father being a pimp. While having not so desirable family background and un-ending trauma experiences over the course of his lifetime, he was able to grow strong mentally and be the successful person he is now, holding a ‘Bachelor of Science in Business Administration (Purchasing & Materials Management and New & Small Business Ventures) from California State University, Hayward (East Bay); a Master of Science in Financial Analysis from Portland State University; and also completed the Cornell Certified Diversity Professional (CCDP) program at Cornell University.’ (Winters Group, n.d.). In the TED talk, he also shared ways and perspectives that helped him overcome the traumas. For example, he shared about how it was perfectly fine with how if someone ‘was a victim but not being a victim’, suggesting that one way to deal with adversities was to choose to focus on the future and what can be changed instead of immersing yourself in past troubles. Also, another way to overcome challenges is to ask for help, through partnerships.
According to the APA Dictionary of Psychology, resilience is defined as the “the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioral flexibility and adjustment to external and internal demands” (APA,2020). Hunt’s experience mirrors this definition. From youth, he encountered advertises such as undesirable family background and losing his loved ones. However, he was able to adapt to those situations and not let it drag him down by seeking support from others and focusing on step-by-step improvements.
We also learn in this course, the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Richardson, 2022). In this theory, one starts at the stage of Homeostasis, which is the comfort zone for most, and a disruption may happen, which is a stressor or a difficult life event. Eventually, there can be 4 different outcomes: Resilient Integration, Homeostatic Reintegration, Reintegration
with Loss, Dysfunctional Reintegration. Firstly, resilient integration is the ideal outcome when one grows stronger where they have acquired new skillsets and strength and improve their situation beyond what it was originally. Secondly, homeostatic reintegration is where, while the disruption does not carry about repercussions, the individual does not gain much from it either. Thirdly, reintegration with loss happens when the individual returns to homeostasis, albeit with certain permanent damage to their lives. For example, the trauma may cause one to lose confidence in their own abilities and thus become withdrawn. Lastly, dysfunctional reintegration, which is the worst outcome where the individual does not successfully cope and adopt harmful behaviours or habits such as drug abuse, alcoholic tendencies, etc. Drawing parallel to Hunt, we can see two different outcomes when adversities happen. Hunt, facing all these undesirable backgrounds was able to reach resilient integration where he was able to move out of that environment and becoming an inspiring figure for many. However, we can also see dysfunctional reintegration in the case of his parents. Hunt’s parents, likely faced certain traumas previously, resorted to substance abuse which led to them landing in prison. More specifically, Hunt’s mother created an even worse situation where her family was thrown out of the social initiative due to the discovery of her drug abuse. Hunt’s father also faced a bad situation where he was jumped in prison and died from that without being able to see his son before his passing. Hence, we can observe that while one may face disruptions in their lives, it is important to choose the way we cope with it as it may lead to differing outcomes.
However, while Hunt’s TED talk is motivating and empowering as he was able to succeed despite all those traumata, it may undermine the importance of environmental risk factors in cultivating resilience. Sameroff and Rosenblum (2006) found that economic hardship, antisocial peers, poor parenting, and living in low-resource communities are environmental risk factors which stifle the development of resilience in children. While Hunt was able to break out of the poverty cycle through his mental resilience, many others don’t. Without the proper guidance and necessary support, it is highly likely for one to find it more comfortable to succumb to the temptations of settling into such situations and not finding ways to improve. From research, it is concluded that ‘poverty and income inequality are each associated with violent crime’ where ‘homicide and assault may be more closely associated with poverty or income inequality than are rape and robbery.’ (Hsieh & Pugh, 1993) Hence, while it is possible for one to overlook their hard natural circumstances, these circumstances often break individual, causing them to adopt extreme ways to cope with the stress.
From personal experience, there are many times where I face problems, often sudden and unpredictable. However, there was one incident that struck my mind when I first see this assignment. For context, I was always deemed and viewed as one of the ‘smarter’ one in class, someone who only needs to read the textbook 30 minutes before the test to ace the test, someone who would not face troubles in his studies. In primary school and secondary school, this was often the case. I was what many called, a ‘genius’. Naturally, this cultivated a sense of pride in me, causing me to have an extremely bad study habit where I do not engage in active revision. After all, why revise 1 week before the test when I can do it the night before and still ace? This situation continued for both PSLE and ‘O’ Levels where I achieved results many others, who have been putting in efforts, dreamed of. Hence, I brought this habit into Junior College (JC). However, JC is a whole other ball game compared to primary and secondary school. Revision the night before was no longer sufficient. Not listening in class was detrimental. Minimal efforts were costly. Before long, I realised every lecture was just me going into class and listening to my teachers speaking in alien. Going for test was a torture, the papers was filled with words that, while separated I could recognise, combining them made me completely clueless. Despite all that, I still managed to scrap by all the test and still managed to pass papers that others could not. The balloon of ego slowly expanded, launching me into the deep black hole of false security. Well, as all story needs an end and life is not a fairy tale, my balloon popped. This came during the release of the ‘A’ Level results. On the certificate, I could only see ‘C’s and ‘D’s. Academically, this was one of the biggest setbacks I encountered. Me? The mighty genius? The feeling of despair and upset was overwhelming. How am I going to go into a local university? While I thought this was the end of my life, I was lucky. I had a group of friends that was there for me, ready to continue the journey with me. The same people I thought lightly of when they were putting in the hours revising was the same people who encouraged me in this dark time. Eventually, after much encouragement by my friends and advice given by my family, I decided to retake my ‘A’ Levels. While the journey to retake my A levels was filled with hardships and obstacles that will take up another whole 5 page, I was able to triumph this time with no credits to myself but to everyone that was with me. Hence, through this experience, I learnt that while it is inevitable to make mistakes and have a giant trip in life, it is important to find out ways to get around the obstacle. It can be as simple as taking a small break when things get chaotic to asking for help from trusted ones. What matters is, always take action. Afterall, the problem and trauma would not solve itself, would it?

            The video correlates to a section on stress in the course materials. Nina introduced three stress relieving strategies which centres around emotion focused coping techniques. Similarly, the study guide explains the transactional model of stress and coping by Lazarus and Folkman(Ong, 2025). However, the video lacked substantial information about the concept of stress. For instance, the course materials cover a greater scope such as problem focused, emotion focused, approach and avoidance coping. Moreover, it emphasises how stress can be managed to reach a flow state for optimal performance (Ong, 2025). 
Strategy one proved to be beneficial amongst the other techniques, based on other research conducted. According to Schultchen et. al. (2019), their research proved that physical activity reduces stress. This is because dopamine, serotonin and endorphin hormones are secreted which account for mood regulation. Therefore, there is substantial evidence to support Nina's strategy whereby engaging in physical activities reduces stress and redirects negative emotions. 
However, I made three critical observations regarding the video and I will share my explanation hereafter. Firstly, Nina’s strategies do not cater to a wide spectrum of her viewers. Her techniques only benefit individuals who are stressed while completing a task, which can be observed through her examples. It does not benefit individuals who are suffering from other forms of stress such as episodic acute stress, chronic stress and psychological stress (Kapur, 2021). Therefore, these individuals would not relate to the video, and would deem the strategies unsuitable for their stressful situations. Secondly, the video showcased three strategies which support emotion focused coping techniques, but failed to incorporate any problem focused and approach focused coping strategies. Since the video title mentions ‘overwhelmed’, Nina focuses on intense emotions instead of the situation being the reason for such feeling. By introducing problem focused coping techniques, individuals will understand that they can cope with stress by focusing on cultivating positive emotions or the root cause of the situation. Otherwise, Nina could introduce approach coping techniques which aim to target the root of the problem and manage the negative emotions (Ong, 2025). Lastly, Nina failed to mention the possible implications if strategy three is not utilised strategically. For instance, if an individual decides to engage in social activities each time they face stress, they would feel a sense of dopamine and it alleviates their tension (Samuel Centre for Social Connectedness, 2017). Thus, they would begin their task with a fully rejuvenated state of being while utilising the refound energy to focus. However, this has the potential to be an avoidant coping mechanism as they would constantly crave the sense of pleasure. Individuals would choose to escape from their stressful duties which eventually leads to procrastination. In due time their stress levels are bound to accelerate, further inducing overwhelming emotions. Nina should address the possible implications of the strategy and ways to channel stress into a motivating factor. 
In conclusion, the strategies appear easy to follow but upon closer observation, it is not informative and lacks depth for individuals to understand stress. Therefore, the strategies are not highly effective for individuals to follow to reduce their stress in overwhelming situations.

I found a full time job as an assistant preschool teacher and applied to SUSS with a successful application outcome. Eventually, I was able to redirect my life. This would have been a healthy coping mechanism to release my overwhelming emotions, pertaining to my experience. I enjoy acrylic and watercolour painting, but failed to utilise that as a coping technique to de-stress. For instance, I could play calming music and let my brush flow with different colours on the canvas. It could simply be splashes of red or black paint to reflect my stress. It is not necessary to paint with a reference as that would defeat the purpose of expressing my inner emotions. This would have provided me an avenue to release my stress and reframe my mindset regarding the situation (Wang & Abdullah, 2024). I resonate with strategy one introduced in the video as it would have been an ideal emotion focused coping mechanism, rather than my initial avoidant coping.
The course explains the fundamental concept of stress by introducing the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman. I was stressed as my expectations of pursuing a  degree at an autonomous university failed, because I was unable to attain remarkable A level results. Furthermore, the course made me realise that I should have used emotion focused, problem focused or approach coping. I would have been able to manage my negative emotions and navigate the root cause of my stress, respectively. In my perspective, both the sessions of the study guide on stress and managing expectations should be read conjointly as it complements each other. When an individual sets highly unrealistic expectations, they are bound to face disappointments when they do not attain it. To reinforce this idea, Kao (2024) highlighted that stress derives from having high expectations.

Essay:
Kelly McGonigal talked about how perceiving stress positively can improve our wellbeing. She cited a study revealing that individuals who experienced high stress but did not view it as harmful had lower risk of dying than those who perceived stress negatively. Believing that stress is detrimental can be more harmful than the stress itself. She also stated how our body’s reaction changes as we change our view on stress. For example, our blood vessels remain relaxed during stress when we view stress as helpful, which is healthier for our cardiovascular system. When going through stress Oxytocin is released, a hormone that encourages social bonding and support seeking behaviour. Oxytocin helps protect our hearts too, by reducing inflammation and aiding in heart cell regeneration. McGonigal mentioned that individuals who spent time helping others show no stress-related increase in dying, highlighting the protective effect of social support. She also emphasises that pursuing meaningful activities is beneficial for health. She advices that choosing a path that aligns with one’s values and trusting oneself to handle the associated stress leads to better outcomes than avoiding stress altogether. 
Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk connects well with the ideas covered in NCO112, especially the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984). This model says that stress doesn’t just come from what happens to us, it depends on how we see the situation. First, we ask ourselves if the situation is a threat (primary appraisal), and then we ask if we have what we need to handle it (secondary appraisal). In her talk, McGonigal encourages us to change how we think about stress, like seeing a fast heartbeat not as panic, but as our body preparing us to cope. This idea matches what we’ve learned in class about reframing our thoughts (cognitive reappraisal) to help us feel less overwhelmed.
She also talks about how stress can be a good thing, which relates to the difference between eustress (positive stress) and distress (negative stress). McGonigal shares research showing that people who think stress is helpful actually live longer, even if they go through a lot of it. This connects with the coping strategies we’ve studied, especially approach based and emotion focused coping. When McGonigal says we should face stress and talk to others, she’s describing the kind of healthy coping we’ve learned about in this course.
However, while her message is uplifting, it may come across as too simple for real life problems. Changing your mindset is helpful, but not always enough, especially if someone is facing long term stress like financial problems, family issues, or illness. For example, Pascoe et al. (2020) found that students dealing with long-term school stress often experience anxiety, poor sleep, and low grades even if they try to stay positive. In the same way, Colligan and Higgins (2006) found that stress at work can cause burnout and people missing work which these are not something that mindset alone can fix.
Another important point comes from Robert Sapolsky (2004), who studied stress in animals. He found that long term stress can harm the body, weaken the immune system, and even damage the brain. And these effects happened no matter how the animals “thought” about the stress. This shows that while changing how we think is helpful, it’s not enough on its own. People also need real life help, like support at work, mental health services, and fairer systems.
In conclusion, McGonigal’s TED Talk shared many useful ideas that match what we’ve learned in NCO112. Her focus on mindset and support is backed by theory and research. But to truly handle stress in a healthy way, we need both a positive mindset and changes in the systems around us. Reframing stress is a good solution but it is not the complete solution.
There were many moments in my life where I experienced stress. The most recent one would be the past semester when I first started university. I felt completely overwhelmed as everything was new to me. I had lectures, group assignments, and individual assignments all piling up and everything felt so foreign. During the assignment submission and exam period, I barely had time to rest, and I started getting headaches and couldn’t sleep well. Back then, I saw my stress as a sign of weakness and that I wasn’t doing well enough. I honestly thought it meant I just wasn’t suitable for university.
After learning about stress in the NCO112 course, I realized that I was using avoidant coping strategies. I was putting things off, kept my worries to myself, and imagined the worst. The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping helped me understand now why I felt so helpless. I kept thinking the challenges were too big and that I do not have the capacity to handle them, what the model calls a negative secondary appraisal.
Watching Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk changed the way I look at stress. She said that things like a racing heart or anxiety before a big task don’t mean we’re failing, they mean we care. I remember the night before my Statistical Analytics exam, I couldn’t sleep and my heart was pounding. Looking at it now, if I convinced myself that it was my body trying to help me get ready and told myself that this means I’m prepared and I care, it may have helped me calm down and complete my exam with confidence. That time, even after the exam I was still feeling the stress and anxiety. I talked to my girlfriend about how I was feeling, and her support made a big difference. She reminded me that I didn’t have to deal with stress all on my own.
Now, I would try to doing things differently by breaking big tasks into smaller steps, planning ahead, and reaching out when I needed help. Like now when I am doing this assignment, I feel more in control, and I got into this deep focus where time just flew by. That’s something we learned about in class, a flow state, where you’re so focused and engaged that you lose track of everything else. It showed me that stress, when handled well, can actually help us perform better.
Now, I see that resilience doesn’t mean having no stress it means knowing how to work with it. This course and the TED Talk taught me that I don’t need to fight stress or fear it. I just need to understand it, change how I respond, and build support systems around me. In my road ahead, I would definitely still get stressed, but I would try not to see it as a weakness but as a part of life, one I can manage and even use to grow.

Essay:
The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw)
(a)Lucy Hone conducts this TED talk in Christchurch, and she covers the major reasons for overcoming tough situations and trauma through the value of resilience.
She begins her talk by asking the audience if they have ever faced some form of misfortune or unfortunate event. Most audience members stand up; Lucy highlights a strong and valid point: adversity does not discriminate. She explains that you must confront some tough times if you are alive. Lucy Hone studied resilience research ten years ago at the University of Pennsylvania. She enrolled in this course when the university accepted a contract to train 1.1 million American soldiers to be mentally fit, just as they are physically fit. After completing her studies in America, she returned to Christchurch to continue her doctoral research. It was at that time that the Christchurch earthquakes struck. She had to pause her research to engage in community aid work. Just when she thought it was her moment to apply her valuable research, she faced the ultimate test of time. She lost her daughter in a tragic car crash. She became a victim of her line of work. She had to confront societal pressures as those around her negatively affected her situation. At that moment, Lucy needed to find light at the end of the tunnel. She took proactive steps to understand her grief and dared to conduct a self-experiment based on the research she had undertaken. Research has shown that parental bereavement is one of the most difficult losses to endure. Despite this, Lucy emerged from that adversity five years later. Drawing from her real-life experience, she advocates that anyone can rise from grief through the proven techniques and strategies she has utilized. She employed three methods to navigate some of her darkest days.
Firstly, Lucy states that resilient people accept that adverse events are bound to occur and are a part of our life journey. Understanding this concept helps individuals avoid feeling discriminated against during tough times. Secondly, resilient individuals are thoughtful and wise in directing their attention. They focus wisely on changing things while accepting those they cannot. Lastly, self-regulation through asking questions that help put the positive in perspective, for example, “What am I doing, helping or harming myself?”—is beneficial. She practiced “benefit-finding,” as it is called in psychology. To conclude, Lucy’s takeaway message is that living and grieving coexist. It is not a trait but rather a set of behaviours. Altering our mindset towards adversity is crucial for our mental and physical reactions to pain and suffering; we can change how we perceive these situations.

(b)(b) The TED talk covers specific resilience areas that were taught to us during our first seminar. Let me discuss the shared values and ideas presented in Dr. Lucy's TED talk, which align with the course content. Dr. Lucy explained how resilient people employ three strategies to cope with trauma. Before that, she mentioned that adversity does not discriminate. This aligns with our course content, emphasizing that resilience is a positive adaptation during adversity (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). In Dr. Lucy’s coping mechanisms, she also addresses concepts like those discussed in the course. In her talk, she mentions “benefit-finding” and changing how we think in response to adversity. These ideas resonate with our course content, which explores the metatheory of resilience and resiliency (Richardson, 2002). In this theory, we examine the disruption of homeostasis leading to the most desired outcome of resilient integration. To elaborate further, one way to build resilience is to identify the positives in adverse situations. This is what Dr. Lucy meant by “benefit-finding.” 

Self-efficacy is another concept that Dr Lucy shared that aligns with what we learned. She smartly phrases, “What am I doing? Is it helping or harming me? "This question invites reflection on how motivation and behaviour influence one’s ability to succeed in specific situations. It also provides a sense of agency.
Through my research, I found similar notions shared by other resilience researchers who believe in the value of resilience and its impact on individuals facing severe adversity, as Dr. Lucy teaches us.

The theory of resilience (APA PsycNet, n.d.-b) synthesizes four resilience patterns from the individual resilience literature: dispositional, relational, situational, and philosophical. In this context, Dr. Lucy’s discourse explores the philosophical pattern of resilience, which examines the individual's worldview and life paradigm. It revolves around beliefs such as optimism, self-awareness, and purposefulness.

However, I have a drawback to this oral discourse. Through my personal story of overcoming trauma, I feel that resilience encompasses more than just a positive mindset shift and redirecting attention to relevant aspects. The healing process is a delicate phase for anyone, and the types of interactions, conversations, and people we choose to associate with make a significant difference. Apart from emotional regulation and having a growth mindset, turning the tables and fostering meaningful connections with diverse individuals is equally pertinent. External factors also impact how resilient one can be. This was absent in Dr Lucy’s scenario.
Research has backed this perspective of mine. Resilience as successful adaptation relies on effective responses to environmental challenges and ultimate resistance to the deleterious effects of stress. Therefore, a greater understanding of the factors that promote such effects is relevant. (Wu et al., 2013) Other factors that affect resilience, apart from mindset building, that were not discussed in the TED talk, include Genetic factors, which contribute significantly to resilient responses to trauma and stress. A range of human genes and polymorphisms associated with NPY, HPA axis, noradrenergic, dopaminergic, and serotonergic systems, and BDNF have been linked to resilient phenotypes (Feder et al., 2009; Russo et al., 2012). 

Genetic studies on resilience provide new insights into the interaction between genes and the environment (Genes × Environment). The development of mental disorders has long been associated with genetic predisposition combined with an individual’s past and present life experiences and environments. Even more surprising is evidence that social experiences can lead to substantial and enduring changes in gene expression that may affect a person’s later behaviour and be transmitted to the next generation. Herrman et al. (2011)

Hence, in this TED Talk, Dr Lucy talks about the personal and systemic sources of resilience; however, she does not explore the environmental and biological sources. 
 
(c) My personal experience of overcoming severe adversity dates to 2013, during my junior college years, when I was overwhelmed by depression. I struggled to cope with the stresses and demands of the A-level examinations. I only passed my papers and did not clear the first round of the ‘A' Level examinations. Consequently, I had to repeat another year in junior college. Those were some of the darkest days of my life, as I felt extremely daunted. I did not understand why I could not comprehend and retain knowledge like my peers. My depression worsened, and I found myself in tears almost every day in the restroom. I experienced major breakdowns as I wondered why I was not mentally capable like others. Things did not turn out well for me. I graduated without a full certificate, which prevented me from entering any university. I was too young to understand or cope with my emotions at that time. I felt emotionally handicapped, unsure how to rise above the adversities and societal pressures I faced. In 2018, I became schizophrenic. Yes, I became a mentally ill patient. I had to be treated and underwent severe medication to recover. However, as I grew older, my desire to enrol in a university and pursue tertiary education became stronger than ever. My medications and support from my family, especially my mother, who has been my most significant source of strength, allowed me to recover from my mental illness. I returned to school and earned a diploma. I found a decent job and successfully enrolled in a university that suits my learning capabilities. This is the story of my resilience, the positive adaptations, and intrinsic motivation to acquire knowledge, which enabled me to rise from my mental trauma. Today, I am honoured to share my story in a university module that teaches critical life skills, offering me a valuable opportunity to reflect on my lived experiences with resilience.
I resonate with Dr Lucy’s findings, which state that we focus on areas we can change.
During the times I was diagnosed with schizophrenia, I focused on reminding myself that I could return to a state where I could acquire knowledge. I practiced resilience with each doctor’s visit. After taking my medication, I took time to heal and concentrate on learning again. Scientifically, I believe the brain synapses strengthened with every effort, and magically, I recovered and relearned how to learn. In my case, the disruption to my homeostasis resulted in a resilient integration, the ideal outcome. Aside from what was discussed by Dr. Lucy, some major contributing factors are the support systems we need to surround ourselves with. In Dr. Lucy’s case, when she lost her daughter, she did not have a proper support system. This resulted in her struggle to return to normalcy being even more difficult. However, I feel that if she had a proper external source of support, her bounce-back ability would have been faster and stronger.
Dr. Lucy discusses how our mindset and behaviours can influence resilience. I believe that external factors, such as the environment we choose wisely during adversity, can also help to ease the pain and restore faith.

In conclusion, resilience develops due to various factors and strategies. As noted in this video, Dr. Lucy focuses on the emotional and mental strategies that help individuals overcome trauma. However, there are many facets of trauma apart from personal adversity. Different strategies are required depending on the type of adversity one is facing. Hence, while Dr. Lucy’s strategies are useful, they may not be relevant in other situations. External and biological factors also affect resilience building.

Essay:
Video Reference: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://youtu.be/NWH8N-BvhAw?si=CaNnjoxzwlpKcMe5)

(a) In Hone’s (TEDx Talks, 2019) talk, her main message was that resilience can be built and strengthened through intentional thoughts and actions, even in the face of adversity. Drawing on her experience as a resilience researcher and a grieving mother, Hone shared how she coped with the tragic loss of her daughter. She outlined three key strategies for overcoming hardship. First, acknowledging that suffering is a natural part of life. Second, instead of dwelling on the negative, focus on what we can control and what we are grateful for. Third, asking ourselves whether our actions will help or harm our well-being, so that we can make choices that support healing and self-compassion. While these strategies did not change the reality of her pain, they helped her navigate the process of grieving while continuing to live a meaningful life.

(b) Hone’s three secrets for building resilience are largely relevant and accurate in supporting the development of resilience in individuals. In her first strategy, she emphasised that resilience begins with accepting adversity as an inevitable part of life – something everyone is likely to encounter at some point (TEDx Talks, 2019). This message prompted me to reflect on how we often personalise hardship, viewing it as something we must face alone, rather than recognising it as a shared human experience. This perspective is reinforced by the course, which highlights that even successful individuals experience repeated setbacks throughout their journeys (Ong, 2025). Adopting this realistic and growth-oriented mindset enables individuals to respond more constructively to disruptions in their homeostasis – a concept described in the course as “bouncebackability” (Vella & Pai, 2019). To build this capacity, I believe we must rely on our internal qualities like hardiness and a strong sense of coherence, which form the foundation for resiliency. As outlined in the course, these traits would help us stay mentally prepared for adversity and find meaning during challenging times, thereby strengthening our ability to adapt and recover over time (Ong, 2025; Mc Gee et al., 2018).

Next, Hone’s second strategy of focusing on what we can control and practicing gratitude resonated deeply with me (TEDx Talk, 2019). It reminded me of how easily we can become overwhelmed by negativity during tough times and made me realise that maintaining a hopeful mindset could influence the way we recover from adversity. This strategy is supported by the course, which mentions that attributes like optimism and positive emotions are contributors to “bouncebackability” in adverse circumstances (Ong, 2025). It also aligns with the broaden-and-build theory, which suggests that having a positive outlook enhances our adaptability and aids us in developing coping mechanisms, ultimately strengthening our resilience over time (Fredrickson, 2001). Additionally, according to Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, as introduced in the course, developing such a mindset helps us achieve resilient integration, the highest form of resilience. This is because reframing the situation and finding meaning in a setback, helps develop our cognitive flexibility, allowing us to not only recover, but also grow (Nakhostin-Khayyat et al., 2024). Overall, this strategy shows that resilience is not only about enduring hardship; it is also about how we choose to respond to it.

The final strategy of determining whether our actions are beneficial or harmful to us struck me as one of the most insightful approaches Hone shared (TEDx Talk, 2019). It reminded me of the importance of learning to pick our battles – choosing how to respond in ways that protect our well-being (Li, 2025). As someone who tends to be headstrong in my actions, I realised how easy it is to fall into habits that feel comforting but are actually unhelpful in overcoming the problem, such as holding onto anger or avoiding difficult conversations. By cultivating this strategy and making more intentional choices, it strengthens our capacity for active coping as we directly engage with adversity in a proactive manner, which the course highlights as a key aspect of resilience (Lieber, et al., 2023; Ong, 2025).

However, when viewed through the lens of Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, this final strategy does not fully align with achieving resilient integration, which requires both internal and external resources (Ong, 2025). In contrast, Hone’s strategy relies heavily on individual insight, which may be a challenge for some people. Factors like stress, limited social resources, or a pessimistic mindset can impair decision-making (Southwick & Charney, 2012; Ho et al., 2008). Therefore, while I find this strategy personally helpful in building resilience, I believe it is most effective when supported by structured coping strategies.

(c) I vividly recall a learning experience from the first month of my internship at a preschool centre during my diploma studies. One of my first responsibilities was to plan a lesson for a class of four-year-olds. As an ambitious intern eager to prove myself, I spent days preparing what I believed would be an engaging activity – a music lesson where the children would play with instruments. I had high hopes that the lesson would go smoothly. However, it turned out to be more challenging than I had anticipated. I struggled to manage the children’s behaviour, as many refused to follow my instructions. I became flustered, trying to stay on track with the lesson plan while feeling overwhelmed by the chaos unfolding in front of me.

After that tough teaching experience, I struggled to persevere. I felt demoralised and began to question whether I was cut out to be an educator. Looking back five years later, I now see how this experience connects closely to the course concepts of resilience. During that time, I had developed a pessimistic mindset in which I took the setback personally and blamed myself. As a result, instead of learning and adapting from the incident, I remained stuck in self-doubt. Through this course, I have learned how adopting such thinking can hinder my ability to recover from adversity and impede my progress toward resilient integration, the ideal outcome outlined in Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory. As such, staying optimistic is crucial, as it is associated with “bouncebackability,” which can help me respond more constructively to future challenges and continue growing as an educator (Ong, 2025).

Besides that, Hone’s strategies also helped me make better sense of the experience in hindsight. Her first strategy – accepting setbacks as an inevitable part of life – taught me to view the incident not as a personal failure, but as something many educators face, especially early in their careers (TEDx Talks, 2019). Recognising that challenges are a normal part of the learning process, I have come to see that resilience means viewing setbacks as opportunities for growth rather than signs of inadequacy. Also, Hone’s strategy of selective attention further reinforced the importance of being a reflective practitioner in this field. I now see how developing habits like journaling what went well and what I would do differently the next time, might have helped me cope more effectively. I also recall receiving feedback from my mentor, which gave me clarity in handling similar situations. These reflective practices promote active coping and play a valuable role in my professional growth (Ong, 2025).

All in all, both the course and Hone’s insights have deepened my understanding of resilience, helping me see challenges as opportunities to become a more adaptable and confident educator. As I continue my degree in this field, adopting this mindset encourages me to embrace growth through setbacks and stay committed to improving my practice in pursuit of peak performance.

Essay:
Selected TED Talk: How to Relieve Stress when You’re Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly
 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc 
Part A
In the TED talk, speaker Nina, who is a work stress and burnout prevention consultant, currently studying for a PhD studying work-related stress, shares practical strategies to relieve stress effectively in daily life and work. Nina introduces three keys to stress relief, which are to let tension out, limit information in, and lower the barrier to entry for stress relief. Some examples of letting tension out are exercising and letting emotions out by journaling or talking to a friend. When relieving stress, it is important to limit taking in information as it may be a contributing factor to additional stress. Barriers to entry for stress relief should be reduced such that relieving stress is accessible at any time. Nina also believes that excessive or stressful media would compound stress rather than alleviate it by highlighting neuroscience research that shows proper breaks lead to better brain focus and reduce stress markers. By incorporating manageable and intentional stress relief, energy levels, focus and well-being will be boosted. 
Part B
Nina’s approach to stress relief of letting tension out, limiting information in and lowering the barrier to entry for stress relief are a form of emotion focused – approach coping, based on the two-dimensional coping framework (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). Emotion focused approach coping refers to actively managing and improving one’s emotional reactions to a stressful situation. (Ong, 2025) Nina’s strategies fit the emotion focused – approach coping category as they do not solve the problem itself but instead, actively engages and improves the emotional responses relating to stress by promoting intentional activities such as physical movement, creative expression, reducing stress through limiting information intake, and making stress relief more accessible and easier to integrate into daily life. Nina believes that incorporating these intentional stress relief will increase energy levels, focus and well-being of the individual. This aligns with the course content as research has shown that individuals who employed approach coping strategies instead of avoidance coping strategies experienced better wellbeing, quality of life and lower levels of perceived stress. (Budimir et al., 2021) Nina believes that scrolling social media and consuming the internet will not relief stress and will instead contribute to stress by such content may trigger unhealthy comparisons or activate the fight or flight response which will disrupt proper rest and recovery and does not alleviate stress levels. However, I disagree with Nina as I believe that social media can be used as a coping strategy and consuming certain information can help to relief stress. 
Social media can be used as a coping strategy for both emotion-focused approach and problem-focused approach coping. For emotion-focused approach coping, individuals may watch uplifting videos, or engage in funny or relatable content as a way to relief tension and improve mood. For problem-focused approach coping, social media can be used to seek practical solutions, gather information or even connect with online support groups to help address the root cause of the stressor. (Lara et al., 2022) What should be avoided is emotion and problem focused avoidance coping methods though escaping and distracting from the problem through mindlessly scrolling and doomscrolling through social media and binge-watching videos to escape stress, which has been proven to have lower wellbeing, quality of life and higher levels of perceive stress (Ong, 2025) 
According to the transactional model of stress and coping, when an individual appraisal of potential stressful situation as stressful, a coping strategy will be used, leading to psychological changes within an individual as an outcome of coping with stress. (Ong, 2025) The use of social media does not necessarily contribute to stress when an individual’s primary appraisal does not perceive the content as threatening or relevant. When the individual views the content as entertaining, relaxing or supportive, it would be seen as helping to relieve stress rather than as a stressor. The example given by Nina is that watching content that trigger unhealthy comparisons or activate fight or flight response will not contribute to stress when content perceived is not threatening. 
Overall, I agree with Nina that letting tension out and lowering the barrier to entry for stress relief are great ways to regulate emotional needs from stress. However, certain information intake and the use of social media can also be great emotion focused approach coping methods when used appropriately. 
Part C
As a student, I often get stressed out from assignments and exams, especially towards the end of the semester. During these periods, I face time constraints and need to priories tasks effectively, which require time management. In the past, I often chose to skip track and field sessions to dedicate more time to studying. 
After watching the TED Talk and going through the course content, I realized that I was relying heavily on problem-focused approach coping, where I directed all my energy and focus towards solving the stressor, which is by revising exams and having neglected emotional regulation. Nina’s TED Talk taught me that letting tension out through physical activities is also a form of stress reliever and I am missing out on the emotion focused approach coping strategy, which can help me better regulate stress and perform better in my learning. 
Moving forward, I plan to incorporate more emotion-focused approaches to cope better and manage my stress effectively. I will intentionally continue to go for track and field sessions during stressful academic periods as a way to manage my emotional response to stress, like how Nina went to a party to relief tension when burdened with many academic tasks. Rather than perceiving it as lost time for studies, I will view it as a way to recharge, regulate my emotions and improve my overall well-being and performance. 
Another strategy that stood out to me from Nina’s TED Talk was the idea of using a “mad book”, which can be picked up and scribble in at any time to release tension. I find this approach very interesting and would be keen to try it out myself. This appealed to me due to the low barriers to entry, which unlike activities such as my track and field sessions that require waiting, can be used immediately whenever I feel stressed. This emotion-focused approach coping strategy is highly accessible which I can incorporate easily into my daily routine. Whenever I am stressed out from studying, I can just take a few minutes to scribble my thoughts and emotions which can help me regulate my stress in a simple and creative way.

(b) A section where you discuss whether the TED talk content aligns with what we have covered in the course (on either resilience or stress). In your reflection, consider the premise of the TED talk, critique the content, and if possible, find articles/sources that might offer a different point of view. All in all, there should be a coherent argument for the conclusion you derive at the end of your reflection. (40 marks)
(c) A section where you practice reflection and identify one of your own personal experiences relating to resilience or stress, and explain how you can better understand and learn from that experience using what is covered during the course, as well as what you have watched in the TED talk. (Please note: when sharing your personal experience, refrain from sharing any confidential or overly sensitive information. Try to use pseudonyms when referring to other people.) (40 marks)
Essay:
The pervasive experience of stress in human life, theorised as an imbalance between perceived demands and available resources, often elicits negative associations (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). However, health psychologist Kelly McGonigal, in her compelling TED talk 'How to Make Stress Your Friend' (TED, 2013), reconceptualizes this conventional thought. This essay will critique McGonigal's arguments, analyse their alignment and divergence with established psychological theories of stress and coping covered in the course seminar, explore alternative perspectives such as the influence of oxytocin, a neurohormone, and apply these insights to my personal experience of stress management.
Citing Keller et al.’s (2012) longitudinal study, McGonigal highlighted that perceiving stress negatively is far worse than experiencing the actual stress itself (TED, 2013). By reappraising these stressors as energised body signs and to treat their stress response positively (Jamieson et al., 2012), people will become more confident and less anxious, leading to a healthier physical response. According to McGonigal, stress can also make a person feel more sociable, motivating people to seek and strengthen social support. Interestingly, McGonigal points out the influence of oxytocin, a neurohormone that is released when a person feels stressed, highlighting its roles in encouraging prosocial behaviours and fostering social connection. Furthermore, caring for others can help an individual build resilience against stress. In conclusion, embracing stress positively and using it to build courage and connection is the success road to a meaningful life.
The information shared on the TED talk aligns mostly with the lecture contents on stress. McGonigal asserted that if reappraised stressors can be seen as energised body signs, people will become less anxious. This directly echoes the core principle of Lazarus & Folkman’s (1984) transactional model of stress and coping. Lazarus & Folkman (1984) asserted that if the stressor is not perceived as a threat, then there will be no stress. Thus, McGonigal's strategy of cognitive reappraisal aligns with the fundamental idea that by altering one's perception (reappraising a threat as a challenge), the stress response can be fundamentally altered.
McGonigal also spoke about the importance of social support to help combat stress. This corresponds to Lazarus & Folkman’s (1984) model of whether they are perceived resources to cope with the stress, which is more clearly defined in McGonigal’s talk. This highlights a key alignment between McGonigal's perspectives and Lazarus & Folkman's theory: the critical role of appraisal and available resources in shaping the stress response (McGonigal, 2015; Niedenthal & Ric, 2017).
The other part is with regards to coping strategies. McGonigal asserts that if individuals can rise to life challenges and trust themselves to handle them, then their stress response will be healthier. In the seminar, the framework by Nes & Segerstrom (2006) was discussed. They provided a two-dimensional coping framework: problem and emotion focused coping and avoidant focused coping and approach focused coping, which is similar to McGonigal’s “fight” coping strategy (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). McGonigal also emphasised positive social support as a form of coping, which was not covered in Nes & Segerstrom (2006)’s framework. Given that Nes & Segerstrom’s framework was developed approximately two decades ago, it is plausible that the growing recognition and empirical validation of social support has been established as a crucial coping strategy in more recent research (Labrague, 2021; Li et al., 2021)
Other factors that may influence coping include personality and individual differences, government and social policies, chronosystem (Bronfenbrenner, 1979; Chen et al., 2022; Childs et al., 2014). To cite an example, a hikikomori (an individual who is isolated at home for a prolonged period and refuses to step out of their house) may be stressed because he does not have money to buy food and his parents have passed away. While McGonigal offers strategies to empower people to take on the challenge, it is crucial to acknowledge situations where reappraisal alone cannot help to resolve the situation. As illustrated by the above case of a hikikomori, broader societal and governmental policies can create inescapable stressors, like lack of social support funds that transcend individual cognitive control (RocketNews24, 2014; Saito, 2019).
Another example where McGonigal’s framework may not be applicable is for individuals experiencing warfare, such as in Ukraine. For those whose houses have been destroyed by the bombs, experiencing war trauma and financial challenges daily, befriending stress on an individual basis may not be appropriate or sufficient given their profound trauma, instability and inescapable physiological burden (Bronfenbrenner, 1979; Długosz, 2023; McEwen & Gianaros, 2011; Seleznova et al., 2023). Such severe circumstances often necessitate deeper psychological interventions and systemic support. 
As a personal reflection, a recent incident was that the Japanese language school that I manage had problems finding more students. I was very distressed with concerns about what is going to happen to the school and the students. While we have a comfortable pool of 70 students across two full-time teachers and one part-time teacher, we have a meticulous process of selecting students, making it even more difficult to recruit students easily.
After watching the video and attending the seminar, I realised that perhaps it is futile being distressed. If I had adopted McGonigal's perspective, I realise I can reframe my anxiety not as a debilitating emotion, but as my body's positive response, preparing me to proactively address the challenges of student recruitment. By reappraising the situation and adopting both problem-focused and approach-focused coping strategies (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006), I can redirect my attention towards the marketing process of attracting more students. Furthermore, re-evaluating our student selection and course marketing methods can help me navigate through this stressful period (Niedenthal & Ric, 2017; Troy et al., 2018). Reflecting on McGonigal's point about the social aspect of stress, I realise I can benefit more by seeking more support from my colleagues, leveraging the oxytocin response to strengthen our collective problem-solving. 
This essay has given me a chance to relook at stress from a different perspective. Although being a feeling-oriented person may make me more susceptible to stress and perceiving it negatively (Benham, 2006; Joo et al., 2012), I am confident that with better understanding and improved applications of these strategies, I can navigate stress positively throughout my life. This navigation, however, may be an ongoing process that requires continuous and conscientious effort, especially when confronted with external uncontrollable stressors such as financial challenges.

Essay:
Psychologist Kelly McGonigal challenges the belief that stress is bad and inherently harmful. She shows research that stress is detrimental to our health only if we believe it is indeed harmful. In a broad-based study about stress, those who experienced high stress levels but did not perceive it as harmful had far lower mortality rates than even others with low stress. McGonigal posits that altering our mindset and perception of stress can make our physiological response better and healthier, transforming stress into something that energises and prepares us for challenges, rather than something debilitating. 
She mentions the hormone oxytocin, commonly known as the love hormone. However, it is instead a hormone released during stress, encouraging us to seek social support, strengthening our heart emotionally and physically. Reaching out while under stress or helping others improves resilience and wellbeing. Embracing stress and connecting with others transforms its potentially negative impacts into positive ones, making us stronger and more compassionate. The overarching message is that our perception, thoughts and response to stress is more important than stress itself, and cognitive reframing to view stress as helpful will lead to better health and a more meaningful life. 
McGonigal states that our perception and response to stress alters its impact on our health and wellbeing. This aligns with the course content, especially the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), and the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework (Nes and Segerstrom, 2006). The model shows our cognitive appraisal and coping strategies affect stress levels as well and is not solely due to external factors. McGonigal highlights the importance of mindset, where perceiving stress as a challenge rather than a challenge leads to healthier psychological outcomes. 
This aligns with the Transactional Model which posits that stress is a dynamic interaction between an individual and their environment, and not solely a direct response to an event. The model includes cognitive appraisal to evaluate how a situation affects one’s wellbeing, and if a situation is deemed stressful, a secondary appraisal is done to assess what can be done. If there are sufficient perceived resources to deal with stress, this results in eustress. If not, it causes distress. This matches McGonigal’s argument that stress is a subjective experience, shaped by how people interpret situations and their perceived ability to navigate them. Additionally, positive stress beliefs and a resilient mindset correlate with adaptive coping and lower distress (Chen et al., 2022). Cognitive reframing is to be aware of how we think, then to intentionally and actively alter how we interpret stressors. This relates to the goal setting theory, which proposes that specific and challenging goals with appropriate feedback leads to higher task performance and motivation. Through perceiving stress as a method to achieve our goals, this allows a flow state, performing optimally under eustress to bring positive outcomes, fostering a sense of control and resilience. 
However, McGonigal’s argument does not account for all individuals, especially those under chronic or overwhelming stress. Prolonged stress exposure can cause neurotoxic effects like impaired memory, increased risk of depression and physical illnesses such as cardiovascular disease (Lupien et al., 2018). This highlights that while mindset is indeed powerful and transformative, it cannot circumvent the physiological consequences of chronic, prolonged stress, especially for those with weak social support. Furthermore, a shift in mindset is only effective for those who have strong self-belief. It is difficult to change those who are chronically pessimistic, as they cling to the familiarity of their thinking and lifestyle. 
Ultimately, McGonigal’s message is important. Reframing stress as a resource to create eustress empowers individuals and increases resilience. This closely ties to the Two-Dimensional Framework of the Problem-focused and Emotion-focused approach coping. She suggests seeking support, positively reinterpreting stressors, and developing a plan to counteract and resolve stress, achieving peak performance in the process and to create a positive feedback loop for a more successful future. However, mindset shifts do have limits. For those facing chronic adversity, a perception shift is insufficient as it could be a genuine health risk. Though, effective coping, social support and interventions are essential. Hence, mindset shifts should complement efforts to reduce stressors for a more effective outcome. 
In my own life, stress has been a constant and it has greatly affected my life. As a deeply introspective and reflective person, my insight has led me to realise many things about myself. I often am hesitant to start on projects or work which I feel unconfident in, which is ironically due to my perfectionism. If I perceive the product to be insufficient given my perceived current ability, I tend to lean toward avoidance and leave the work to be done only when the stress of the deadline is greater than the stress of perfectionism. Over time, strides have been made, but this is a continual journey of improvement, aided by this course.
One notable event was my procrastination on one of my group projects. It was difficult as it required high technical knowledge and understanding of the topic. At the time, I had perceived this stressor as a threat while perceiving that I lacked the resources for coping, resulting in distress and emotion-focused avoidance, as I would procrastinate or distract myself to reduce the negative feelings. However, this left me constantly dissatisfied and there was a constant nagging feeling within me.
The deadline neared, and my groupmates were starting to get anxious as well, which caused additional stress. Some began to chase me to complete my share of the work. I was aware that I did not want to live my life this way, and that I needed to take a first step toward change, however uncomfortable. After reflecting, I understood the mechanisms of my thinking and actions. There was a fear of failure, and a fear of falling below expectations of both myself and others. After overcoming various mental hurdles, I accepted that to succeed, it would first require failure and various setbacks. There was a clear perception shift due to a new goal of wanting to do better (aligning with Goal Setting theory), where I internalized that failures were not indicative of negativity about my identity, but rather was a step forward and a sign of courage that I was willing to put in effort to improve. This aligns with the mindset shift mentioned by McGonigal, where the cognitive reframing allowed me to view my stressors as motivators instead, putting me on an upward trajectory with each challenge overcome. 
I used failure as fuel, devising a plan for myself to remain productive to achieve better performance in my work. I intentionally schedule “focus time” into my day to actively engage in flow state. I break down tasks into manageable components of sufficient difficulty to challenge me at my current skill level, and accomplishing the tasks gives me a great sense of control and satisfaction. Doing this allowed me to keep up to date on tasks, and to fulfil my responsibility in the project, achieving a desirable result. I am also very fortunate to have a strong support network, where I can discuss my views, talk about my stresses and receive advice accordingly. I also actively give back and support peers as I feel it is only right and courteous to do so. Through the TED talk, I have come to realise that part of the reason that support systems work so well is due to the release of oxytocin and its physiological benefits where it buffers against stress (Takayanagi & Onaka, 2021). This has yet again increased awareness of how my environment affects me and can direct me to improve as a person. 
A key takeaway from my experiences, learning and reflection is that our mechanisms largely decide our outcomes. The way we perceive and deal with problems is vital to whether we perform well or not. Though there are many factors involved, I believe that if one has strong enough self-belief while acting in alignment with their goals, if they are intentional in their actions and willing to sacrifice for a better result, they will be able to overcome any self-induced stress. However, we must be cognisant that stress may indeed be overwhelming, limiting one’s ability to cope adequately.
