When she was grieving, she realized the advice given to her by the authorities and experts was not helpful but instead hurtful. Thus, she self-experimented with her knowledge in resilience research and summarized what helped her to build resilience and overcome this difficult period of her life.
She summed up her learnings with 3 takeaways. The first takeaway is acknowledging that adversity does not discriminate and is a part of life. The second takeaway is choosing to focus on the aspects we can control instead of those we cannot, and to recognize and pivot to the positive sides of a bad situation. The last takeaway is assessing whether a particular action we are doing is helpful or harmful to us and letting go of it if it is harmful (TEDx Talks, 2019).








Alignment of TED talk content with the course coverage on resilience
The TED talk content, where Lucy Hone mentions three strategies of resilience, aligns with what we have covered in the course on resilience. The first strategy adheres to what is covered in this course on resilience, like how success does not always happen. Everyone, including successful people, faces failures and setbacks on the route to success (Ong, 2025).
The second strategy adheres to what is covered in this course on resilience, where adversity and positive adaptation are necessary for resilience (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). It also aligns with the areas associated with resilience under the concept of ‘bouncebackability,’ such as optimism, cognitive flexibility, and positive emotions (Kunzler et al., 2020). Resilience is built on staying positive and dealing with difficulty positively.
The last strategy aligns with ‘sense of coherence’ under the key areas of resilience building mentioned in the course (Kunzler et al., 2020). Being able to differentiate actions that help positive growth in resilience makes it easier for someone to pivot their attention towards it.
Different views on building resilience
An alternative approach to building resilience, compared to what the TED talk speaker Lucy Hone adopted for her grief recovery, includes joining social support groups. It consists of sharing sessions by others who are grieving, where participants learn how others in similar situations go through and cope with grief (Schwartz, n.d.). This is in line with how social support is important to accelerate recovery and build more resilience mentioned in the course content (Ong, 2025).
Similarly, another article mentions that resilience can be shared. We can motivate ourselves to cultivate our resilience by watching others overcome setbacks (Threads of Life, 2025). This is a fairly new viewpoint as it is not mentioned in the TED talk or the course content.
Personal experience relating to resilience 
My personal experience relating to resilience is when I was a new member of the rock climbing club in secondary school. I faced the setback of performing much worse than my teammates during our first national climbing competition, even though we joined the club at the same time. I was at the bottom of the chart against 50 other competitors and the last among my teammates in school. I was disappointed in myself when I learnt that I fared worse than my teammates. I considered giving up the sport because of my poor performance during the competition. I was plagued with self-doubt. 
However, after further thought, I started to recognize that I was just a newcomer, and one setback does not determine my success or failure in the future. There are steps I can take to improve, surpass my teammates and, most importantly, surpass myself to attain a better performance. This is in line with the course content and the first strategy of the TED talk, which helps me better understand that one has to recognize that success does not always happen. Failures and setbacks are likely to happen before achieving success.
I focused on the things that I can change and control, like keeping a positive attitude and looking forward to training sessions. I proactively sought advice from my coach on how to improve my climbing technique. I took a different perspective on the outcome of the climbing competition; at least I remained safe and injury-free, this allowed me to immediately return to training and get better after the competition. This was similar to the second strategy of the TED talk and the concept of resilience in the course content. It helps me better understand what I did was appropriate to build resilience, that I should focus on what is controllable, and look at the positive side of a difficult situation. The course content helps me learn that facing setbacks head-on instead of avoiding them, is a sign of positive adaptation to adversity, and in doing so, I am developing resilience.
There are times when I plateau with my climbing progress and get stuck at a particular climbing grade for long periods. My self-doubt builds up, and I start to think of giving up again, as it is the easy way out. However, I set myself back on track and stop thinking of trying to take the easy way out when I realize these negative thoughts are not helping me to improve. The last strategy of the TED talk made me realize I could identify what was not helpful to me. I was able to put the self-doubt aside and keep it from distracting me from improving myself.
Aside from the TED talk and course content, I was able to experience how resilience can be shared, as mentioned previously. I was motivated to press on and keep improving myself while observing my teammates overcoming their own struggles. Having a supportive social support network, which included my teammates and coach who encouraged me along the way, also helped me recover from my disappointment and self-doubt.
The course content on bouncebackability helps me better understand the areas I can adopt for future setbacks, such as self-efficacy and meaning in life, which I may not have displayed during this particular setback. I was finally able to surpass my peers and perform better at the climbing competition the following year, by clinching the top place.
 I did this by keeping my mind and body focused on what is important, which is to improve myself and be better, instead of sulking over my past performance.

Essay:
Summary of TED Talk - How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)

The speaker in the TED talk offers three practical strategies to manage stress during work, which she coin: ‘let tension out’, ‘limit information in’ and ‘lower the barrier of entry’. The first strategy is about relieving stress through deliberate activities or breaks from work, which differs for individuals, such as exercising, journaling, or seeking console in others. The second strategy is to avoid taking in too much information, such as media or work-related content, during such breaks as it may add to the individual’s stress; citing that our brain can only focus on a single activity which either relieves stress or accumulates it. The last strategy is to adopt stress-relieving activities that are accessible and requires little effort to do; in doing so, individuals will most likely conduct such activities to relieve their stress even when they are busy.

Reflection on Learning from the Course & TED Talk

After reviewing the content of the TED talk, I made two observations: the credibility of the strategies shared, and its alignment and relevance to what was covered in the course.

	I assess the strategies, and the associated activities, shared by Nina Nesdoly to be credible as it is supported by credible academia and reliable sources. Harvard Medical School conducted clinical trials proofing that physical and mental exercises relieves mental stress, in both chemical and behavioural aspects. Endorphins produced during exercise induce feelings of relaxation and optimism. Meditation reduces one’s heart rate and blood pressure, allowing the body to relax (Harvard Medical School, 2020). This is synonymous with Nina’s sharing that exercise and meditation will relief one of stress - ‘letting tension out’. A review on studies conducted on workplace breaks, reported in Harvard Business Review, also supported her remaining claims about the benefits of taking frequent micro-breaks and to avoid social medial, which can lead to emotional exhaustion (Lyubykh & Gulseren, 2023).

	While the strategies shared in the TED talk were credible, the content on stress and the coping mechanisms was rather broad-brush and limited in application. In the talk, Nina alluded only to the detrimental effects of stress and seemingly suggested that stress can only be managed by the three strategies articulated. Conversely, the content in this course offered a wider coverage by (1) defining a theoretical model to explain how stress arises and the resultant outcome, and (2) illustrating a more encompassing and robust coping strategy in dealing with stress.

	The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping explains that stress arises from an imbalance between the demands that an individual faces, and the resources that the individual possesses to cope with it; it also involves a transaction between the individual and the environment, which elicits a response (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). If the individual perceive that he has sufficient resources and the ability to cope with the demands, he may experience eustress – a positive form of stress which facilitates performance; accentuating the fact that not all stress are bad to individuals.

	In coping with stress, Nes and Segerstrom (2006) proposed a two-dimensional framework that comprises of problem- and emotion- focused coping, and approach- and avoidant- coping (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). Studies has also shown that an individual’s reaction to stress is greatly determined by his personality (SingHealth, 2024). As such, when in a stressful situation, one individual may find solace in regulating his emotional reactions, such as confiding with friends, while another manages it better through solving the problem at hand. This offers more insights on the approaches individuals may take when they need to ‘let tension out’ shared in the TED talk. 

Reflection on Personal Experience

	About fifteen years ago, I was promoted to a position akin to that of a manager, for an outfit of no less than sixty personnel, at work. It was the first time I took on a supervisory role of that scale and with that level of responsibility. Prior, I had consistently performed well in my individual work and was assessed to have high potential, with plans for me to take on higher positions after that managerial role. I was eager to perform well in my new role. At the same time, in my personal life, my second child was just born and my spouse expected me to spend more time at home with my two year old toddler and newborn. 

	I was able to perform reasonably well for the first six months, putting in extra hours at work and providing guidance to my team, when required. Having tasted success hitherto, I was confident, positive and energetic. However, fatigue started to set in while the demands of work continued. At times, I will not be able to concentrate at work or perform as effective as I had wanted to. Other times, after a long day at work, I would return home tired, not wanting to interact with my family socially, and engage in personal activities such as drinking or watching TV. As this continued, and having not met the expectations I set for myself, I even degraded to taking sick leave at times, avoiding work but only to have it piled up during my absence at work.
	Needless to say, my performance review for that year were abysmal, and the relationship with my family was tense. Fortunately, the episode also alerted my supervisors of my situation, who in turn offered advice and provided me with the much needed support to see me through in the role. I also opened up to my family about the challenges at work. Since then, I learnt to prioritise my time and resources better and also sought assistance from others.

	Referencing Lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model of stress and coping (1984), I realise that the model would have been a useful model for me to assess my level of stress during that period of time. The model depicts that an individual will make a primary and secondary appraisal, of which the latter involves evaluation of the resources available and the coping options available to address any stress (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). During the first six months then, I was probably still able to perform well, performing under eustress, as I was positive and the demands of work was still manageable. After that, as I got tired from the demands of work and my personal life, I did not recognise the signs of distress, in that I did not had sufficient resources, physical energy and time, and not being equipped with adequate coping strategies, such as emotional support, to overcome my stress.

	Also, on hindsight and with reference to Nes and Segerstrom’s two dimensional coping framework (2006), I realised that I had avoided the distress I faced at work and emotionally, ignoring work and engaging in drinking. Thankfully, I was able to arrest the situation, facing my stressors through approach- coping means – getting support and asking for resources from my superiors and seeking emotional support and acceptance from my family then. I could also have benefitted from the stress coping strategies articulated in the TED talk - undertaking approach-based and stress-relieving activities such as exercising or talking to my spouse, and spacing such activities throughout the duration to manage the level of stress I faced then.

Essay:
1. （a）
This TED video mainly tells about a weekend in 2014, when the speaker Lucy Hone and two other families planned to go out for fun. However, Lucy Hone's 12-year-old daughter, her 12-year-old best friend, and her best friend's mother died on the spot due to a car accident. After that, Lucy Hone's world collapsed, and she refused to listen to any theories and advice about resilience. She went through the five stages of facing sad events: anger, bargaining, denial, depression, and facing reality. Finally, with the help of self-adjustment and the support of society, relatives and friends, he walked out of the darkness. He believes that resilience is very important and anyone can become resilient. He also summarizes three strategies for dealing with the darkness and lows in life: 1. Pain is part of life; 2. See the positive side of things; 3. Is what you do self-harm or self-help? This is to encourage everyone to overcome difficulties and lows.

2. （b）
I watched Lucy Hone's TED talk, which summarized three strategies for getting out of the darkness: resilient people understand that bad things are part of life; think about the positive side of everything, and when taking action feedback, consider whether the action is helpful to yourself or hurts yourself more and gets you into trouble. The speaker believes that resilience is not innate, but something that everyone can have. Pain is part of life, and it is most important for us to face pain. This is consistent with the definition of resilience in our class - resilience is not just "bounce back", but also the ability to maintain psychological, emotional and behavioral flexibility when facing challenges (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013).
The phrase "choose to focus on what you can control" from TED reminded me of the active coping and cognitive flexibility we discussed in class. The course also noted that optimism, self-efficacy, and meaning building are crucial aspects of resilience (Kunzler et al., 2020). This lecture, in my opinion, is incredibly practical and allows us to apply abstract theory to real-world situations.
However, I noted that this TED talk was essentially about changing one's thinking and mostly disregarded the value of external support systems. Lucy Hone lost a daughter, but she still had two lovely sons, a high degree, a successful career, and the support of her family and society, She mentioned in the video that everyone who knew her story thought she was a victim and gave her advice and warmth, which brought a lot of attention to her story. She had a good support system and she was wise enough to internalize the difficulties and suffering. The external and internal aspects complemented each other. which was an important reason why she was able to get out of it. We reviewed in class how a person's social context, cultural history, and resource acquisition all have a significant impact on their ability to "adapt actively." For example, people who have been stressed or distressed for a long time cannot heal simply by "changing their minds" (Kunzler et al., 2020).
Furthermore, as Bessel van der Kolk (2014) noted in his book " The body keeps the score" ，long-term impacts on the neurological system and brain from severe trauma can make rehabilitation a challenging process that frequently necessitates medical intervention, physical therapy, and community support. This supplements TED's perspective: it's not that Lucy Hone's views are wrong, but not everyone has the conditions she has, so the differences in individual conditions still need to be considered. For example: If a person is in a very bad economic situation, has a low social status, is not well educated, and does not have access to higher quality information, when he experiences darkness and low points in his life, he may not be able to get through it relying solely on his resilience. 

3. （c）
The past year has actually been the lowest point in my life. A long, stable relationship ended, and coupled with personal academic pressure, unstable income, and strained family relationships, I was exhausted physically and mentally. I had to face everything as soon as I opened my eyes every day, and my trust in people dropped to negative, so much so that I closed myself off and had to rely on myself to get through it all. I didn't show weakness or give in to anyone, and didn't tell them that I needed help. So I had to face life in a strong and invulnerable state all the time, which made me feel even more tired.
Looking back now, I had a more avoidant coping style at the time, which was somewhat similar to the "emotion-oriented + avoidant" strategy mentioned in the course. Although in the short term I seemed to have wrapped and protected myself very well, in the long run, I put myself in an isolated and helpless situation. Later I realized that I couldn't go on like this, and I needed to find an outlet for my emotions, so I wrote down these experiences and pains, made them into videos, and posted them online. Although I was attacked by some strangers, most people encouraged and understood me, and shared with me privately that they had encountered the same pain and difficulties. Slowly, I opened myself up more and more, and was more willing to share and face my experiences calmly, and day by day I found confidence and relaxation in life.
When I was watching the TED talk, I agreed with what was said in it: "Pain is a part of life, and the important thing is to see the positive side." After sharing my own story on self-media, I found that everyone will encounter lows in life. We can express ourselves boldly and attract people with the same frequency. We can even learn from how people who have had the same experience as you got out of it, so that we can face life more optimistically.

By relating this experience to Richardson's Metatheory of Resilience, I realized I had reached a moment of ‘reintegration with function'. Whether I could progress toward ‘resilient reintegration' depended on whether I made certain critical internal and external changes. The three ideas described in the TED talk effectively provided a pathway toward resilient reintegration.
To sum up, I have truly realized that resilience does not mean making a great transformation, but rather mustering up the courage to move forward a little bit again and again, and slowly accumulating your self-confidence. When you believe in yourself, you will believe that you can get out of the trough.

TED Talk Title: The Three Secrets of Resilient People
Speaker: Lucy Hone
YouTube Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw 
(a)Summary
In Lucy Hone’s TED Talk, The Three Secrets of Resilient People, she shares three strategies to aid individuals in managing and recovering from adversity. As a resilience researcher and after experiencing the sudden death of her 12-year-old daughter, Hone outlined three key habits of resilient people. First, resilient individuals have accepted that suffering is a normal part of life. Second, they focus their attention on what they can control and what is good in their lives instead of dwelling on negativity. Third, they ask themselves whether what they are feeling or doing is harming or helping them. Hone stresses that resilience is not a ‘fixed trait’ but willingness to give resilience a try (Hone, 2019) and overcome their adversities. 

(b)TED talk contents alignment with course on Resilience
Premise
The premise of Lucy Hone’s TED Talk is that resilience is a practical, learnable process that involves ordinary processes and a proactive mindset. This aligns with the NCO112’s definition of resilience with reference from the American Psychological Association (APA, 2020), which describes it as “the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioral flexibility” to derive this definition “individuals who can successfully adapt to the challenges that they face in life are able to cultivate resilience.” Hone conveys this by emphasising that resilience is not a rare, fixed trait but an accessible mindset that anyone can cultivate through deliberate daily practices (Hone, 2019).
Critique and others’ perspectives
Academic research supports a wider perspective where external variables aid in resilience training. For instance, Fletcher and Sarkar (2012), in their study on Olympic athletes, found that resilience stemmed not just from personal traits like optimism and focus, but also from external resources, such as high-quality coaching, structured training environments, and team camaraderie. To exemplify, a gold medallist athlete gave credits to his parents for protecting him from the pressures of elite sport by giving him the opportunity to air his grievances arose from injury and not being selected (Fletcher & Sakar, 2012, pg 674). Similarly, Kunzler et al. (2020) reviewed resilience interventions for healthcare professionals and found that while techniques like mindfulness or cognitive restructuring can help, their impact is often modest unless paired with secondary social support (Kunzler et al, 2020). These findings reinforce that while Hone’s strategies are useful, they represent only one aspect of resilience on the individual level. A more complete understanding should include both personal mindset and external support systems that enable sustainable resilience training.

(c)Reflection
Personal experience relating to resilience
As a student-athlete at the Singapore Sports School, I trained and competed as a bowler with the goal of representing Singapore and getting into the National Development Squad then. This environment exposed me to intense competition, both locally and internationally, where success was almost never guaranteed despite months of preparation. I often found myself facing disappointment after devastating tournament results, especially when comparing my performance against international athletes. The emotional impact of repeated underperformance was discouraging and mentally draining.
I was fortunate to receive strong external support from my coaches, teammates, and parents, all of whom played a vital role in keeping me grounded during difficult periods. This aligns with Fletcher and Sarkar’s (2012) findings that resilience is shaped not only by personal mindset, but also by the presence of a supportive environment. Their study on Olympic athletes highlights how elements like constructive feedback, emotional encouragement, and well-structured training systems significantly contribute to building resilience is something I can relate to from my own journey.
Better understand from that experience using what is covered in course / TED Talk
After engaging with the course materials and watching Hone’s TED Talk, I’ve come to view resilience as more than just “bouncing back” from setbacks. In the past, I relied mostly on just external motivation and feedback to stay focused. But Hone’s third strategy of asking oneself whether what they are “doing is helping or harming them” offers a mindset I had not consciously practiced. I realize that internal dialogue and self-regulation are just as important as external support. Instead of fixating on losses, I can redirect my attention to what I can control. This includes continuously developing my technical skills, learning from failure, and staying emotionally composed in difficult situations.
The course also reinforces this perspective through concepts like having a growth mindset, self-talk, and goal setting in SU3 (Ong, 2025, pg 34). Together with Hone’s three cognitive strategies, I now see resilience as a combination of both own self’s mindset and external environment. With more competitions upcoming for me such as the SUNIG in September, I will integrate questioning myself whether my thoughts help or harm me when coping with setbacks pre, during and post competition. This will not only help me to perform better during my competitions but also protect my mental wellbeing when faced with setbacks.

Essay:
(a)	The Three Secrets of Resilient People expounds on how adversity and experiences shape us tremendously, reflecting the strategies and assimilations we undergo in order to cope (Hone, 2019). In 2014, Lucy Hone’s life radically transformed, thrusting her from a researcher into the position of a grieving mother. This left her feeling like a victim, powerless to change the circumstances. The centrality of her message is on the theme of hope—journeying through the wide spectrum of emotions such as anguish, pain and longing. She assuredly asserts her identity as an “active participant in the grief process” (Hone, 2019). 
Hone presents three strategies for being resilient. The first strategy is acknowledging that suffering is part of the human experience. Secondly, she elaborates on how resilient individuals are selective in their attention, to realistically appraise situations to change or accept the potential outcome. Lastly, posing the question of ‘Is what I am doing helping or harming?’ allows us to reclaim our autonomy and agency. All of these strategies demonstrate a personal journey for the speaker in overcoming grief, turning every situation towards goodness. She concludes with a call to action, compelling the audience to draw strength from the possibility of hope and a willingness to try—driven by a grateful heart.
(b)	Resilience is defined as the assimilative process that individuals undergo to accommodate challenges and adversity (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). At the beginning, by calling every individual to stand if they had experienced some form of adversity struck a chord and resonated deeply. Adversity is a shared encounter of many, despite our differences. Hone (2019) speaks of how our innate cognitive response to positive and negative emotions differs, and adapting is the process of “tuning into the good”. In seeking encounters to experience goodness and gratefulness, the speaker identifies the psychological perspective called benefit-finding. Drawing parallels to the account of Yip Pin Xiu, her landmark wins at the Paralympics are attributed to the various support systems she relied on, along with role models she looked up to in her sporting career (Yip & Goh, 2021). These coping mechanisms emphasise the positive potential for individuals to derive benefit from disability or grief alike. Individuals develop the psychological and social resources to enhance personal well-being, serving as a stronger cognitive structure compared to problem-focused or emotion-focused coping (Tan et al., 2021). Similarly, Fletcher and Sakar’s (2013) posit positive adaptation as a core factor of resilience that is contextualised within adversity, citing Olympic champions' consecutive humiliating defeats contributing to psychological resilience. This precedes sports performance as an outward expression of an inward characteristic—handling adversity and employing strategies to overcome external stressors (Gould et al., 2002). Positive adaptation is also measured through social competence and fulfilling expectations, and operating within these contexts might be more prevalent in a grieving mother or a struggling athlete, compared to a student in Singapore. Therefore, as the nature of the adversity differs, the approach must be informed through realistic and relevant means, framed in context.
In seeking the experiences that bring people joy, the experiment Marty Seligman (2010) conducted in 2005 measured elevated gratitude, happiness and less depression over the duration of the study, which required participants to share three good things that they experienced. Making an intentional and deliberate effort to tune into what’s good in the world is an area of self-efficacy that fosters resilience (Tan et al., 2021). Although the success of these coping mechanisms is measurable within the scope of experiments, it acknowledges the limitations of these benefits beyond a controlled environment. Self-maintenance is required of individuals to habituate high-performance strategies in the long term (Seligman, 2010). 
Self-talk is also used by Hone (2019) during moments of solemnity, when poring over old photos and asking, "Really? Is this helping you or is it harming you? Put away the photos, go to bed for the night, be kind to yourself." Lev Vygotsky (1978) postulates private speech as a gradual cognitive development from egocentric speech during the early years, guiding children’s thinking for self-communication. Even in adults, it's an evolving concept of self, as the sociocultural theory is evident in the environmental circumstances we navigate. Such self-regulating behaviour is important to manage interpersonal relationships and develop personal efficacy. Emerging from a more reliant state towards independence is further described in Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development, which pushes an individual’s threshold for potential development. The balance for internal and external regulation equips individuals with the capacity for evolving and adapting to future contexts and situations (Pasqualotto, 2015).
In summation, strategies require an individualised approach towards trauma, adversity or challenges. Contextual relevance and realistic expectations enable these strategies to be effective for resiliency, coupled with the “willingness to give them a go” (Hone, 2019). Resiliency is to adapt and detach ourselves from a state of permanence and stagnant comfort to foster resilience.
(c)	The time I overcame the challenges of feeling inadequate as a teacher required gumption and a tenacious spirit. I entered the classroom as a 13-year-old volunteer teaching Gospel stories to a young audience of Primary Three students. Five years later, I would enter my first Nursery 1 preschool classroom as an intern teacher. My characteristics of teaching largely emulated the educators in my schooling years, and I was suddenly thrust into a position where I would be judged on every minute detail of classroom management and instructional pedagogy. It became a frequent barrier for me to surmount due to the need to keep many different segments of the lesson plan focused, fulfilling every objective I set out to accomplish. After my first semester of studies, the feedback from my lecturers devastated my confidence as an early childhood educator. Doubts compounded in my teaching competence, inseparable from the utter disappointment of my grades.
	It was a humbling experience, inadvertently leading me to share this testimony countless times thereafter. Despite the circumstances, I began seeking feedback spontaneously from my colleagues and peers after every interaction to identify the blind spots unknown. Gradually, I realised that setting unrealistic expectations of myself to conduct pristine lesson implementations triggered discouragement time after time. Ultimately, it was necessary to let go and find joy in learning alongside the children. I began experiencing the child-like awe and wonder to immerse myself with the child’s perspective, holding on to every precious encounter of discovering new ideas, bravely exploring the unknowns. Such a hopeful outlook on teaching and learning as a cyclical process of highs and lows made it possible to regain my confidence. Holding fast to my convictions to press on further enhanced my ability to inspire my peers as educators and leaders in their own right.
	Furthermore, the teaching practice feedback I received transformed. I viewed these opportunities critically and introspectively, in a continuum to hone my craft and adapt to the needs of the classroom environment. The past dread of receiving poor results turned into encounters for professional growth. Finding stability through critical reflection enabled me to achieve resilient integration. As a reflective practitioner, I have become increasingly open and willing to receive judgment of my teaching competence, as an avenue to positively cultivate reciprocal and responsive teacher-child relationships. Although my crisis of identity is distant from the anguish felt by Hone, the indistinguishable feelings of inadequacy and helplessness began to fade over time. Strengthening our resolve to perceive everything through a positive lens is not a matter of disillusionment, but overcoming the personal barriers of our worth and value. 
	In summation, I delight in Hone’s perspective to see the good in everything I do. I endeavour to “make an intentional, deliberate, ongoing effort to tune into what’s good” in my world (Hone, 2019). I now embrace these challenges because I know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope. My hope remains unwavering, sure and steadfast.

Essay:
a)
The TED talk discussed by Hone (2019) highlights three characteristics of resilient people, with the first being that resilient people understand that adversities and setbacks are part and parcel of daily life, and do not feel personally maligned by the setbacks they face. The second secret shared by Hone (2019) was that resilient people focus their attention on productive thoughts rather than allowing their thoughts to revolve around negativities. In doing so, resilient people do not necessarily disregard negative events, but rather remain aware of these while also attuning themselves to positive events. Hone (2019) described this as benefit-finding, a process through which individuals sieve through events to search for things to be thankful for. The third and final secret shared was that resilient people question themselves about whether their current actions and thoughts are detrimental or beneficial to themselves. In exercising this questioning, resilient people charge of their thinking and decision making, engaging in productive behaviours and patterns of thinking. Finally, Hone (2019) ended her talk by sharing that resilience is not a predetermined attribute that individuals do or do not possess, but rather something attainable that can be achieved through a simple desire to embark on.

b) 
Richardson’s (2003) metatheory of resilience and resiliency plays a large role in defining resilience and how it develops. This model posits an individual’s state of equilibrium as homeostasis, which when affected by stressors, could lead to various outcomes spanning from the ideal resilient integration, to the undesired dysfunctional reintegration (Ong, 2025). Factors hindering the ideal resilient integration from occurring could include a pessimistic explanatory style (PES), defined by Ho et al. (2008) as the propensity to viewing negative events as occurring due to intrinsic factors such as oneself, and having influence over various parts of one’s life. With relation to Richardson’s (2003) model, Hone (2019) experienced a disruption in her homeostasis after the death of her daughter, but was able to overcome it, leading to resilient integration, where she was able to overcome the adversity she was facing and develop new understandings on how to face her grief head-on. Hone’s (2019) discussion of the first trait of resilient people is supported by its contrary link to the PES. The PES is referenced - albeit indirectly - in Hone’s (2019) talk, where she mentions that resilient people understand the inevitability of setbacks, and thus do not get caught up in pessimism or feel personally victimised by them. This example of a resilient person directly contrasts the PES, and leans more towards an optimistic explanatory style, wherein individuals view negative events as occurring due to external factors out of their control, with a limited influence on their life; given their higher level of optimism, these individuals are shown to demonstrate greater resilience when faced with major life stressors (Ho et al., 2008). Additionally, Hone’s (2019) sharing on the second trait of resilient people practicing benefit-finding aligns with Tennen & Affleck’s (2002) ideas that finding small wins during adversities alleviates feelings of pessimism, and is pivotal in sustaining well-being and building mental resilience. By sharing her example of how she chose to focus on her family, and her daughter’s painless passing, Hone (2019) served as a real-life example of how benefit-finding serves to develop resilience.
Prominent figures in the course material on resilience are Kunzler et al. (2020), who note certain factors that may facilitate resilient integration, through evidence-based methods. With regards to this, Hone’s (2019) ideas show clear links with these factors, and methods. Cognitive flexibility is defined by Kunzler et al. (2020) as positive reappraisal, where individuals are motivated to challenge harmful thoughts in favour of positive ones. This could be seen in Hone’s (2019) third ‘secret’ of appraising whether her actions and thoughts were harmful or helpful. In discerning these thoughts, Hone (2019) was able to identify better alternatives and prioritise helpful actions and thoughts over harmful ones. Optimism, as defined by Kunzler et al. (2020), could also be referred to as a positive attributional style, not unlike the optimistic explanatory style mentioned by Ho et al. (2008). Hone explained this in her second ‘secret’ in encouraging the audience to not lose track of positive aspects of their lives.

c)
One experience that tested my resilience would be when my father was diagnosed with stage 3 colon cancer. This event came as a shock as I had always known my father to be sturdy, in spite of some unhealthy habits. As we were living apart at the time, I was wrought with guilt at not having been able to spend more time with him before his diagnosis, and being unable to contribute financially to his medical bills. In my woe, I resorted to rather unhealthy coping strategies in hopes of temporary respite from my negative feelings. Looking back on this experience and linking it to Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory of Resilience and resiliency, my father’s diagnosis presented as a major stressor in my life and disrupted my homeostasis.
During this time, I lacked proper intervention such as social support, due to a fear of oversharing details about my personal life. Coupled with this was my constant pessimism regarding the matter; I blamed myself for being unable to do more to alleviate my father’s suffering and feared that should the worst case happen, my whole life would be perpetually turned upside down, defined as a PES (Ho et al., 2008). Due to this closed mindset, I was unable to look past the situation and think of more productive methods to cope. These factors hindered my ability to develop resilience when faced with this matter, which resulted in me going through a dysfunctional reintegration, defined as an inability to cope with adversity, leading to engagement in unhealthy behaviours (Richardson, 2002). My eventual hospitalisation as a result of these unhealthy coping strategies served as a turning point - potentially the start of my resilient reintegration - and I was able to receive social support from people who were able to help me cope better with my father’s situation. At this point in time, rather than homeostatic reintegration, I felt that I had developed a capacity to view the situation in a positive light, which enhanced my ability and confidence to deal with it (Richardson, 2002).  While I did not have these resources at the time, looking back on this experience allows me to draw conclusions between the coursework and the coping strategies I used at the time. To start, I engaged in religious activities like praying for my father’s health. In doing so, I did not feel so helpless in my actions. Additionally, by having a sense of coherence, I was able to transform my initial guilt at being unable to spend time with my father into motivation to visit him more often. These methods of building resilience align with Kunzler et al. (2020) who note religiosity, sense of coherence and social support as important factors in allowing individuals to recover from setbacks. 
Drawing links to Hone’s (2019) talk, I realise that although I was unable to embody any of the three traits of a resilient person, being aware of them would have helped me greatly during that situation. To start, the first ‘secret’ of knowing that adversity does not discriminate would have alleviated my sense of guilt and I may not have felt so despaired in that situation. The second ‘secret’ of focusing on positive aspects would have allowed me to be relieved that my father was diagnosed early, which allowed him to seek timely treatment, instead of focusing on the negative aspect of his diagnosis. Finally, the third ‘secret’ of critically evaluating my thoughts and actions would have undoubtedly allowed me to make wiser decisions regarding my coping methods.
In retrospect, I would have appreciated having this knowledge to cope with the situation more effectively. However, I am confident that the knowledge I currently have from the course material and Hone’s (2019) talk will be able to serve me in responding appropriately should similar situations arise.

Essay:
Title: The Three secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw) 
Summary of TED Talk: 
The Lucy Hone (2020) in her TED talk explores the traits and skills that resilient people have to get through adversity. 
Firstly, resilient people accept that life doesn’t always goes the way we wanted . They understand that adversity and challenges in life is a norm as aptly put by Hone (2020) “suffering is part of every human existence”. This shift in mindset allows them to think less negatively and push forward through tough times. 
Next, resilient people can deliberately choose where they should focus their attention on. They adopt a realistic lens when faced with a challenge and accept that some factors are uncontrollable. This allows them to tune into the positive as describe by Hone (2020) as benefit-finding, as a result allowing them to overcome the challenge and improve their resilience.
Finally, resilient people deliberately ask if their actions are “helping or harming” them. This allows them to be more in control of their life decisions. 
Alignment with NCO112 content: 
The content covered in the TED talk, as summarised above, aligns with the concept of resilience covered in the course. 
Hone’s (2020) story encompasses 2 key components of resilience taught in the course — adversity and positive adaptation (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). Hone (2020) set the premise of the TED talk around her experience of losing her daughter. She covered in extent how it negatively affected her and her lived environment. This presents the adversity component. To overcome her bereavement, she utilised the 3 key traits (as summarised above). The first trait that Hone (2020) teaches — the acceptance that challenging times are constant in life. This is similar to positive adaptation which explains that the people who are resilient are not afraid of difficulty or hardship and is able to succeed in such conditions (Ong, 2025). 
Next, the skills taught in the TED talk can assist people to achieve the ideal potential outcome as stated in the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR) (Richardson, 2002). The theory states that everyone starts at their comfort zone known as homeostasis and a setback, hardship and challenge in life can push them out of it.  There are four outcomes, and the most ideal outcome is ‘resilient reintegration’ which increase their overall level of resilience and resiliency, but such is an ‘ideal’ outcome as there are many challenges that impede such growth. The techniques taught to inculcate resilience in the TED talk can assist one in achieving this ideal stage. It is evident as Hone (2020) describe it as it allows one to “live and grieve at the same time”, this means that they gleaned valuable lessons which allow them to create a new comfort zone. Thus, the TED talk supplement the content taught in the course.  
Next, the skills taught in the TED talk and course focuses in shifting mindset. Hone’s (2020) three techniques focus on grounding oneself to reality and shifting the mindset from hopelessness and bleakness to hope and optimism. This is similar to how the course highlights the importance of tapping onto “innate resources” and “social support” to create and inculcate resilience when facing setback (Ong. 2025). 
However, Hone’s (2020) teaching failed to account the different environment and circumstances that people lived in . The premise of the TED talk solely revolves around the bereavement of losing a loved one. The hardship is universal, but the circumstance might differ from people to people. In our course, we explore that there are different “environmental risk factors” such as socio-economic statuses (SES), friends and upbringing (Sameroff and Rosenblum, 2006) that affect how one might cope with hardship or challenges in life. To elaborate further, Noor & Alwi (2013) highlighted that low SES adolescent who have resilient resources such as strong maternal relationship, teacher and school support gained higher resilience scored as compared to those who does not have such resources. This study highlights the importance of these other factors in creating resilient people. Thus, Hone’s (2020) methods failed to account for these environmental and circumstantial differences. 
To summarise, The TED talk by Lucy Hone mostly align to the course content, however it does not account for the different circumstance or environment one lives in.   
Reflection:
 The TED talk had aptly described the feeling of pain and anguish of losing a loved one. My grandmother’s death was sudden and not accounted from her myriads of illnesses from stomach cancer to kidney failure. On 16 May 2025, my grandmother had passed away due to a gallbladder stone. The night before, she wanted to speak to me, but I was in a project meeting till late at night. I was not able to speak to her for the final time. That is one of my life’s biggest regrets. As I am writing this reflection, it has been a week after my grandmother’s death. This reflection is as real and raw as it can be. 
My grandmother was a role model in my life, she taught me the basics of being a boy in a traditional and orientalist Malay community, which allowed me to navigate and fit into social groups easily. She pampered me like I was her own child with love and tender care. She cooks for me whenever I said I am hungry or when I craved for something. She was like my mother when my mother was busy working the 9 to 5 to earn a living for me and my family. However, as I grew older, I further distanced myself from her due to school and other commitments I have to survive and thrive as a student in this small city-state. 
Her death was something I could not accept and the past few days I was full of regret, self loathe and self-doubt — always asking if I was a filial grandson to my grandmother and if she knows I love her. 
As Hone (2020) mentioned that “suffering is part of life” and that we need to accept this to excel. I understand that death is inevitable for any living being and that my grandmother’s death will free her from the pain and ordeals she had to suffer from medical treatments such as chemotherapy and dialysis. This shift in perception allowed me to take back control of  my emotions and understand that what I am going through is normal and it can heal. 
The course taught us about the different “social support” to build up resilience (Ong, 2025) such as religiosity. Born and raise in a Malay-Muslim household, God has been a pillar of my life that guides me through the toughest of time. The loss of my grandmother is no different, and I lean heavily on prayers and seeking help from the Asatizahs (religious teachers) in my community. It was a painful process, but I was able to keep my emotions in check, gain clarity and find closure. 
The process is still ongoing. Some nights I feel a sense of emptiness and others I reminisce the good time with her and imagine the possibility of spending time with her if she was still alive. However, I try to actively practice Hone’s (2020) third lesson – asking myself is the process helping me or harming me – which allowed me to take control of my process of grieve. 
Overall, as I am still navigating in this ‘new world’, the techniques taught in the TED talk and course has helped me gain stability in overcoming this adversity and building my resilience. I believe its going to be a long process to overcome this adversity but at least I will be able to live and grieve and hopefully achieve the ideal outcome of MRR.

Essay:
TED Talk on Resilience 
YouTube Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw 
Title: The Three Secrets of Resilient People
Speaker: Lucy Hone
Part (a): Short Summary of TED Talk
In this TED Talk, resilience researcher Lucy Hone shares three of her go-to strategies to navigate tough times and rise from adversity. Firstly, she mentioned that resilient people understands that suffering is a part of life. Terrible things is a part of human existence, and it happens to everyone. Hence, we should accept it instead of being resistant to tough times. Secondly, she highlighted the importance of focusing on the things that we can change and accept those that we can’t. We should direct our attention towards situations that are within our control and act on it. Last but not least, resilient people often ask themselves "Is what I'm doing helping or harming me?". This is a simple yet powerful question that can be applied to many different contexts in life, allowing us to have some control over the situation and be kind to ourselves.
Part (b): Discuss 
The TED Talk aligns closely with the course content on resilience. According to Fletcher and Sarkar (2013), the two key components for resilience are adversity and positive adaptation. The Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency suggests that disruption (e.g. stressor or difficult life event) is necessary for growth. We must be able to step out of our comfort zone to build resilience and achieve resilient integration, in the most ideal situation (Ong, 2025). This relates to what Lucy mentioned with regards to her first point where suffering is a part of life.

The second point on focusing on the things that we can change relates to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984). The model suggests that there is a transaction between the person and the environment, which evokes stress response (Ong, 2025). Two main stages are involved, namely the primary appraisal (where the person evaluates whether a situation is significant and will threaten them) and secondary appraisal (where the person will figure out how they can cope with the difficult situation). For instance, as mentioned by Lucy, resilient people tend to assess situations realistically and are good at selecting where to focus their attention on. This involves both primary and secondary appraisals. Thereafter, we should use problem and approach focused coping as an active form of coping to help to improve the situation (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006).

Lastly, we should strive to achieve a flow state, as described by Csikszentmihalyi (1990) which includes the experience of deep engagement, absorption, and enjoyment (Ong, 2025). Lucy’s personal story of losing her daughter in a car accident and her decision to focus on what helps instead of what hurts demonstrated a form of self-regulation which aligns with the flow. Her third point can help to provide individuals with a sense of control over the outcome (one of the nine dimensions of a flow state) in guiding their mindset and actions. Apart from that, to cultivate resilience, we should adopt an optimistic attitude towards life and utilise positive emotions to overcome the negativity in difficult situations (Ong, 2025). These are what we can do that are helpful instead of harmful.

Despite the three strategies mentioned by Lucy in the TED Talk, there are also environmental risk factors that are not within individual’s control that could hinder the development of resilience. This includes poor parenting style, family structure, economic situation, community inclusion, and social conditions etc. (Robert Land Academy, n.d.). Individuals who operate in these unfavourable environments may lack the ability to react positively to adverse situations. As such, although Lucy offers valuable insights to navigate tough times, it does not address more complex situations and the environmental barriers that people may face.
Part (c): Practice Reflection and Identify Personal Experiences
One personal experience that stands out in relation to stress was during my polytechnic internship three years ago. As it was my very first corporate job, I was nervous and did not know what to expect. My first two months were not as smooth sailing as I thought it would be, with mistakes made along the way. It also drained me mentally every day as the stress was overwhelming. I even began to doubt my abilities and felt inferior compared to my peers, especially when I saw that they were all doing well. There were also a lot of miscommunications along the way. However, things started to improve, and I eventually found joy in my job. I learnt how to better cope with stress and manage my tasks in an efficient manner.

I think that I can better understand and gain from that experience by pondering on “What can I learn from this?” instead of asking “Why me?” whenever I am met with challenges. For instance, understanding what I can learn from the mistakes, interpersonal skills, problem-solving skills and stress management. This shift in mindset aligns with the course concepts that are covered in NCO112 and Lucy’s sharing on her personal experiences.

During that period, I reduced social gatherings with friends and can go a few days without replying to text messages which is an avoidant focused coping style. However, had I asked myself this question "Is what I'm doing helping or harming me?" according to the third strategy shared by Lucy, I would be able to reconsider these actions and make better decisions.

In addition, I learnt to not have pessimistic explanatory style by constantly attributing unfavourable events to internal factors (“the problem lies with me”), global factors (“this negative event affect my entire life”), and stable factors (“the negative effects of this event will last a long time”), which deters the cultivation of resilience (Ong, 2025). For example, I should trust myself when I was faced with those obstacles during my internship, believe that I will be able to overcome it instead of feeling inferior and doubting myself. 

Therefore, having a positive mindset is important in managing stress, allowing me to transform difficult situations into learning opportunities.

Essay:
“The three secrets of resilient people”, by Dr Lucy Hone
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw 
(a)
The TED Talk by Dr Lucy Hone, a resilience expert, explains 3 strategies that she personally used after losing her daughter to a car accident. Firstly, Dr Lucy shares that resilient people accept that life is not always smooth sailing and no one is exempt from pain and hardships. This mindset prevents a victim mentality and “why me” attitude, which helps one not to feel singled out by adversity. Secondly, resilient people selectively choose where to focus their attention on. They focus on what they can change and look for positive aspects even in tough times while accepting what they cannot change. This approach allows resilient people to notice the good things happening and practice gratitude. Lastly, Dr Lucy shares that resilient people question if their actions are in fact doing more harm than good. This strategy is the most beneficial and impactful one as it provides an individual an avenue to remain in control over their decision making. This simple strategy thus steers one away from self-defeating habits and guides them toward healthier choices. In conclusion, Dr Lucy believes that anyone can learn these strategies easily and face their own challenges with greater resilience.

(b)
Yes, the TED talk content largely aligns with the course content on resilience. Dr Lucy’s TED talk provides a personal and practical perspective on resilience. Her strategies for resilience align with the course content such as APA’s definition of resilience and Richardson’s Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Ong, 2025). 

For example, Dr Lucy’s first strategy of accepting that adversities are universal and suffering is part of life aligns with the course’s definition of resilience. The American Psychological Association Dictionary of Psychology defines resilience as “the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioural flexibility and adjustment to external and internal demands” (APA, 2018). This definition emphasises that adversity will occur. Hence, encountering obstacles and failures is part and parcel of life for everyone. This notion is further reinforced by Glen Richardson, who describes how individuals will experience disruption to their comfort equilibrium and then undergo one of several outcomes of reintegration (Ong, 2025). Ideally, the individual experiences resilient reintegration and bounces back while gaining new strengths in the process. His Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency outlines how nobody escapes from adversities, and what actually defines a resilient individual is how they rebound and learn from it. Dr Lucy’s view that suffering is part of life directly echoes this academic insight that adversity is universal and perhaps even necessary for growth. Her message combats the myth that resilient or successful people do not undergo failures and challenges. For example, Thomas Edison, the inventor of the lightbulb, famously said “I have not failed. I have just found 10,000 ways that will not work.” (Thomas Edison Foundations, n.d.). This quote exemplifies accepting adversity as part of the process, as Thomas Edison failed countless experiments before successfully inventing the lightbulb. He did not view those 10,000 attempts as true failures but as learning points. He demonstrated what Dr Lucy and the course content were emphasising – failures and challenges are inevitable, hence we must not be demoralised by them. Furthermore, this example illustrates the concept of “bouncebackability”, which is the ability to recover and persist after failures (Ong, 2025). Thomas Edison was able to have a positive mindset and turn failures into motivation rather than despair, resulting in success. Therefore, Dr Lucy’s message that suffering is part of life is consistent with the course content and the foundation definition of resilience as bouncing back from hardships. 

However, Dr Lucy’s TED Talk does not explicitly address the full picture of resilience in peak performance. Her talk focuses on the psychological dimension, while the course emphasises a biopsychosocial approach (Ong, 2025). This means that resilience arises from a combination of biological, psychological and social factors. For example, social support is also a crucial component of resilience. A high quality network of family, friends and neighbours to give psychological, physical and financial help can enhance an individual’s resilience to stress (Ozbay et al., 2007). In the context of peak performance, a professional athlete’s support network can be the difference maker in his success. His network can provide encouragement and advice during tough times, allowing one to withstand and rebound from adversity. From Dr Lucy’s first strategy, it also implicitly recognises a social aspect. Knowing that suffering is part of life can encourage one to share their struggles and draw comfort from the fact that they are not alone. Dr Lucy only drills down on the idea that false images of perfection on social media can isolate us, whereas recognising that everyone hurts can foster connection and empathy. Sharing about life’s struggles and challenges with peers or trusted adults can be healing in nature. Since Dr Lucy’s professional work involves community and organisation resilience, this is why she may most likely appreciate the broader systemic factors. Therefore, I view that Dr Lucy’s TED talk is complementary to the biopsychosocial approach. Her message is valid, but the full picture involves additional layers beyond the individual mindset. 

(c)
I faced one of the toughest challenges of my life in National Service (NS), where I retook my A Level examinations in both years of my NS. I always did well in school, so I was complacent in Junior College (JC) and left my revision too late, eventually attaining poor results. However, I was driven by my deep conviction in my potential and to not disappoint myself or my parents. This experience exemplifies several resilience principles from this course and Dr Lucy’s TED talk. Almost failing my A Levels was similar to the disruptor that knocked me out of homeostasis as explained in Richardson’s Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Ang, 2025). It threatened my self belief and my future. However, I chose to embrace resilient reintegration instead of spiralling into despair. I came up with a study plan and made necessary sacrifices, eventually doing well enough to study my preferred course in university. Looking back, I “followed” Dr Lucy’s 3 strategies. Firstly, I accepted that setbacks are part of every high-performer’s journey, just like how Thomas Edison failed countless times before succeeding. Secondly, I did not dwell on my past errors which I could not change. I used to spend lots of time aimlessly re-reading old notes and instead concentrated on a new path. I created a structured revision timetable and practiced revision papers under timed conditions, and clarified my doubts with my peers. This positive focus transformed my anxiety into actionable steps. Lastly, I noticed that I had a bad habit which was to cram information late into the night. This left me feeling lethargic and inefficient. I asked myself if this was sustainable and if it was helping or harming me. I soon changed my ways and adopted a healthier routine where I slept early and took small breaks along my revision. This improved my concentration and memory retention. 

Dr Lucy’s TED talk allowed me to enhance my understanding and learnings from this retaking journey. It gave me the clarity that I am progressing along the right path with the right mindset. I have come to appreciate that setbacks are not roadblocks, but springboards to success, provided that I remain resilient. In future, I will continue to apply these insights whenever  presented with a high pressure situation, such as when tackling a demanding project during my university internships. I will remain committed to having the right mindset and take purposeful action, while embracing the courage to adapt to embody true resilience.

Selected TED talk: How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc) 
Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk is all about handling stress when you are feeling overwhelmed. She shares her personal story where, instead of powering through her to-do list, she chose to go to a party, and it actually helped her feel more focused and energized afterward. She is a stress and burnout prevention consultant. In the TED talk, Nina Nesdoly outlines three key principles to help reduce stress in our daily lives. 
Firstly, to let the tension out. Whether it is going for a walk or doing something creative, releasing physical and emotional tension is important. Secondly, limit the information in. We are constantly bombarded with content, from social media to work emails. Taking a break from all these can give our minds the mental space they need. Lastly, lowering the barrier to entry. Stress relief does not have to be a huge time commitment. It can be as simple as doodling for a minute or having a quick chat with anyone you want. These activities have to be easily accessible. By prioritising stress relief, we are not just managing stress but also making ourselves more energized and productive.
Reflecting on Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk, I realised that it is related to Seminar 2 on “Coping with Stress”. Her main message is that stress management is not complicated and everyone can proactively use easily accessible strategies to lessen the feelings of being overwhelmed. This strongly aligned to the discussion on stress management in NCO112. In Seminar 2, the emphasis on stress and recovery cycles for peak performance highlights the importance of actively engaging in recovery which directly aligns with Nina Nesdoly’s first principle: letting tension out through activities like moving, talking to someone or creative outlets.
The coping strategies in Seminar 2 also further reinforce Nina Nesdoly’s point that we can always take concrete steps to manage our response to stress. From here, I can infer how the emotion focused strategies like engaging in activities to release tension, can be directly related to Nina Nesdoly’s advice. Letting tension out is aligned with the strategies that help us manage how we feel about stress. Nina Nesdoly’s approach also fits well with the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping that was discussed in class. This model explains that stress happens when we think the demands around us are more than we can handle. Her strategies seem to be able to boost our coping management by giving us practical stress management techniques. Her emphasis on releasing tension aligns with emotion focused coping, while limiting information feels like a way to engage in problem focused coping by reducing stress sources. The idea of lowering barriers to entry seems to encourage us to adopt coping strategies which makes it easier to engage in activities that help us recover.
While Nina Nesdoly offers self-help strategies for immediate stress relief, focusing on simple, actionable tips, it can be critiqued for implying that these readily available methods are sufficient for all forms of stress. In contrast, the Healthline article delves into professional therapeutic interventions, such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and group therapy, underscoring the crucial point that stress sometimes can only be effectively managed with professional guidance, particularly when it is chronic impacting daily functioning (Cherney, 2024). Furthermore, Nina Nesdoly’s steps might be critiqued for presenting an overly simplified view of stress management that does not fully account for the complex physiological processes involved. In contrast, the NCBI article provides a crucial scientific perspective and systemic impacts of stress on the body. This deeper understanding reveals that stress is not merely a feeling to be managed with simple techniques, but a profound physiological reaction that, particularly in chronic forms, can have significant and widespread bodily effects, potentially necessitating approaches beyond basic self-help to address its underlying biological manifestations (Chu et al., 2024).
Unlike the systematic review on work-related stress in healthcare professionals, which delves into evidence-based organizational and individual interventions tailored to a demanding occupational environment, Nina Nesdoly's advice largely omits the nuanced impact of systemic stressors or the necessity for structured, evidence-based therapies often required in professional settings. Her focus on individual, readily applicable tips, while beneficial for mild, general stress, might inadvertently suggest that all forms of stress, including chronic occupational burnout or stress requiring organizational changes, can be adequately addressed without deeper, context-specific, and professionally guided interventions (Catapano et al., 2023).
Thus, Nina Nesdoly's advice effectively offers accessible self-help strategies for daily stress, aligning with key course concepts on coping. However, her approach is limited as it oversimplifies the complex physiological and systemic aspects of stress. For chronic or work-related stress, a deeper scientific understanding, professional therapeutic interventions, are often crucial for effective management.
One stressful experience I encountered was during a business project in ShenZhen, where I had only six days to carry out four business experiments. The pressure was intense, as at least one of them needed to succeed for the trip to be considered worthwhile. The tight timeline and high stakes caused a surge of stress. I felt overwhelmed and constantly anxious. By using the Transactional Model discussed in Seminar 2, I understand how this stress manifested. In the primary appraisal, I perceived the situation as a direct threat to my goals and personal sense of competence. During the secondary appraisal, I judged that I lacked the time and resources to manage the demands effectively, which led me to experience distress instead of the more productive form of stress. In terms of coping, I retreated into avoidance, trying to suppress the stress instead of facing it head-on. I did not speak much about how I was feeling and avoided dealing with the emotional weight of the situation. 
Reflecting on Nina Nesdoly’s TED Talk, letting tension out, resonates with what I could have done differently. Emotion-focused coping can be a healthy outlet when used constructively. I now see that short breaks could have helped me regulate my emotions and stay more grounded. During that project, I allowed myself to become distracted and overloaded by updates and unnecessary details that added to the pressure. Applying a more problem-focused coping approach by prioritizing only the most essential information might have eased my mental load.
Her final point, lowering the barrier to entry, highlights how small, consistent self-care habits can make a big difference. I realize now that I didn’t need to wait for a perfect moment to decompress. A quick walk, a few deep breaths, or even a light conversation could have helped me manage the pressure more effectively throughout those intense six days.
Ultimately, this experience taught me that stress is inevitable in high-stakes situations, but how I respond to it makes all the difference. By incorporating both emotion-focused and problem-focused coping strategies, I am now more prepared to face future challenges with resilience, clarity, and control.
