The TED talk of choice is by Charles Hunt. It is titled What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience, and its link is https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qELiw_1Ddg. 

This TED talk discusses the significance of resilience in our lives. Hunt starts off with his background, setting the context for which resilience personally was, and is applied in his life. It was communicated that the unpleasant and even traumatic encounters one goes through in life are a rite of passage for establishing one’s tenacity, as they are the circumstances where resolve is tested. In contrary, smooth sailing situations were framed to be lacking in strengthening perseverance. It was claimed that there was nothing that within the latter that would inspire striving towards a better state, trauma is often a better opportunity for one to cultivate resilience. He highlights the value of having an “irrational” hope of emerging victorious that rejuvenates oneself in dark times. To supplement that, the perspective one has is crucial in influencing the responses one has. When accumulated, said responses create an outcome – positive or negative. Resilience is a transformative element in perspective that could alter life trajectories. Ultimately, trauma is a prerequisite for tenacity. 


The notion that difficult times are a breeding ground corresponds with content taught in the course. 

Hunt proclaims that adversity is where resilience is relevant, which coincide with Fletcher and Sakar (2013)’s sentiment of adversity being an indispensable component for resilience to be applied. Zhang et al. (2022) presented that resilience was a “process” in which distress was managed and tackled. Similarly, this idea is represented in Hunt’s speech, right from the start: “Resilience… is built through some of the most painful moments”. Furthermore, treacherous journeys are foundational to the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, which proposes that when trials and tribulation occur, one’s homeostasis is dysregulated, as Ong (2025) shares. From which, resilient integration, a possible resulting stage where the person has managed well with such events, gained insights and raised their homeostasis to a higher threshold, corroborates Hunt’s belief that “precisely because of” trauma, that one becomes better.

Both Hunt and the course material have emphasised adversity’s undeniability within the construction of resilience, which suggests its vitality. There is a dependent relationship between resilience and hardship. Resilience is inherently reliant on the presence of difficulty, and the active participation of the respective person within said hardship. Therefore, adversity is framed as a journey in which tenacity is to be developed, as an aftermath of persevering. The Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency posits that resilience has something that emerges from prior circumstances, and with Hunt leveraging on his personal experiences he deems excruciating, he doubles down and refines the parameter of prior circumstances to adversity. Adversity is not merely a factor for resilience, it is the basis on which it is created. Thus, the reliance of nurturing resilience based on the existence of trauma is underscored. That said, the focus of the talk might be too concentrated on the significance of resilience, a personal factor, without crediting other factors that play a part in moving past trauma and possibly work in conjunction with resilience, to lift a person back up on their feet after turbulent events. these factors include but are not limited to: access to support communities and resources to revitalise one’s spirits and master grit. Instead, Ungar (2013) advocates for a more holistic view of surmounting obstacles and tribulations, where various sources for support are leveraged on for support and resilience being one of them, instead of a sole contributor to overcoming hardship. 

As the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency establishes, I believe the connection of adversity to resilience is indeed valid and substantiated. 

My personal experience with resilience would certainly apply to coping with family dynamics and academic load in 2024, which have led me to find truth in the significance of Hunt’s beliefs about resilience and trauma. 

To be specific, dealing with the awkwardness, anger – residue of arguments with, and expectations of parents, whilst dealing with meeting the submission date for three assignments that fell on the same day was unprecedentedly packed and anguishing. In foresight, it had honed my resilience. Knowing my own emotional regulation skills and time management, it was a pressing period of time where both were really tested. However, it was because of it that my resilience to new experiences and challenges skyrocketed. I have faith in applying the same perseverance to weather distress, ideate and achieve success regardless. It attests to the value of adversity in spearheading resilience, which Seery et al. supplements  that it can be transferred to other aspects of our lives, facilitating enhanced outcomes in said aspects too. I believe I have a better endurance for academic pressure now, reflecting resilient reintegration as per the Metatheory as that used to be discomfort, but heavier academic workload is within my comfort level with discomfort now. That would be my definition of success from this experience. Those were not characteristics that were ingrained within me, prior to this experience. Personally, resilience comprises of being resistant to overwhelming negativity, striving for better days and taking action to actualise said better days. Had I not gone through that period, I would still possess lower resilience against adversity, aligning with the concept of difficult periods being a journey to establishing tenacity. This is supported by Seery et al. (2010), who found a directly proportionate relationship between trauma and perseverance. 

With an understanding of Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency and Hunt’s words, I can see that my experience is valuable, should I choose to leverage on it, which I did. This would be a good quality to take with me and make a conscious effort to further hone, so as to optimise and enhance other experiences and outcomes of endeavours I embark on. 

In conclusion, Hunt’s talk and the course content has elucidated that the origins of resilience is hardship, what it entails, how it ripples into future life and above all, how it has immense power to influence our lives – whether with, or the lack thereof.

Selected TED Talk : The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw)  
The TED talk is centered around building resilience in times of adversity which is something that all of us as humans have to go through at some point in our lives as mentioned by the speaker. She starts off by talking about how adversity does not discriminate and that there is a great need to build resilience within us so as to endure the various struggles in life and overcome them with an optimistic outlook on the future. Lucy mentions three different strategies that are really simple to put into practice and readily available for us all. The first is to acknowledge that suffering is a part of every human existence and this stops you from feeling discriminated against during tough times as you realize that the situation is not unique to you. Secondly, she talks about the fact that resilient people are really good at carefully selecting where they choose to channel their attention to. This means acknowledging situations that can be changed by our efforts and those that are out of our control. Lastly, Lucy mentions an important question that resilient people ask themselves which is “Is what I am doing helping or harming me”? Such a question puts one in control of his or her decision making and goes a long way in helping one to recover from a difficult situation.
The content of the TED talk fully aligns with what has been covered in the course on resilience. The TED talk begins with Lucy describing a life changing event which was the death of her daughter, daughter’s friend and the mother of the friend who was also Lucy’s close friend. By definition of the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR), this difficult life event caused a disruption in Lucy’s homeostasis (Richardson, 2002), causing her to deal with a newfound adversity. The speaker mentions that this adversity is also not an ordinary one as parental bereavement is widely recognized as the hardest loss to bear (Field and Behrman, 2003). 
She then goes on to say that all the supposed help in terms of advice and feedback that she received from social service groups only made her feel worse and this led her to formulate three key strategies that enabled her to ultimately find hope in such a tough situation and actively take part in the grieving process. These strategies are innate ones that positively shapes the individual’s mindset towards life and enables one to achieve resilient reintegration. 
To begin with, Lucy mentions that resilient individuals have to be brutally honest with themselves with respect to suffering as it is a part and parcel of life. Such a mindset allows one to no longer question oneself why such an event happened to him or her thereby preventing any possible feeling of discrimination. It also allows the individual to have a realistic view of life unlike the warped or distorted portrayal of life that is shown on social media (Samra et al., 2022). This also creates a sense of coherence in the individual whereby one is able to focus on the positive side of adversities in life. 
Secondly, Lucy mentions that resilient people are able to realistically appraise situations, which means that they acknowledge that there are situations that they can control and those that they cannot. As such, they choose to focus their attention and efforts on the former as nothing can be done about the latter since it is not in their power to change certain circumstances. Lucy also mentions negative emotions tend to naturally stick with us and threat focus and stress response is permanently dialed up for us humans in this modern day. This shows that it is important for us not to be fixated on situations that cannot be changed as that simply worsens our anxiety and increases our stress levels. Hence, the best we can do is to make use of cognitive flexibility and positive emotions to utilize challenging circumstances as opportunities for growth.

Lastly, Lucy states the most important of the three strategies based on client feedback that she received later on, which is to continually ask whether one’s actions are helping or harming oneself. She states that this is extremely important as it actively puts the individual in control of his or her decision making. Although the individual may not be able to control the event as in the case of the speaker, he or she is able to regain control over how to respond to the event which removes the initial feeling of powerlessness during traumatic events. This also promotes self-awareness as one may come to realize the harmful effects of unhealthy behaviors such as rumination and self-criticism and encourages self-compassion by choosing healthier choices to cope with the loss such as gratitude journaling or practicing various forms of self-care (Lacey, 2025). Thus, by utilizing this active coping strategy, individuals going through a rough period can develop a more optimistic outlook towards life. 
A personal experience of mine that I would like to share would be having to cope with the loss of my maternal grandmother while I was in Junior College. It was an extremely difficult period for me as prior to her death, I had flown to India to see her in the hospital, and it saddened me to see her in so much pain. I had booked my return tickets in advance and so was ready to leave when I heard the news of my grandmother’s passing on the way to the airport. It was such a shock to me as I never expected that her death was so imminent. It was made even worse as I realized that I along with my sister would be the only ones to miss her funeral as all my other relatives were staying back for it. I had come back to Singapore under the impression that I would not be able to promote to JC2 if I did not attempt my JC1 promotional examinations, which was what was communicated to me by my home tutor prior to leaving for India. It was only after I reached Singapore when she told me that I could in fact be promoted since I had done quite decently for my other JC1 examinations.
This made me really angry, and I started to question myself as to why this had to happen to me out of all people. It was hard for me to fully let go of this episode due to the constant rumination over what happened. I was only able to let go after praying about it, going to church for mass and confession and talking to my friends for support.
As I look back on this traumatic situation I had to go through, there are several things that I could have done to better understand and learn from the experience which are to implement the strategies laid out by Lucy. To begin with, instead of asking myself as to why this had to happen to me, I could have adopted a growth mindset and acknowledge that everyone has to go through tough times, and this is not something unique to myself. This would have enabled me to have an optimistic outlook and recover quicker from the difficult situation. To add on, it would have been useful to identify that this is a situation that is out of my control and what I can do is to focus on what I can control which is how I choose to respond to the situation and move forward in life. This would have enabled me to truly achieve “bouncebackability” in life (Foster, 2018). Lastly, by questioning myself as to whether what I am doing to cope with the situation is harming me or helping me, I could have realized the negative impacts of rumination much earlier and this would have enabled me to focus more on positive coping methods such as gratitude journaling.
To conclude, by implementing the three key strategies mentioned by Lucy in her TED talk, one would be able to face any and all forms of adversity in life and positively adapt to it which is resilience in action (Fletcher and Sarkar, 2013). By implementing the above-mentioned strategies, one would be able to achieve resilient reintegration and move ahead with life, knowing that what doesn’t kill truly makes you stronger.

(A)
Ted Talk Title: How to relieve stress when you're overwhelmed
YouTube Link: https://youtu.be/9G1zyFoAaMc?si=2Pi2cradI_5QVP1j
Speaker: Nina Nesdoly 
Summary:
	In her TED Talk, Nina introduced three key methods for relieving stress. The first key, “Let tension out,” involves physical activities such as exercising, journaling, meditation, and talking to a friend. These actions help release built-up tension and provide one with a break.  The second key is, “Limit information in”. With the constant influx of information in today’s digital age, it can quickly become overwhelming. Hence, Nina suggests limiting the amount of new information consumed to help reduce mental overload and stress. The last key is, “Lower the barrier to entry”. This key focuses on simplifying tasks to make it easier to build momentum and enhance productivity. With a smaller and more achievable task, it reduces the amount of stress one feels as the task will seem less overwhelming. 

(B)
	Study Unit 1 (Chapter 2) in the course explores the stress and recovery cycles, which closely align with the key themes in the TED talk. One key similarity between the course and the TED talk content is the shared focus on an example and definition of stress, and how it affects performance. The course notes define stress as “mental or emotional tension or strain,” a concept that was further brought to life through personal examples shared by my classmates during the Zoom session, highlighting the various sources of stress encountered in daily life. Nina had also begun her TED talk with her personal example of stress when she was studying for her bachelor’s degree and had two options: pushing through or going out to party. Despite her choosing the latter, she recounted how it resulted in her having better energy and being less stressed as she let tension out of her body, allowing her to focus on her work better. However, a difference between what was covered in the course and the TED talk was the negative effects of stress. Nina may not have covered it due to time constraints as she only spoke about her three key methods on how to relieve stress. In contrast, the course provided a more comprehensive overview of the importance of stress management. It highlighted negative effects such as reduced work/academic performance and poor quality of family and friends relationships. 

	In her three keys to relieve stress, Nina emphasises active strategies such as engaging in physical activities, limiting the amount of information in, and breaking down barriers to entry. It is worth noting that all three keys involve taking deliberate action. However, an alternative perspective highlights the importance of rest-based recovery methods, such as sleeping or napping, are equally or even more effective in reducing stress. For instance, a 2019 study conducted at a Saudi medical college found that sleep plays a crucial role in managing stress (Alotaibi et al., 2020). The study concluded that “poor sleep quality was significantly associated with elevated levels of stress” (Alotaibi et al., 2020). This posits that passive strategies are equally valuable in reducing stress. 

	Another alternative viewpoint is that maintaining a healthy diet can help to reduce stress and improve mental health. For example, a study found strong evidence that individuals who follow healthy eating habits, such as having a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins, experiences reduced symptoms of stress (Hill et al., 2021). This nutritional approach highlights how the quality of what is being consumed can influence stress levels, offering a different method to stress management.

	Overall, by incorporating healthy sleep habits and dietary choices alongside Nina’s three key techniques and the course materials, it allows individuals to adopt a more holistic approach in managing stress. As Nina’s strategies focus on active methods only, research suggests that other methods, such as quality sleep and a healthy diet, are effective too. This allows me to derive the conclusion that there is no one-size-fits-all solution to relieve stress, and instead, individuals should combine multiple strategies to be tailored to their unique needs to enhance their overall well-being and relieve stress. 

(C)
	Personally, one of the most stressful experiences I faced was during my preparation for my GCE “O” level examinations at 16 years old. The minimum requirements to enter a local polytechnic were to score 26 points and under and obtain a D7 in both English and Mathematics. At that point, my L1R4 score (one language subject and four relevant subjects) was above 26 points. Throughout the year, I experienced intense pressure from both my peers and family, which led to a buildup of stress and tension. I was sleeping less than five hours on school nights, which affected my ability to focus and significantly reduced my productivity. My stress levels peaked during the mid-year parent-teacher meeting, when my form teacher told my mother, “Rita is stagnant in her studies while all of her classmates are improving”. This moment heavily impacted me and stressed me further as my mother sent me to more tuition classes to improve my grades. 
	Looking back, I had coped with the stress by scrolling through social media and playing mobile games. However, as mentioned during Nina’s TED talk, this form of distraction may have added to my stress rather than relieving it. Her second key, “Limit information in,” highlights how new information can overwhelm the brain as I flooded it with more stimuli, making it harder to relax and focus. From the lens of the TED talk and the concepts covered in the course, it allows me to better understand and learn from that experience that I should have instead used relaxing and proactive strategies, such as exercising or resting to relieve stress. Moreover, I had also turned to overeating and eating unhealthy foods to relieve stress. This coping mechanism ended up having the opposite effect as I felt sluggish and bloated. I had also gained weight, leading to a decrease in my self-esteem and an increase in stress. Based on the alternative viewpoints and research as discussed in part B, my eating habits at that time were not helping me recover from stress but intensifying it. 

This reflection has helped me realise that some of the coping mechanisms I adopted previously were not beneficial, and in fact, were doing more harm than good. The course content on the stress-recovery cycle has deepened my understanding of how prolonged stress can lead to long-term health issues and decreased productivity. Therefore, it is important to learn and combine stress management strategies, such as Nina’s three key methods, adequate sleep, and a healthy diet, to support my mental well-being and relieve stress.

Essay:
(a) Introduction and Summary of the Selected TED Talk
For this essay, I have chosen to reflect on the TED Talk titled “The Three Secrets of Resilient People” by Dr Lucy Hone (2019), presented at TEDxChristchurch. Youtube link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw. 

Drawing from her academic research and the tragic loss of her 12-year-old daughter, Abi, Dr Hone (2019) outlined three strategies that resilient individuals employ to navigate adversity. The first is to accept that adversity is an inevitable part of life. The second is to focus on what can be changed rather than dwelling on circumstances beyond control. The third is to pause and ask whether one’s thoughts or actions are promoting well-being or adding to one’s distress. This reflective practice aims to promote choices that support healing and personal growth. Dr Hone (2019) concludes by emphasising that resilience is not an innate trait but a skill anyone can learn and develop, albeit it is not easy to do so.

(b) Discussion on the TED Talk
Resilience is defined by the online Oxford dictionary as “the capacity to recover quickly from
difficulties; toughness” (Robertson & Cooper, 2013). It is widely researched and taught, as demonstrated in both Dr Hone’s TED Talk and the Peak Performance course (Hone, 2019; Ong, 2025). Upon reflection, the insights from both sources appear to be closely aligned. 

Firstly, both sources address the importance of acknowledging adversity as a foundational aspect of resilience. Adversity refers to a difficult or unpleasant situation, typically involving hardship, misfortune or significant challenge (Seery et al., 2013). Dr Hone’s (2019) first strategy involves “know[ing] that suffering is part of every human existence,” which prevents a person from “feeling discriminated against when the tough times come.” A similar point is made in the course content, which highlights that everyone, regardless of status or occupation, faces adversity and that it is necessary to build resilience (Ong, 2025). Hence, both sources agree that adversity is unavoidable and that recognising this fact helps individuals shift from a victim mindset to one of agency and growth.

Secondly, both sources encourage shifting one’s focus as a way to remain resilient. Dr Hone’s (2019) second strategy highlights that “resilient people (...) have a habit of realistically appraising situations and typically managing to focus on the things they can change and somehow accept the things that they can’t.” This aligns with the course’s teaching on positive adaptation (Ong, 2025). Adaptability refers to the “capacity to adjust thoughts, behaviours, and emotions in response to changing or uncertain circumstances” (Martin et al., n.d., as cited in Fullerton, Zhang, & Kleitman, 2021). Positive adaptation thus involves reframing situations to maintain psychological well-being (Ong, 2025). Therefore, both sources advocate for the change of perspective in order to cope with adversity effectively.

Finally, both sources emphasise the significance of self-reflection in building resilience. Dr Hone’s (2019) third strategy involves asking, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” This encourages individuals to evaluate their thoughts and actions and make changes that support their well-being. Similarly, the course introduced the concept of sense of coherence, which is associated with resilience. It “promote[s] the ability to make sense of life’s challenges and how they can contribute to positive growth,” which is a process that likewise requires ongoing self-reflection (Ong, 2025). Thus, both sources highlight that resilience involves cultivating inward awareness and thoughtful reflection.

These three resilience strategies not only align with the course teachings but are also supported by numerous studies (Falon, Kangas, & Crane, 2021). For instance, they are integral to the Skills-Based Model of Personal Resilience. A feasibility study involving trainee psychological well-being practitioners found that applying the model led to notable improvements in resilience (Nelson, 2019, as cited in Baker, Baker, & Burrell, 2021). This proves the value of the strategies.

However, these strategies are not without limitations. Jones and colleagues (2013) argue that “centring the processes of resilience available to an individual in the face of systemic-level problems like racism is insufficient.” In the context of this discussion, encouraging acceptance, shifting of focus and self-reflection places emphasis on internal processes. An overemphasis on inward focus may unintentionally dismiss or downplay systemic barriers such as discrimination or injustice (Derickson, 2016; Holtmann et al., 2023; Jones et al., 2013). Therefore, while the aforementioned resilience strategies are valuable, they must be applied with sensitivity to context and supported by external resources when necessary.

(c) Reflection and Personal Experience
Dr Hone’s (2019) three strategies reminded me of a personal experience that cultivated my resilience. I once worked with an elderly patient who had experienced significant functional decline and was assessed by the medical team to need a caregiver. As a Senior Social Work Assistant in the hospital, I was responsible for ensuring she had the necessary post-discharge support. Given that she was living alone and had no informal social support, I explored formal care options, such as residential services. However, despite several attempts to explain the risks, she rejected all available options. Over time, I felt emotionally exhausted and defeated and began to question whether I was making any meaningful difference.
Now, having learned more about resilience through Dr Hone’s TED Talk and the course, I can better make sense of my experience. At the time, I internalised my patient’s resistance as a reflection of inadequacy. In hindsight, I came to recognise through Dr Hone’s (2019) first strategy and the course material (Ong, 2025) that setbacks like this are a normal part of the professional experience. This reframing allowed me to shift from self-blame to understanding the limits of my role, which is a perspective I intend to carry into future practice. 

Dr Hone’s (2019) second strategy and the course’s teaching on positive adaptation resonate with how I navigated this situation. Rather than giving in to frustration, I acted within my area of control. I sought supervision, tried different communication styles and collaborated with the medical team. Eventually, my patient agreed to hire a helper. While I already applied the second strategy in practice, it feels affirming to understand positive adaptation in theory.

Finally, Dr Hone’s (2019) reflective question, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” would have been a helpful tool at the time, as I had been holding onto negative thoughts and emotions. The course’s emphasis on the sense of coherence also enabled me to understand that such challenges can serve as opportunities for growth and professional development (Ong, 2025). For instance, I now feel more equipped to manage similar situations in my work. As such, this experience has made me more willing to embrace challenges.

To conclude, I have a renewed appreciation for what I have learned from both sources thus far. This is further reinforced by a literature review on resilience in health disciplines, which recommended that “resilience theory should be part of the educational content and taught in a way that promotes reflection and application in order to give students strength, focus and endurance in the workplace” (McAllister & McKinnon, 2009).

Essay:
The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)
Resilience can be Trained
The speaker starts off by establishing the fact that everybody has had bad experiences at some point in their life, contrary to the false image often portrayed on social media. She shared on her personal journey, on how she coped with her traumatic experience and proposed three strategies that helped her through it. In gist, the speaker suggests that resilient people are generally good at accepting that bad things happen to everyone, selecting where to focus their attention on and having the metacognitive ability to self-reflect and make better choices. Rather than focusing on the things that cannot be changed, resilient people are able to weigh their options and objectively decide the best course of action. Instead of dwelling on the things they had lost, they are able to lean into their social support and be grateful for what they still have. The speaker suggests that resilient people were not born this way. Instead, their willingness to think outside the box is crucial in the shifting of mindsets to deal with the undesirable circumstances they may face in life.
Strategies for Resilience
The sharing by Lucy Hone on the secrets of resilient people is generally relevant and targeted to most, if not all, populations of different cultures and contexts. The sharing focuses on the strategies that are readily available for the public to use at anytime and anywhere but does not claim that it is by any means easy. The overarching message aligns well with the course content, signalling the notion that perceptions and mindsets matter more than the actual circumstances themselves.
There are numerous factors that can contribute to greater resilience, but the few that really shone through in this sharing was cognitive flexibility, optimism and social support (Kunzler et al., 2020). An example of a cognitive flexibility exercise is to identify negative thoughts and replace them with positive or more useful thoughts (Ludolph et al., 2019). Lucy mentions that terrible things happen to everybody, and it is a personal decision whether to wallow in despair or to start moving on. The experiment conducted by Martin Seligman in 2005 was brought up during the sharing as an example of how optimism can help increase levels of happiness and gratitude while decreasing the symptoms of depression, proving once again how powerful the mind can be. Social support from family and friends was specifically mentioned by the author as an important aspect to be grateful for and is one of the critical motivating factors for people to strive for a meaningful life. 
Regrettably, not all the highlighted resilience factors can apply to all contexts, especially in the case of social support. As mentioned in the journal by Sundström, Blomqvist, and Edberg (2021), the aging population is on the rise worldwide which may eventually lead to challenges in combating loneliness. However, the loneliness epidemic does not only apply to older people. As suggested by Patulny and Bower (2022), global phenomenon such as the COVID-19 pandemic led to the rapid technological advancements as well as the increase in digital interactions using tools like social media, which can allow people to be more interconnected than ever before. However, this predictably had a part to play in the decrease in in-person interactions, hence the mixed results with regards to recent studies on technologies’ influence on loneliness. Recent studies conducted by countries worldwide provide worrying results (Kannan and Veazie, 2023).
In conclusion, the author’s message is widely applicable to the masses and the proposed strategies are convenient to use to help as many people as she can. It was an effective and meaningful sharing that will hopefully be able to reach the intended audience and help people from all walks of life. 
Personal Reflection on Resilience
As I am an Army regular in the SAF, my job scope often involves the usage of heavy machinery, and I clearly remember this incident where one of my subordinates got seriously injured during one of the local training exercises. A small portion of his ring finger had been severed off and the tip of the bone was visible. 
At the scene, I think I did well to remain calm and gave instructions for his evacuation to the hospital while trying to calm him down, but the true test of resilience came after the whole debacle was over. Though investigations revealed that it was his own fault for not following safety procedures, I cannot help but think if there was anything more that I could have done to prevent this from happening and how would I explain the situation to his family members in a way that is acceptable to them.
In hindsight, the crucial factors that helped me to get through was exactly the resilience strategies mentioned in the TED talk by Lucy Hone. Firstly, case studies of previous injuries are shared often in my industry for learning purposes and to increase safety awareness. Thus, I had no qualms believing that bad things happen to everyone, not just me. As a matter of fact, the actual victim was not me and many other colleagues and superiors were also affected in some way even though they were not physically at the scene. The environment I was working in covered the first secret of resilience mentioned in the TED talk, which was the ability to accept that terrible things happen without discrimination.
The second strategy is about focusing attention on what I can control rather than what I cannot. Initially, negative thoughts like “could I have done more?” and “is this my fault?” filled my mind, affecting my ability to perform at work. Fortunately for me, I had many peers around me that checked on me, asking if I need any help. The abundance of social support snapped me out of the spiral early and enabled me to focus my attention on looking ahead and to do what I can, instead of dwelling on what has already happened. This was mentioned in the TED talk as the second strategy and a vital skill for resilience, but in my case, I received quick and ample assistance from my social support, so I am not sure how long would I need to take to be able to snap out of it by myself if I am left to my own devices. 
In relation to the last strategy, the idea of asking myself whether what I am doing or going to do will lead to a desirable outcome before execution seemed to me like something that we are constantly doing subconsciously. Weighing the pros and cons of making simple daily choices like whether to give in to the desire for an extra snack or to stay disciplined in our weight loss plan is one such example. Conversely, I feel that this strategy will work better as a reminder rather than trying to forcefully apply it to every single decision. For instance, we can put up this message as one of the motivational quotes around the workplace in poster form or even just using post-it notes, to trigger people’s thoughts in hopes of bringing someone out of the negative spiral in the future. This initiative can be especially useful to help those who may not be as inclined to seek help or those lacking in social support.
In conclusion, watching the TED talk and reflecting on my experiences provided me with plenty of insights regarding resilience. I had always thought that working in the high-risk environment automatically meant that I had built up a certain level of resilience and I will be able to handle any situation, but it was eye-opening to be humbled during this incident. Reflecting on this, I found that gaining the knowledge to be able to identify exactly what contributes to greater resilience, what are some ways to maintain resilience as well as what does it mean to emerge stronger from the challenges faced in life will certainly be beneficial as I face future challenges, as I continue to strive towards more resilient reintegration (Richardson, 2003).

Essay:
My chosen TEDx Talk featured a personal story of resilience shared by Dr. Lucy Hone, a research and leading expert on resilience who experienced devastating tragedy and profound grief following a fatal car accident involving her twelve-year-old daughter, Abby, Abby’s best friend, Ella, and Ella’s mother, Sally. Drawing upon her research and her own journey through grief, she identified three core strategies, or “secrets”, used by resilient people in the face of adversity. The first secret is acknowledging that difficult things happen in life, accepting reality rather than fighting against it. The second is the ability to choose our focus by intentionally directing our attention away from unhelpful thoughts or circumstances. The third strategy involves asking ourselves the practical questions, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?”, which encourages meta-cognition (TEDx Talks, 2019). Through these strategies, resilience can be understood as the capacity to actively navigate adversities, suggesting that it is a learned ability rather than an inherent trait. 
Lucy Hone’s three strategies or “secrets” of resilient demonstrate notable alignment and connection with many key concepts on resilience and stress presented in the course, such as the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR), the Transactional Model of Stress (TMS), and concepts of coping with adversity as reviewed by Kunzler et al. (2002). 
Lucy’s first secret emphasises the need for acceptance of adversity and suffering as inevitable realities of life aligns with the core premise MRR, which sees resilience as a process initiated by disruption to homeostasis caused by stressors or adversities (Richardson, 2002). In reality, resilience is studied and occurs in the contexts of adversity (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2012; Leppin et al., 2014; Ungar, 2018), thus, acceptance of suffering is acknowledging the necessary condition for the resilience process to begin according to this metatheory. This acceptance strategy is also a key prerequisite for realistically appraising demands and resources in addressing any adversity, which aligns itself with the appraisal component of the TMS (Biggs et al., 2017), as it can be seen as the foundational stance that can influence initial appraisals. Accepting that bad things can happen prepares a person for potentially appraising stimuli as threatening without falling into denial. This first secret also aligns well with the understanding that resilience is shown despite significant stress as Kunzler et al. (2002) list “acceptance” as a component of cognitive flexibility, which is a well-evidenced modifiable psychosocial resilience factor. Hence, given the above alignments, the first secret serves as the groundwork for making resilience possible through grounding individuals in the reality of a situation and pushes back against the idea that resilient people are simply lucky or avoid problems. 
The second secret involves acknowledging the negative while consciously seeking out positive aspects or moments in difficult experiences. One suggestion from Lucy is to do a daily gratitude practice of listing three good things (TEDx Talks, 2019). This secret aligns with the MRR’s emphasis that growth can happen during the resilience process and its idea of finding meaning and purpose in disruptions (Richardson, 2002). Proactively seeking out positive aspects in one's reality contributes to resilient reintegration, which increases the baseline of homeostasis and nurtures beneficial characteristics (Ong, 2025). This secret ties strongly with the TMS as it is a direct application of cognitive appraisal described in this model (Biggs et al., 2017). Although an initial appraisal might identify a threat, this secret helps to reappraise an event by actively searching for potentially positive aspects. It also ties strongly to the concept of Cognitive Flexibility as positive reappraisal is included as a key factor in coping; this directing of attention helps manage the emotional response to stressors (Kunzler et al., 2020). I think that this secret operationalises the idea that attitude and focus greatly influences navigating stress and adversity. It moves beyond passive endurance towards proactive meaning-making and the building of internal-resources.
The final secret is an encouragement of introspective and self-examination of one’s state of being and actions in response to adversity with the aim to regain control. This aligns itself with the choice stage in the MRR’s second wave (Ong, 2025) as after disruption and readiness for reintegration, an individual must choose how they will reintegrate. Lucy’s suggested question helps inform that choice by evaluating the efficacy of one’s current responses. It aligns with MRR’s focus on “practical paradigms” to increase personal agency and choice (Richardson, 2002). Aligning the TMS, this secret being a meta-level evaluation of coping strategy, prompts a conscious assessment of whether one’s current coping approach is adaptive or maladaptive. This corresponds to the TMS assertion that appraisal initiates coping strategies to manage emotions or stressors (Biggs et al., 2017). This self-examination is an act of active coping itself as it involves directly addressing stressors and managing emotions (Kunzler et al., 2020). This is a practical tool for self-regulation that increases the agency of individuals facing adversity, shifting individuals from being passive recipients of stress to proactive participants in shaping their experiences and response, which echo the process-oriented and modifiable nature of resilience and coping taught in this course. 
I have chosen Dr Lucy Hone’s TEDx Talk as the content for review in this assignment because of how her experience resonated with my recent personal journey with grief, distress and resilience. I was able to relate to Lucy’s loss with the loss of my elder brother through a violent and unnatural death in late 2024. This occurrence threw my whole being, daily routines and relationships off-balance, into a state of immense distress. This experience is reflected and described by the TMS where the demands to meet the diverse and wide-ranging difficulties became overwhelming, leading to enormous levels of stress. With these stressors, I experienced acutely the disruption to my state of homeostasis, as set out in MRR (Richardson, 2002), pushing me into alien and difficult circumstances, leading to instability in major aspects of my life — emotionally, psychologically, physically and socially. However, with the passing of the initial shock, came awareness of both internal and external resources available to me for responding constructively to my circumstances. It is here the TMS also offered insight where the initial demand outweighs my perceived coping resources, yet through activating my internal strengths, such as personal faith and habits of self-reflection, and external support from friends, church and mentors, I was able to regain a sense of agency and hope gradually. 
Relating to Lucy Hone’s first secret of accepting suffering as part of life’s reality helped me to normalise my grief rather than resisting it. This acceptance allowed me to bear and abide with my grief and distress with patience and self-kindness, which made a reframing of perspective that relates to the second and third secret possible. The second secret of being intentional about where to focus my attention in life is a lifeline. I was able to reframe my mind by intentionally choosing to remember my late-brother's kindness and legacy rather than to be consumed by the trauma of losing him. Lastly, the third secret’s question to ask “Is what I am doing helping or harming me?”, has been immensely helpful in anchoring my self-reflection to examine how I responded to thoughts, conversations, relationships, and daily-living while navigating this healing process. 
This experience of grief and distress, and the course content have taught me, and continues to teach me, that resilience is not about avoiding pain, but choosing to grow in the presence of pain. My personal journey of grief is not a deviation from performance or well-being but a crucible where resilience and compassion can be forged.

(A)How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal
In the TED Talk, Kelly McGonigal (2013) challenged the common belief that stress is harmful, arguing that its negative effects are largely contributed by how we perceive it. She supported this claim with a study showing a correlation between higher mortality rates and the belief that stress is bad for one’s health. She also referenced another study suggesting that reappraising stress responses—such as viewing the fight-or-flight reaction as helpful for addressing challenges—can reduce anxiety, increase confidence, and improve performance. She interpreted that the correlation could be explained by the physiological changes observed in the participants who reappraised their stress; they had more relaxed blood vessels despite elevated heart rates. Finally, she concluded the talk with three pieces of advice on managing stress while building resilience: (1) connect and help others, (2) reframe how we interpret stress, and (3) pursue meaningful options over easy convenience options.
(B)Discussion on TED Talk 
McGonigal promoted the approach-focused coping strategy, specifically the emotional-focused approach i.e. the stress reappraisal intervention and discouraged avoidance-focused coping strategy. This aligns with the course materials, which also favour approach-focused strategies. These strategies are also supported by Jamieson et al. (2012), study cited by McGonigal, where individuals who were instructed to reappraise stress outperformed those who were told to reorient their attention away from the stress instead.
However, the TED Talk and the course materials differed in their specific instructions and views on stress responses. McGonigal specified how acute stress responses can be beneficial from a physiological standpoint. For example, a racing heart and quickened breathing are signs of energy and readiness rather than signs of failure. On the contrary, the course materials only mention the negative side-effects of what is presumably chronic stress. 
As McGonigal claimed, the reappraisal method has been shown to be effective, though mainly for acute stress (Keller et al., 2012; Jamieson et al., 2012). She has overlooked the effectiveness of the reappraisal strategy for chronic stress and the mechanism behind the strategy. This is crucial because chronic stress is equally, if not more, harmful than acute stress.
The first essential aspect she has overlooked is that stress responses can occur independently of a person’s perception and reframing the stress response is only applicable when the response is clearly noticeable at the moment. Thus, the strategy is applicable to acute stress, as the typical physiological signs of distress are visible or obvious to oneself when the body starts to operate at a significantly faster pace. The strategy however falls short for less detectable yet gradual and prolonged effects of chronic stress, such as aches, pains, decrease in energy, social isolation, disrupted sleep patterns, impaired concentration, substance abuse, changes in emotional reactivity, and emotional withdrawal (Liu et al., 2019; Yale Medicine, 2019). Additionally, such symptoms of chronic stress are difficult to be spun off as beneficial when they impair a person’s daily interactions and performance, and their prolonged effects can harm immune (Alotiby, 2024; Niharika et al., 2024), cardiovascular (Hinterdobler et al., 2021), and cognitive health (Girotti et al., 2024). 
Secondly, she did not address the mechanism behind the reappraisal process. A meta-analysis of the efficacy of stress reappraisal interventions by Liu et al. (2019) found that reappraisal intervention is more likely to be effective for active stressors (i.e. acute stressors) than for passive stressors (i.e. chronic stressors). Additionally, significant variations in scores were found among the samples for both active and passive stressors; indicating differences in stress-handling abilities. These differences are further supported by a study by Perchtold et al. (2017), which found that a person’s ability to generate quality reappraisal is associated with a specific pattern of brain activation, particularly left-lateralized activity. The complexity of the reappraisal intervention and stress was further highlighted by a study on military veterans with Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, where successful cognitive reappraisal is found to be associated with a person’s emotional clarity—the ability to accurately identify and understand one’s emotions at the moment (Boden et al., 2012). Therefore, reappraisal is not a mere act of reframing the stress response; it involves complex workings of the brain that are beyond our direct control, though some aspects that can be accessed through practices such as emotional mindfulness (Boden et al., 2012).
In conclusion, McGonigal’s claim was partially true as stress reappraisal intervention is an effective approach for managing acute stress. However, she has oversimplified the relationship between stress and the reappraisal by failing to address chronic stress and the actual complexity of the reappraisal process.
(C)Reflection
The most memorable acute stress episode I had was during a group presentation in my first semester at the Singapore University of Social Science. That was memorable because I had not experienced such a severe anxiety attack before. Despite believing that I was well-prepared and that it was an ungraded class activity, I found myself shaking, short of breath, and my voice faltering during the presentation. In the end, I could not finish my presentation and I had to hand over the remaining slide to my groupmate.
At the time, I perceived these physiological symptoms as signs that I was failing under pressure and believed that something was wrong with me. I suspected that a part of me has weakened over the years as I had never experienced such an intense reaction in the past. However, after watching Kelly McGonigal’s TED Talk and reading the course materials, I began to reinterpret that event with more clarity and understanding.
McGonigal’s talk helped me understand that my racing heart and quickened breath were my body’s way of preparing for a challenge, not signs of incompetence. If I had been able to reframe my view on my physical reactions in that moment—as signs that my body was getting ready to perform—I might have been more confident and could have been able to recompose myself.
This aligns with the emotion-focused approach strategy discussed both in McGonigal’s talk and the course materials, where individuals reframe their emotions to change their impact. McGonigal specifically supported the reappraisal strategy, which Jamieson et al. (2012) found to be effective in improving performance under acute stress.
However, my experience also highlights the limitations of reappraisal if not practiced beforehand. According to my research, reappraisal is not simply a thought pattern—it involves emotional clarity, brain activation patterns, and contextual factors that influence whether the strategy can be accessed right at the moment. In my case, lack of prior experience in managing public speaking anxiety resulted in poor emotional clarity and made it more difficult for me to apply reappraisal effectively. 
In hindsight, it would be beneficial for me to expose myself to more stress-inducing scenarios where I can practice stress reappraisal deliberately. Additionally, mindfulness-intervention techniques such as meditation and journaling, which enhance emotional clarity, may help me to better regulate my emotions during future high-pressure moments. 
In summary, this experience has help me understand the true nature of the stress response during acute stress. The course materials and McGonigal’s TED Talk have helped me recognise that such stress response is not a sign of failure, but a signal that my body is gearing me up for the challenge— and that with the right strategies, I can turn anxiety into my advantage.

Summary
The TED talk I have selected is How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc). The TED talk highlights three keys of stress relief . Firstly, letting out tension. One can engage in activities that may involve physically extracting something from our bodies, such as words and sweat, as doing so relieves the tension in our body. Secondly, limiting information by taking a break from the Internet and social media platforms. Doing so can also prevent social comparison, which may lead to dissatisfaction with one’s life and increased stress levels. Lastly, lowering the entry barrier. One can come up with easier and more accessible ways to relieve stress, making it seem less of a burden and encouraging individuals to follow through with stress-relieving behaviours, rather than continue to complete tasks despite experiencing significant stress.

Evaluation of the TED talk content
The key points of the TED talk are supported by various research and offer accessible techniques for stress relief. However, it may oversimplify the relationship between stress and information consumption, and overlook individuals experiencing prolonged or severe stress.
Firstly, Nesdoly highlights how information overload from excessive media consumption and social media comparison can lead to increased stress. This is consistent with research which has found that high levels of social media usage is associated with high levels of negative emotions and stress, due to exposure to negative content online (Taskin et al., 2024). Various studies have also shown that online social comparison leads to distress, lower self-esteem and dissatisfaction with one’s life (Liu et al., 2017; Ojha et al., 2021; Robinson et al., 2019). However, this perspective can be criticised for oversimplifying the association between stress and consumption of information. While excessive information consumption may have negative consequences on one’s stress level, information consumption can be an effective stress relief method. During the COVID-19 pandemic, activities on social media platforms, such as consuming content made by others, helped users regulate stress and negative emotions (Bae, 2023). Hence, information consumption is not always detrimental, and it can lead to either positive or negative impacts depending on not just the quantity of information consumed, but also the quality of information consumed. 
Nesdoly’s other two keys of stress relief, lowering the entry barrier and letting out tension, are closely linked to approach coping (Ong, 2025). Lowering the entry barrier to stress relief by simplifying stress-relieving activities highlights the actions taken by individuals to improve their situation. A study has found that workers who experience high work-related stress in the intellectual disability sector face barriers, such as difficulty taking time off to access mental health care (Carter et al., 2025). Similarly, when individuals are feeling overwhelmed, they may struggle to engage in complex stress relief strategies. Hence, it is crucial to lower the entry barrier to stress relief and empower individuals to take small steps to relieve stress. However, it is important to note that prolonged or severe stress is associated with increased vulnerability for procrastination, and simpler coping strategies may still be overwhelming for people under such circumstances (Sirois, 2023).
Additionally, Nesdoly’s point on letting out tension aligns closely with emotion focused coping (Ong, 2025). This point is well-founded as it aligns with research on the significance of expressive support coping, which refers to individuals engaging in social interactions to seek advice and support, during the COVID-19 pandemic for the alleviation of stress and negative emotions of individuals (Bae, 2023). Furthermore, activities like journaling and expressive writing have been found to have positive effects on life satisfaction, relationships with others, and mental health aspects like anxiety and burnout, reducing stress (Lukenda et al., 2024). 
Overall, the TED talk’s three keys to stress relief are generally well-backed by research, and reflect various concepts taught in the course, such as emotion focused coping and approach coping, highlighting the validity of Nesdoly’s points. However, a more holistic view of stress relief can be achieved by incorporating both the positive and negative impacts of information consumption, as well as recognising the challenges faced by individuals experiencing severe or prolonged stress.

My personal experience with stress
I experienced significant stress during my first semester at SUSS. As a freshman, I did not know what to expect for my workload, and took on too many commitments. At the time, my part-time job required me to work at least three days a week and additionally, I was involved in volunteering events for most weekends. I also joined the Public Safety and Security Interest Group and was required to plan and attend many events. These commitments, together with academic responsibilities, made me feel overwhelmed. Furthermore, I was unable to spend much time with my loved ones due to my packed schedule, reducing accessibility to social support, which is a key strategy for stress relief as highlighted in Nesdoly’s point on letting out tension.
Initially, I ignored the stress and hoped that it would be alleviated when I eventually adapt to my hectic schedule. This parallels problem focused-avoidance coping, which refers to when people ignore the problem they are facing (Ong, 2025). However, my fatigue persisted, making me realise that ignoring the causes of my stress was ineffective. Hence, I adopted problem focused-approach coping by being proactive and quitting my part-time job. Instead, I took on flexible event-based jobs that fit my schedule. I also learnt to set aside time for social interaction and leisure. These changes gave me a sense of control over my situation and tasks. Additionally, I reached out to my close friends for emotional support and advice on how to better manage my commitments. This parallels emotion focused-approach coping, and the encouragement and advice I received made me realise the importance of letting out tension, as highlighted by Nesdoly, as social support helped me restore a sense of control over my life and lowered my stress.
Reflecting on this experience, I recognise that I could have tried to relieve stress using the other two keys of stress relief highlighted by Nesdoly — limiting information and lowering the entry barrier. Frequent notifications from Canvas, group chats and emails led to constant exposure to  information regarding my modules and assignments. This was a possible stressor as information overload could have overwhelmed my cognitive capacity and distracted me from effectively completing my tasks. Taking breaks from my phone could have allowed me to gain some mental space, enhancing my ability to concentrate on my tasks. Moreover, I could have considered lowering the entry barrier to stress relief. During that stressful period, I felt that taking time off for my hobbies or arranging to meet up with my loved ones would add to my burden. However, I failed to realise that I could have chosen simpler methods to relieve stress, such as listening to music or arranging a quick call with my friends to seek advice and share my concerns. I will keep in mind Nesdoly’s point on lowering the entry barrier to stress relief as I have come to realise that failing to simplify coping strategies into more accessible forms can end up detering me from engaging in stress relief completely.
Overall, my experience with stress during my first semester at SUSS made me realise the importance of active coping strategies that address the problem or attempt to deal with negative emotions. Moving forward, I aim to apply what I have learnt from this course and the three key stress relief strategies from the TED talk more intentionally to my future experiences with stress.

Essay:
Title and speaker of the TED talk: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone
Resilience expert Lucy Hone delivers a moving message shaped by academic research and personal tragedy, the sudden death of her 12-year-old daughter. She shared three key strategies that resilient people consciously adopt to navigate adversity. Resilient individuals understand that suffering is an inevitable part of life. Rather than asking, “Why me?” they change their perspective to “Why not me?” Recognising that adversity is universal and not personal injustice fosters emotional resilience and avoids self-victimization. They are deliberate about where to direct their attention and consciously seek out positives and gratitude even amidst pain and however minor. It acts as a beacon of hope. They focus on what they can change and let go of what they cannot. It helps them avoid dwelling on negativity and uncontrollable circumstances. They ask themselves: “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” This straightforward yet impactful question empowers them to be resilient by giving them agency over their healing process.
Hone’s talk offers a concise and pragmatic approach. Her central premise emphasises that resilience is not an innate trait but a set of learnable skills and behaviours. Her talk serves as a powerful and heartfelt reminder that while pain is unavoidable, our response determines our capacity to heal and grow.. Through deliberate actions, habits, and mindst, we can cultivate resilience and find strength even in the darkest times. Her message reflects the definition of resilience as “the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioural flexibility.” Her personal story exemplifies resilient reintegration, a concept from Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency, where individuals appear stronger after adversity. Her deliberate emphasis on self-control and introspection aligns with ideas of self-awareness, cognitive flexibility, and positive emotion focus. She chose to confront and manage her loss. The work of Fletcher & Sarkar (2013) echoes these tactics, pointing out that high-achieving people frequently use them to deal with stress and hardship. Hone chooses to be an active participant in her grieving journey taking deliberate steps in managing her grief, instead of an over-fixation on unchangeable events, maintained hope and finding a meaning in her work. She paused to reflect before reacting. Benefit-finding and the principle of positive reappraisal shows that reframing is a critical element. 
While Hone’s talk is empowering and grounded, its individual-centred view warrants criticisms. Her emphasis on personal choice and mindset overlooks systemic and socio-economic constraints limiting a person’s capacity.  People from disadvantaged backgrounds face stressors, such as poverty, racism, or unstable families, that cannot be mitigated by mindset.  It underplays external and structural challenges and not all individuals have equal access to the resources, such as social support and financial security . Ungar (2011) poses that resilience is not only shaped by internal traits or behaviours but influenced by external environments. Masten (2018) argues in Ordinary Magic that access to relationships, community infrastructure and social safety nets are often more predictive of resilience than individual effort. In a nutshell, Hone’s talk is compelling, emotionally resonant, and are helpful but neglects broader social and cultural factors. It is crucial to consider social and systemic factors to allow for a holistic, inclusive and broader understanding to avoid pitfall of framing resilience solely as a personal responsibility. Despite this, her approach supports the central message that resilience is not something we are born with — it is something we can cultivate. 
A defining test of my resilience occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic when my family faced financial instability. My father, the sole breadwinner, lost his income due to business closures, forcing my mother, who has been a full-time homemaker, to renter the workforce. As a junior college student preparing for national exams, I took on weekend part-time work to help out. This upheaval means sacrificing dance classes due to costs, losing social connection with friends, and giving up personal time once spent watching shows or playing games, leaving me juggling academics, work, and home responsibilities with little rest and support. The pressure was overwhelming. Over time, the chronic stress and unrelenting demands led to exhaustion and burnout. I became unmotivated and slipped into depression, functioning mechanically, while masking my turmoil. It wasn’t until stability returned that I realise the weight I had been carrying. Even now, I am still in recovery, learning to balance resilience and compassion with therapy and medications. Some days are better than others and I learnt to be kinder to myself and those around me. 
The course and talk illuminate my experience through the lens of resilience and reminded me that healing is not linear. With Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory of Resilience, I understand that the pandemic shattered my psychological homeostasis. I experienced reintegration with loss. I coped functionally but felt emotionally drained.  Over time, with intentional changes, I moved toward resilient reintegration, I prioritised self-care and gradually regained and purpose.  Hone’s message that “resilient people know that suffering is part of life” reframed my pain. I viewed my struggles as a personal weakness and felt life was unfair. It deepened my isolation. Hone’s perspective normalised hardship and reduced the internal stigma I had. Her second strategy, focusing on what is still good, is a mindset I am working to cultivate. During the crisis, I fixated on losses: financial stability, time, joy. I failed to see what remained – my family, my friends, my education. Hone’s emphasis on benefit finding, echoed through concepts like cognitive flexibility, helped me retrospectively recognised the overlooked positives. Balancing grief with gratitude may not have eliminated the pain, but it could have softened its emotional intensity. The most profound takeaway was Hone’s third principle, asking “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” Had I asked myself this during that period, I might have recognised that bottling up emotions, working through sleepless nights, and ignoring my mental health were doing more harm than good. The focus on self-awareness and emotional regulation are skills I lacked, but which I am now trying to actively build. The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping clarified how my initial stress response was shaped by my appraisal of the situation and my perceived lack of coping mechanism. Instead of avoiding and insisting on pushing through without help, the approach of seeking understanding and integrating self-care shifted my perspective and reinterpret the situation.
I have come to know that resilience does not mean being strong all the time. It involves vulnerability, rest, and courage. Failure is not a weakness but a catalyst for change. Emotional regulation is a skill, not a flaw. Resilience does not mean relentless perseverance. It is not a destination I have not reached but a skill I am developing. I once saw resilience as solitary endurance but now, it is a dynamic interplay of mindset, regulation, self-compassion, and self-awareness. I am not fully there yet, but with the tools I have gained, it empowered me to approach future challenges with greater flexibility, knowing that resilience is not about avoiding breakdowns but learning to rebuild with wisdom and grace.

Essay:
Title: What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience 
Speaker of the TED talk: Charles Hunt 
Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qELiw_1Ddg


Executive summary
Charles Hunt opened his TED Talk by sharing his tough upbringing in a drug-abusive and crime-prone environment with limited economic opportunities, setting the stage for a moving narrative on resilience and the journey of overcoming adversity. 
According to Hunt, the key to resilience lies in the mind. Particularly, a proper perspective and attitude that empowers one to overcome negative changes. He placed greater emphasis on negative changes, noting that it is often more difficult to navigate than positive changes. This is due to the emotional responses such changes evoke. Additionally, he emphasised that while disruptions are often beyond our control, we have the power to choose how we respond to them. This underscores the importance of converting adversities into opportunities, and that the future should not be sacrificed because of today’s challenges. However, he cautioned that planning for adversities may not necessarily equate to true preparedness. Thus, there is no textbook formula to becoming resilient; it is a dynamic process developed through experience, introspection, and a willingness to adapt to uncertainties.
Linking to NCO112 content
Resilience is recognised as one of several components necessary to overcome failure. This aligns with the concept of bouncebackability, which refers to the recovery from a setback (Foster, 2018). Resilience positively contributes to achieving peak performance, which is defined as a state of optimal functioning and flow (Wells, 1998).
The two key elements of resilience are adversity and positive adaptation, which together enhance an individual’s ability to thrive from setbacks (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). This resonates with Hunt’s reflection on negative change, which he described as more difficult to navigate than positive changes due to the emotional responses it often triggers. Hence, the perception of adversities plays a crucial role in determining how one copes with hardship.
The Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MMR) proposes that an individual starts from a baseline of homeostasis, otherwise known as their comfort zone (Richardson, 2002). There are four potential outcomes – resilient reintegration, homeostatic reintegration, reintegration with loss, and dysfunctional reintegration. Linking this to Hunt’s recount, he shared that he fell into a depressive state and struggled to cope after experiencing a series of adversities. This reflects one of the four potential outcomes - reintegration with loss – as he grappled with the passing of his father, the loss of a caregiver and his mother’s incarceration. Although, he clung on to an irrational hope that things might get better, truly believing in that hope was a significant challenge.
Fortunately, Hunt drew on his experiences and beliefs to build a robust foundation of resilience. This allowed him to bounce back and achieve goals that once seemed impossible. His journey demonstrates resilient reintegration, where he not only adapts to the disruption but also developed protective factors that raised the baseline of his comfort zone. He emerged more resilient and determined, better equipped to face future setbacks. Hunt’s story illustrates how relentlessness and resilience plays a pivotal role in achieving peak performance.
However, Hunt’s experience stands in contrast to one of the concepts explored in NCO112 and supported by established research. Sameroff and Rosenblum (2006) suggest that financial disadvantage, poor parenting, antisocial peers, and under-resourced communities acts as environmental risk that hinder the development of resilience in children. Children living in such environments may be deprived of the social support or developmental guidance necessary to build resilience and cope effectively to challenging situations. Similarly, a study conducted on victimisation, poverty and resilience resources in adolescents highlighted that limited access to social support, lower socioeconomic status and being a racial minority results in experiencing greater range of adversities and having lower resilience than children from contrasting backgrounds (Nurius et al., 2019). 
Despite lacking key protective factors – such as stable parenting, economic security, and access to positive role models – Hunt demonstrated admirable capacity to adapt, persevere and grow through life’s obstacles. This challenges the deterministic view that resilience is solely on the product of environmental support. What sets Hunt apart is not the presence of conventional resilience-building resources, but his capacity for self-reflection, hardiness and adaptive coping. While risk factors can heavily influence developmental outcomes, they do not rigidly define them. Hunt serves as an outlier – an example of resilience emerging from within, through personal meaning-making and agency rather than external scaffolding.
Self-reflection
Resilience used to just be a term used by my teachers, it did not seem particularly important to me at that time. I had never strived for anything exceptional. I was an average student who did not take things too seriously and stayed within my comfort zone. While setbacks did not affect me deeply, I also did not view them as opportunities to learn or grow. 
That changes during my final year in secondary school when the importance of N-level examinations became clear. I realised that my performance would shape my future pathway. Then came a major shock; I failed my English mid-year examinations – something that has never happened before. This failure negatively affected my confidence and perspective of my capabilities. Further, I was struggling with personal issues that made it challenging to manage. As the N-Level examination drew closer, I began to feel disconnected and overwhelmed.
However, I soon understood that reacting negatively would not change my circumstances. I began asking for more practise papers and becoming more vocal about my doubts. Fast-forward to results day, I was one of the top students in my cohort. That moment became a powerful reminder that I am capable, and that resilience is not just a word – it is a choice I made to rise above adversity.
By using the MMR (Richardson, 2002), I am able to dissect my experience and better understand the dynamic nature of resilience. Initially, my response to the setback aligned with reintegration with loss, as I allowed the disruption to undermine my self-belief. However, the eventual effort into regaining control such as seeking help and active preparation, demonstrates a movement toward resilient reintegration, even if it was not sustained at that stage. However, while I managed to overcome the immediate challenge and achieve academic success, there were no prominent changes to my baseline of homeostasis. I continued to experience similar emotional responses to setbacks in tertiary education, which suggests a homeostatic reintegration outcome. The MMR framework helped me understand that resilience is not a fixed trait, but a continuous journey of growth and adaptation.
Additionally, my experience can be analysed thorough the theory postulated by Sameroff and Rosenblum (2006), which suggests that the lack of protective environmental factors can diminish one’s ability to develop resilience. Growing up in a low-income family, having a strained relationship with my caregivers and susceptibility to victim mentality contributed to a weaker capacity to bounce back from hardships. This is evident in the extended time it took for me to accept the setback and view it as an opportunity for growth. 
Compared to Hunt’s experience – though the circumstances and type of adversities differs – there is a similarity in having a positive mind as the main resource to foster resilience. Despite the odds, we demonstrated that even in the absence of ideal external conditions, personal outlook can play a crucial role in overcoming challenges. Further, in Hunt’s sharing, he highlighted the importance of partnership – the strength to ask for help as a crucial factor in coping with difficult circumstances. Similarly, when I struggled to cope with my own setback, I reached out to my teachers. These conversations gave me the space to verbalise my concerns and receive constructive feedback. This support system empowered me to bounce back and ultimately achieve peak performance.
