This essay will talk about ‘How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)’.
a) Nina Nesdoly shares her strategies for managing stress in healthy and effective ways. Her approach is backed up by neuroscience and psychology, focusing mainly on three ideas: letting tension out, limiting information intake, and lowering the barrier to entry. She also addresses a common misunderstanding many people have about taking breaks. For example, activities like going for a walk, listening to podcasts related to career development, checking emails for work, and scrolling social media may feel like breaks. However, they feed information to your brain to keep you engaged. Real breaks should help the mind rest and recover and not taking in information during breaks.
b) The content of Nina Nesdoly's TED talk mentions her past experience. She begins by sharing a story from her own life: during the final weekend before university exams, instead of studying or writing papers, she chose to go out partying. She explains that this decision was the best choice of her life. Partying allowed her to release built-up stress let the tension out, and return to her studies with renewed energy. Ultimately, Nina Nesdoly’s story shows that stress management is not always about doing more or pushing harder, it is often about doing something that you enjoy at the current moment. 
According to the Two-dimensional coping framework, avoidant-focused coping aligns with Nina Nesdoly’s story. This type of coping strategy is where Nina Nesdoly disengages from stressful situations to protect her mental well-being. At the same time, her choice reflected problem avoidance, she consciously distanced herself from studies to reduce stressful feelings. Rather than denying the reality of her exams, Nina used this as a temporary withdrawal as a way to recharge mentally. She sought social interaction, which helped her relieve tension and regain emotional balance.
While this approach may be effective, Nina Nesdoly did not fully grasp on why this method works for her and not everyone else. For example, introverts might not find going out with others to be a helpful form of stress relief. Instead, activities like playing games or listening to music, which involve processing information and serve better to their coping needs. These hobbies are not just distractions, they also offer meaningful ways to process emotions and regain mental energy.
Enjoying a personal hobby can be far more beneficial than following general tips for stress relief. General advice like taking a break or going out with friends might not be for everyone. When someone engage in activities they enjoy, it provides them satisfaction and relaxation, making coping strategies more effective and sustainable. However, the best general advice to cope with stress is by getting at least seven hours of sleep per day, have a healthy diet and exercise regularly. These habits will benefit you in the long run.
c) Currently as a part-time student at SUSS, the combined academic and work demands become overwhelming during semesters. I often felt mentally and physically exhausted and found it difficult to concentrate on lectures. One coping mechanism that eventually helped me was playing video games with my friends. It allows me to take a mental break from my responsibilities and shift my focus to something enjoyable. This form of mental disengagement helps me clear my mind, lifts my mood, and gives me the energy to return to my tasks the next day.
However, Nina Nesdoly mentioned in her TED Talk, mental disengagement can be similar to running, if you enjoy it and boost your mood temporaily, it can still wear you down over time. This made me realize that although video games offer a brief moment of mood lift, they may not provide a real rest that my body and mind truly need after extended periods of stress.
Through the course, I was introduced to the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping developed by Lazarus and Folkman (1984), which further helped me understand stress. In the primary appraisal phase, I find that the deadlines from my studies and the workload from my work are stressful. Then, in the secondary appraisal phase, I felt that I lacked of energy, motivation, and mental focus to handle everything effectively. As a result, I turned to gaming as a coping mechanism, which provides temporary stress relief. Reflecting on this experience, I realized that I rely heavily on emotional coping rather than problem-focused strategies that could have dealt with the root of the stress. Strategies would be taking a nap during breaks and better time management.

TED Talk Summary
In her TED Talk "How to Make Stress Your Friend", health psychologist Dr Kelly M. McGonigal shares a powerful shift in perspective on stress, arguing that how we think about stress can fundamentally change its impact on our health and well-being. For years, she taught that stress was harmful, which is linked to an increased risk of illness and death. 

However, a landmark study tracking 30,000 adults in the United States over eight years showed that people who experienced high stress but believed it was not harmful had the lowest risk of dying (Keller et al., 2012). This suggested that the mindset surrounding stress could be more dangerous than stress itself.

Dr McGonigal uses this to introduce a new message: stress can be helpful when we believe it prepares us to face challenges. By changing our perception, our physical response to stress also changes where our heart may still pound, but our blood vessels remain relaxed, mimicking the state associated with courage or joy rather than anxiety (Sara et al., 2022). 

She explains that oxytocin, a hormone released during stress, encourages social bonding, empathy, and support-seeking, which strengthens resilience and protects cardiovascular health (Takayanagi & Onaka, 2021). The talk emphasises that viewing stress as a helpful and energising response fosters biological and emotional resilience. 

It also highlights the importance of human connection, suggesting that caring for others and accepting support during stressful times makes us more resilient and physically healthier (Jordan, 2023). Ultimately, Dr McGonigal reframes stress from an enemy to a resource, something we can use to connect with meaning, draw strength, and thrive rather than simply survive.

Alignment to the Course
Dr McGonigal’s TED Talk offers a compelling reinterpretation of stress that aligns well with the NCO112 course's focus on resilience and the psychology of peak performance. Her key claim, that stress only becomes harmful when we believe it is, echoes Lazarus and Folkman’s (1984) Transactional Model of Stress and Coping. This model explains stress as a dynamic interaction between an individual and their environment, where appraisal plays a central role. 

The course emphasises that cognitive reappraisal (seeing stress as a challenge instead of a threat) is crucial to managing stress effectively (Bosshard & Gomez, 2024). Dr McGonigal extends this by showing, with empirical evidence, that this shift in mindset even changes our physiological response, such as keeping blood vessels relaxed during high arousal, thereby promoting cardiovascular health. Her use of oxytocin as a central theme aligns with the course’s emphasis on the importance of social support in managing stress. 

The hormone’s role in strengthening relationships, encouraging empathy, and promoting help-seeking reflects the social dimensions of resilience discussed in Kunzler et al.’s (2020) framework. Furthermore, it affirms the principle that resilience is not just an individual trait but is shaped by the support networks and interpersonal connections available to us (Kuldas & Foody, 2021). The TED Talk’s framing of oxytocin as a “social resilience hormone” reinforces the NCO112 course content, which explores how social support buffers against the effects of stress and enhances psychological well-being (Delgado et al., 2023).

Additionally, Dr McGonigal’s argument can be linked to the principles of growth mindset (Dweck, 2006) and the role of intrinsic motivation in promoting peak performance. By encouraging a shift in how we view stress, not as a threat but as a source of energy and connection, she invokes the idea that challenges, when embraced, can foster growth and meaning. The course similarly advocates for mindset shifts and positive framing to foster resilience. Stress, when linked to purposeful goals, can become a catalyst for learning and personal development (Sridaran et al., 2021).

However, while Dr McGonigal’s perspective is well-supported by evidence and aligned with positive psychology, one could argue that the talk lacks nuance in dealing with chronic or traumatic stress. The TED Talk assumes that most people can access the psychological tools or social support needed to shift their mindset. Yet, for individuals experiencing long-term financial hardship, systemic discrimination, or trauma, mindset shifts may not be sufficient. 

Repetti and Wang (2017) caution against overemphasising personal agency in the context of environmental or structural stressors, where access to resources and long-term exposure to adversity can erode coping ability despite positive beliefs. Moreover, the talk does not address the need for professional intervention in situations involving clinical anxiety, PTSD, or burnout (McNally et al., 2003). While the biological argument about stress responses is persuasive, it may inadvertently suggest that people are to blame for the negative impacts of stress because of how they interpret it (LeMoult, 2020). 

This oversimplification can be harmful, especially to those already feeling overwhelmed. The NCO112 course, by contrast, offers a more balanced view, encouraging both internal mindset change and external support mechanisms, such as counselling services, community engagement, and mental health resources (Gautam et al., 2024). Despite these critiques, Dr McGonigal’s talk is a valuable contribution to the discourse on stress. It encourages individuals to reclaim a sense of agency and to use stress as a means to deepen human connection, develop courage, and grow resilience. 

These themes resonate with key course concepts, such as the Peak Performance Plan, which highlights the integration of mental, emotional, and social strategies for thriving under pressure (Wells, 2010). In sum, the TED Talk reinforces the message that stress, when harnessed thoughtfully, can be an opportunity rather than an obstacle. Still, it should be integrated into a broader framework that includes systemic understanding, access to support, and contextual sensitivity.

Reflection on Experience and Learning
A personal experience that deepened my understanding of stress and resilience occurred during my time volunteering with Heartware’s River Hongbao (RHB) 2023. I served as the Admin Lead for the Youth Liaison Committee, a role that required me to coordinate over 100 volunteers, lead weekly meetings, and handle logistical planning. Simultaneously, I was supporting both the Operations and Media teams, juggling communications, content creation, and on-the-ground decision-making. It was a fulfilling yet immensely stressful experience, and there were moments where I felt completely overwhelmed.

Initially, the stress had a noticeable effect on my performance. I began experiencing physical symptoms such as restlessness, mental fatigue, and tension. My confidence dropped, and I questioned whether I had taken on more than I could handle. These stress signals made me feel incompetent and on the verge of burnout. At one point, I even considered whether I had made a mistake taking on multiple roles. However, over time, I started to shift my perspective.

Although I wasn’t consciously applying theories then, I now realise that I had begun to use ideas that were later introduced in the NCO112 course and Dr McGonigal’s TED Talk. One key shift was how I started to reinterpret my stress. Instead of seeing it as a sign of failure, I began to view it as an indication that I cared about my work, that the stakes were high because the task mattered. This reframing, which Dr McGonigal strongly advocates, allowed me to tap into my energy rather than be paralysed by anxiety.

The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, which I later learnt about in NCO112, perfectly explained my journey. At first, my primary appraisal viewed the situation as threatening and beyond my capabilities. But through experience, reflection, and informal peer support, I unconsciously began to shift into a challenge appraisal. I started breaking large tasks into manageable parts, actively sought help from co-leads, and made time to check in with my team. These were signs of approach-based coping, problem-solving and support-seeking, despite not formally understanding them at the time.

Richardson’s (2002) Metatheory of Resilience also resonates with my experience. Resilience wasn’t just about surviving the experience; it was about growing from it. There were several setbacks, like scheduling miscommunications or last-minute changes during the event. Previously, I would have seen these moments as personal shortcomings. Instead, I started viewing them as necessary disruptions that helped me adapt and learn. This mindset shift helped me recover faster and improve each time.

I also experienced what the course describes as ‘flow’ during high-stakes moments, such as briefing volunteers or designing outreach content. In those moments, I was fully engaged; my stress felt like focus, not fear. Reflecting on this, I see how my performance actually improved under pressure once I shifted my mindset. I began performing at a level I didn’t think was possible. What once felt impossible, managing multiple teams and responsibilities, gradually became energising.

Dr McGonigal’s explanation of oxytocin’s role in the stress response helped me understand why team connection felt so essential. Informal chats, shared meals, and laughs during breaks and in between work helped reduce tension and reinforced that I wasn’t alone. These moments built psychological safety and reminded me of the social side of resilience, a core theme in both the talk and the course.

Looking back, I see that while I wasn’t fully aware of the theories at the time, I had intuitively adopted many of the concepts now taught in NCO112. The TED Talk gave me words and science for what I had gone through. This realisation has empowered me: I now know that I have the tools to face stress more intentionally in the future. I have learnt that resilience and peak performance are not just about enduring but about interpreting stress meaningfully, connecting with others, and allowing growth through challenges.
